option_rationales.A: Overturning beliefs plays no part in the passage's account; the explanation turns on noticing an absence.
option_rationales.B: Difficulty and effort are never mentioned; paragraph 1 explains the point by the impossibility of noticing a gap.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says the account treats curiosity as 'not a general appetite for novelty', so this reverses the account.

common_misconception: Choosing the novelty option because 'appetite for novelty' appears in the paragraph, without noting that the account denies it.

correct_answer: (C) be capable of ruling out some patterns of behaviour instead of fitting any pattern after the event.
explanation: Paragraph 3 objects that if 'any movement of attention whatever can be redescribed after the fact as the closing of a gap', the account 'no longer explains anything in particular' and becomes 'a vocabulary rather than a hypothesis'. The implied standard is that a real hypothesis must exclude some possibilities.

option_rationales.A: The passage makes no claim about where evidence should come from; classrooms appear only in the practical conclusion of paragraph 4.
option_rationales.B: This is the defenders' reply, which the author says preserves the theory only 'at a cost'; the author does not recommend it.
option_rationales.D: The author ranks neither kind; paragraph 4 says 'Both have their place', and the objection concerns how the theory explains, not which kind matters more.

common_misconception: Choosing the many-small-gaps option because it is the content of paragraph 3, although it is the view being criticised.

correct_answer: (B) Leafing through an old atlas in a second-hand bookshop with no particular place in mind.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says the account is weaker for curiosity 'that drifts without a target', as in wandering library shelves, where 'there is no specific question waiting to be answered'. Leafing through an atlas with no destination in mind is of this kind.

option_rationales.A: A 'mystery with a culprit' is named in paragraph 2 as a case where the account 'is at its strongest'.
option_rationales.C: Though it looks like browsing, the visitor is closing a specific, noticed gap, the location of one known painting, which is the case the account handles well.
option_rationales.D: A puzzle with a single solution is a well-defined gap, which paragraph 2 says the account explains well.

common_misconception: Picking the museum visit because it involves wandering, though it is driven by a single definite question.

correct_answer: (A) appreciative of what it explains but doubtful that it accounts for every form of curiosity.
explanation: Paragraph 1 says the account 'has much to recommend it' and lists what it explains; paragraphs 2 and 3 limit its scope to targeted curiosity. The attitude is qualified appreciation.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says this only of the account as stretched by its defenders; the author calls the unstretched account 'a good theory of the first' kind.
option_rationales.C: The author takes a clear position in paragraph 3, 'It seems more accurate to say that there are at least two kinds', so the stance is not neutral.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the account 'fits some cases far better than others', so the author's approval is plainly not whole.

common_misconception: Choosing 'dismissive' because of the sharp phrase 'a vocabulary rather than a hypothesis', which is aimed at the defenders' reply.

correct_answer: (B) trace the familiar sequence back to an origin that differs from the use now made of it.
explanation: Paragraph 1 describes the sequence's current status and then, with 'It began, however', traces it to observations of dying patients and notes its 'migration from the dying to the grieving' and from observations to 'something closer to a timetable'.

option_rationales.A: No comparison of difficulty is made; the paragraph says only that the shift to grief happened 'largely outside' testing research.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says the sequence began as a description of some patients, so it does not deny that the feelings were observed.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says the sequence was 'drawn from clinical conversations' with such patients but makes no claim that it describes them accurately, and presents no evidence.

common_misconception: Taking the reference to clinical conversations as a claim that the model is accurate for dying patients.

correct_answer: (C) may well be grieving in a way that is common and is not a sign of feelings being avoided.
explanation: Paragraph 2 describes people who experience 'intense sorrow that gradually eases over months without passing through anything resembling distinct stages' and says this seems 'for a good number of people' to be 'the ordinary course that grief takes'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says 'Resilience of this kind is not denial in disguise', so the author rejects this reading.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says many people report some of the feelings 'hardly at all', which contradicts the claim that most report every one.
option_rationales.D: This expectation is what paragraph 3 criticises when helpers 'wait for a stage that never arrives'.

common_misconception: Applying the model's own reading of an absent stage, which the passage presents as the error.

correct_answer: (A) researchers stopped studying grief because the model appeared to have settled the important questions.
explanation: The three supported options are the widow, the son and the pressing helpers of paragraph 3. Paragraph 1 says only that the model's spread happened 'largely outside' testing research and paragraph 2 refers to grief being 'studied directly'; nowhere does the passage say research stopped.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says helpers may 'press a grieving person to move on to the next one', so this is stated.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the son who feels relief 'may wonder what is wrong with him', which is this consequence.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 gives exactly this case: the widow who is not angry 'may be told that she has not yet faced her loss'.

common_misconception: Reading 'happened largely outside the kind of research that might have tested it' as a claim that research ceased.

correct_answer: (D) Critical of its use as a norm for how people should grieve, while granting that it once met a genuine need.
explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 argue that the sequence is poorly supported and harmful as 'a standard of what everyone ought to feel'; paragraph 4 concedes that giving people words for hidden feelings 'was a real service'. The attitude is critical but fair.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 explicitly says 'It would be unfair, though, to treat the model's popularity as mere credulity'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the sequence 'has not fared well' when grief is studied directly, so the author is clear about what the research shows.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the harm lies 'less in its inaccuracy' than in its use, but it still describes real harm, and the author wants its fixed order dropped; the author does not excuse the model.

common_misconception: Choosing 'sympathetic' because the author says the harm lies less in inaccuracy than in use, missing that this relocates the criticism rather than softening it.

correct_answer: (A) feeds the child's sense of competence, which is what made the activity enjoyable.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says such praise 'may even strengthen interest, since it feeds the sense of competence that made the activity enjoyable in the first place'.

option_rationales.B: Nothing in the passage says praise removes any expectation; the stated reason concerns the sense of competence.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 gives this reason for the unexpected treat, not for praise about quality; the option transfers one explanation to the other case.
option_rationales.D: Tangibility is mentioned as a condition of the undermining effect, but the passage does not explain the benefit of praise this way.

common_misconception: Confusing the reason given for the unexpected treat with the reason given for informative praise, as both appear in one sentence.

correct_answer: (C) Announcing that the pupil will receive a small gift for every hour of practice completed.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says the effect is most reliable when the reward is 'tangible, expected in advance and given for doing the task rather than for doing it well'. A gift announced in advance for each hour of practice meets all three conditions for an activity the pupil already enjoys.

option_rationales.A: This is praise that conveys information about quality, which paragraph 2 says 'may even strengthen interest'.
option_rationales.B: An unexpected treat 'cannot have been the reason' for practising, so paragraph 2 implies it does not undermine interest.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says rewards cannot crowd out an enjoyment 'that was never there'; the reward is attached to the dull part, not to the playing the pupil loves.

common_misconception: Choosing the reward for scales because it is a tangible, announced reward, without noticing it targets an activity with no prior interest.

correct_answer: (B) can sometimes keep a person at it until growing skill makes the task itself enjoyable.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says a reward 'may keep someone at a dull task long enough for skill to grow and for the task itself to become absorbing, so that interest arrives because of the incentive'. The correct answer states this hedged possibility.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says a reward 'may' keep someone at the task long enough for interest to arrive; 'always' overstates this.
option_rationales.C: The contrast between rewarding the task and rewarding quality belongs to paragraph 2 and is not applied to dull tasks in paragraph 3.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says rewards 'cannot crowd out an enjoyment that was never there', so the undermining effect does not apply to dull tasks.

common_misconception: Turning 'may' into 'always', or carrying the undermining effect over to tasks that had no interest to undermine.

correct_answer: (D) now sees drawing as a job done for the prize, so that without the prize it no longer seems worth doing.
explanation: The phrase describes an activity that has been turned into paid work and then stripped of its pay; paragraph 2 explains that an expected prize 'invites the child to understand the drawing as a means to the prize'. Once the prize ends, the means has no point.

option_rationales.A: Nothing suggests the child is tired; the image is about how the child understands the activity, as paragraph 2 confirms with 'a means to the prize'.
option_rationales.B: Competition with other children is never mentioned; the image concerns the loss of a reward, not rivalry.
option_rationales.C: The passage attributes no resentment to the child; the reduced drawing is explained by a changed view of the activity, not by a grievance.

common_misconception: Reading the image emotionally, as resentment, instead of as a change in how the activity is understood.

correct_answer: (C) the deformation that a load produces in the body that is subjected to it.
explanation: Paragraph 1 says 'stress is distinguished from strain, the deformation that the load produces'.

option_rationales.A: A relation is one of the senses the word 'stress' takes on in psychology (paragraph 1); it is not the engineering definition of strain.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says stress and strain 'are distinguished from the load itself', so strain is not the load.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 gives this as the engineering meaning of 'stress', from which strain is distinguished.

common_misconception: Confusing strain with stress, which is defined in the sentence just before.

correct_answer: (D) argue that 'stress' is worth keeping but that claims using it must be clear about which sense they rely on.
explanation: Paragraphs 1 to 3 show how the word slides between the situation, the reaction and the relation, paragraph 4 rejects abandoning it, and paragraph 5 recommends asking 'which of its meanings is in play'. The correct answer combines the diagnosis, the concession and the recommendation.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says abandoning the word 'would be a mistake', and the author values the breadth the borrowing produced.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the first sense of 'good stress' is 'uncontroversial' and the second 'plausible within limits'; the author criticises a slide between senses, not the claims as such.
option_rationales.C: This is the point of paragraph 4 only, a concession within the argument rather than its purpose, so the option is too narrow.

common_misconception: Choosing the paragraph 4 option, which is accurate but covers only one part of the argument.

correct_answer: (B) borrows a certainty available only when the claim is nearly true by definition and applies it to demanding situations generally.
explanation: Paragraph 2 calls the reaction reading 'close to true by definition' (the first reading) and the situation reading 'plainly false as a generalisation' (the second). Discussion that moves between them sounds as certain as the first while claiming as much as the second, which the correct answer states.

option_rationales.A: The remark concerns moving between the reaction sense and the situation sense; the relational sense based on belief is not what is being combined here.
option_rationales.C: The 'authority' of the reaction reading comes from the claim being 'close to true by definition', which makes it empty rather than trustworthy; the author does not commend it.
option_rationales.D: 'Authority' here means the apparent certainty of the definitional reading, not the standing of experts, and no claim about small samples is made.

common_misconception: Taking 'authority' to mean expert standing, or reading 'first reading' as praise.

correct_answer: (A) Most such advice states plainly that it concerns how people interpret their reactions, and it cites studies that test this claim.
explanation: Paragraph 3 charges that such advice 'slides from the first meaning, which everyone accepts, to the third' and that the third is 'a specific claim requiring specific evidence'. If the advice openly made the third claim and supplied that evidence, neither the slide nor the lack of evidence would hold.

option_rationales.B: This is the first sense, which the author already calls 'uncontroversial'; confirming it does not touch the charge that advice slides from it to the third.
option_rationales.C: Varied usage, if anything, supports the author's concern about confusion; it does not show that the advice avoids sliding between senses.
option_rationales.D: This fits the author's description of the second sense as 'plausible within limits', so it is consistent with the criticism rather than damaging to it.

common_misconception: Choosing the option about physiological limits because it sounds like a scientific qualification, when it matches what the author already grants.

correct_answer: (C) head off an apparently natural conclusion by pointing to a benefit of the word's looseness.
explanation: After three paragraphs on confusion, paragraph 4 raises the obvious remedy, 'abandon the word altogether', and rejects it because the term's breadth 'has allowed researchers' in several fields to see connections. It blocks that conclusion before paragraph 5 gives the author's own remedy.

option_rationales.A: The author says abandoning the word is a mistake 'not only because ordinary language is not so easily reformed', and the main reason given is the term's fruitfulness.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 5 says that failing to keep the senses apart 'has cost a good deal of confusion', so the author does not concede that the harm was slight.
option_rationales.D: The link between working conditions and heart disease is offered as a connection the broad term drew attention to, not as a confirmed hypothesis.

common_misconception: Choosing the ordinary-language option, which picks up a reason the author mentions only in passing.

correct_answer: (D) effortful thinking seems to alter the brain's total energy use only slightly.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says this version 'met an additional difficulty: effortful thinking appears to change the brain's overall energy consumption only slightly, far too little for the proposed mechanism to work'.

option_rationales.A: The passage says nothing about what the replications measured; the 'additional difficulty' is a physiological one.
option_rationales.B: The finding about beliefs in willpower is separate and says nothing about consumption of sweet drinks.
option_rationales.C: The passage never says sweet drinks weakened self-control; the difficulty named concerns the brain's energy consumption.

common_misconception: Running together the separate findings listed in paragraph 2.

correct_answer: (B) a physical store ought to run down with use whatever a person happens to believe about it.
explanation: Paragraph 2 calls the result 'awkward for any theory in which the resource is a physical quantity'. A physical quantity should be depleted by effort regardless of belief, so a depletion that disappears when people believe willpower is plentiful does not fit.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says 'it does not follow' that the experience is an illusion, since people 'do grow less willing to persist', and the findings are only 'reported' by some studies.
option_rationales.C: If beliefs enlarged a physical store the theory would survive; the awkwardness is that belief matters at all to something supposedly physical.
option_rationales.D: The passage does not link the belief studies to the replication attempts; the awkwardness lies in what the result implies.

common_misconception: Reading the belief findings as evidence that fatigue is imaginary, which the author explicitly rejects.

correct_answer: (A) A person's persistence at a dull task recovers only after rest, however the task is framed or rewarded.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says that 'changing how a task is framed, or what it leads to, may restore persistence where rest alone would not'. A case in which only rest helps, whatever the framing or reward, is what the fuel picture would predict and runs against the opportunity cost account.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says tasks that 'feel meaningful or rewarding should be less draining', so this is just what the account predicts.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 contrasts tasks that feel rewarding with 'equally demanding tasks that do not', which is this case exactly.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says weariness nudges attention 'towards rest, pleasure or novelty' as the value of alternatives accumulates, which this describes.

common_misconception: Treating the film case as inconsistent because it describes giving up, though the account explains giving up as a shift in priorities.

correct_answer: (B) A shopper who has spent an hour in one store grows restless as the other stores nearby seem ever more worth the time.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says continued effort 'carries an opportunity cost, the value of everything else one might be doing instead', and weariness rises as that cost accumulates. The shopper's restlessness grows as alternatives look more valuable, not because anything has run out.

option_rationales.A: Stopping because a task is complete involves no rising opportunity cost; the author's account concerns weariness while the task is unfinished.
option_rationales.C: This is the fuel-gauge picture of paragraph 1, the model that paragraph 2 says has 'fared badly', not the account the author favours.
option_rationales.D: This depicts a store used up by effort and restored by rest, which is the resource model rather than a shift in what one is 'willing to pay for'.

common_misconception: Choosing the runner, which looks like the everyday experience of tiredness but mirrors the depletion model.

correct_answer: (D) a real experience that the resource model described vividly but explained wrongly.
explanation: Paragraph 1 offers the evening collapse as the experience the theory matched, paragraph 3 insists the experience is not an illusion, and paragraph 5 says 'a vivid metaphor can capture a real phenomenon while getting its mechanism entirely wrong'. The correct answer joins these.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 presents rationing as the strategy that follows if willpower is a fuel; the author favours the other picture, so the failure of the model does not support rationing.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says 'it does not follow' that this experience 'is an illusion'; people 'do grow less willing to persist'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 5 says the model's decline 'is not a refutation of everyday wisdom about tiredness'.

common_misconception: Choosing rationing, which sounds like sensible advice but belongs to the model the author rejects.

correct_answer: (C) Treat the cup as full inside the game while knowing it is empty, and let events in the game have their fitting effects.
explanation: Paragraph 1 says the child must 'hold two descriptions of the world in mind at once' (the cup is empty; in the game it is full), keep the game's version separate from reality, and 'follow its consequences faithfully'. The correct answer states both requirements.

option_rationales.A: In paragraph 1 a toppled cup is part of following the game's consequences 'faithfully', leaving the bear 'wet'; a spill breaks no rule.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 reports the 'rehearsal of adult roles' reading only to say that it misses 'what is most remarkable about the scene'; it is not what the child must do.
option_rationales.D: This reverses paragraph 1, which says she must 'keep the game's version from leaking into the real one', which is why she does not try to drink.

common_misconception: Choosing the 'rehearsal of adult roles' option because it is mentioned in the passage, without noticing that the author rejects it as incomplete.

correct_answer: (A) keeping track of how things actually are and how they are within the pretence, both at the same time.
explanation: 'This double bookkeeping' in paragraph 2 refers back to the end of paragraph 1, where the child must 'hold two descriptions of the world in mind at once', the real one and the game's, keeping them apart while following each.

option_rationales.B: No adult record keeping is mentioned; the phrase picks up the 'two descriptions of the world' that the child herself holds in paragraph 1.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 stresses that the two descriptions are held 'at once', which is simultaneous, not alternation between play and other activity.
option_rationales.D: Nothing in the passage concerns counting; 'bookkeeping' is a figure for keeping two accounts of the world apart, not for tallying objects.

common_misconception: Taking 'bookkeeping' literally as record keeping or counting instead of reading it through the sentence it refers back to.

correct_answer: (C) narrow the author's claim by conceding what the link between pretence and reasoning does not establish.
explanation: Paragraph 3 opens with 'Some caution is nevertheless in order', grants that the shared capacity does not prove a causal effect of play, admits that much pretence is loose, and states 'The claim worth defending is narrower'. Its role is to qualify and narrow the thesis.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 accepts the shared capacity ('That play and counterfactual reasoning draw on a shared capacity') and only denies that this shows more play makes better reasoners.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says 'much of it is repetitive and loose' but goes on to defend a 'narrower' claim about its value, so saying it lacks any real value is too extreme.
option_rationales.D: This is the opposite of paragraph 3, which warns that the shared capacity 'does not show that more play produces better reasoners'.

common_misconception: Mistaking a concession for a rejection of the whole argument.

correct_answer: (D) a child who senses that a particular answer is expected will stop exploring suppositions and try to read the adult instead.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says that when a game exists to deliver a lesson, 'the child who knows that a right answer is wanted stops supposing freely and starts guessing what the adult has in mind', destroying the 'freedom from consequence' that made pretence valuable.

option_rationales.A: This echoes the 'waste of time' view that paragraph 1 rejects; the author never worries that guided play crowds out reading or counting.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'Some guidance helps' and that an adult who asks what happens next 'can enrich' a game, so the objection is not to any involvement.
option_rationales.C: Measurement is never discussed; the worry in paragraph 4 is that a lesson-driven game 'changes character', not that its outcomes are hard to assess.

common_misconception: Overextending the author's caution into a rejection of all adult involvement, despite the explicit concession that some guidance helps.

correct_answer: (B) The belief that matching lessons to a learner's style improves learning lacks support, and labelling learners by style can do harm.
explanation: Paragraph 2 argues that the predicted crossover 'has generally failed to appear', and paragraph 4 concludes that labelling 'narrows expectations while appearing to widen them'. The correct answer captures both the lack of support and the harm.

option_rationales.A: This is the point of paragraph 3 alone; it leaves out the central critique of the matching claim in paragraph 2 and the cost of labelling in paragraph 4.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 defends variety for other reasons (attention, several routes back to an idea); delivering lessons so that every style is reached keeps the diagnosis the author rejects.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 states that 'That people report preferences is not in dispute'; the author denies only that preferences predict performance.

common_misconception: Picking the option about matching form to content, which is true to one paragraph but too narrow for the whole.

correct_answer: (A) The advantage of one teaching method over another reverses depending on which style a group of learners has been assigned.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says the theory needs a visual learner to learn more from a visual lesson 'while a learner labelled auditory will show the reverse', and that testing it means 'checking whether the advantage flips from one group to the other'.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 compares groups taught in both ways; it says nothing about learners with no preference learning more slowly.
option_rationales.C: A group that wins in every format shows no flip; paragraph 2 says the theory needs the visual group to do better with visual lessons and the auditory group with spoken ones.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the theory predicts that the better method 'flips' between groups; a uniform benefit from mixed lessons is not a matching prediction.

common_misconception: Confusing the claim that visual learners simply do better with the claim that the better method differs by group.

correct_answer: (C) has been borne out by studies teaching learners both in their own style and in another.
explanation: Paragraph 1 names three 'honest reasons' for the idea's appeal, matching the other three options. Paragraph 2 says that when tested in the demanding way 'the predicted crossover has generally failed to appear', so the correct answer is not a reason given; it is contradicted.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says it 'fits the everyday experience that people do prefer some ways of taking in information to others'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says the idea 'gives teachers something concrete to do with that respect'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 lists this first: 'it seems to respect individual difference'.

common_misconception: Rushing past paragraph 2 and assuming the idea's popularity reflects confirming evidence.

correct_answer: (D) Learners sorted by style and taught in both formats showed a reversal: visual learners gained more from diagrams, auditory learners more from talk.
explanation: Paragraph 2 rests on the claim that, under a proper test, 'the predicted crossover has generally failed to appear'. A properly designed test that found the crossover would undercut exactly that claim.

option_rationales.A: Teachers' confidence says nothing about whether matched teaching improves learning, which is the claim at issue in paragraph 2.
option_rationales.B: This supports paragraph 3, where form is matched to content 'whoever the learner is'; it does not show any crossover between kinds of learner.
option_rationales.C: The author already grants this in paragraph 2 ('That people report preferences is not in dispute'), so it leaves the argument about performance untouched.

common_misconception: Choosing the option about preferences because it sounds like support for learning styles, without noticing that the author concedes it.

correct_answer: (A) spares the learner the decision about which procedure a problem needs, a decision a mixed examination requires.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says block practice lets the learner apply one procedure 'without ever deciding which procedure the problem calls for, the very decision a mixed examination demands'.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the reverse: it is mixing problem types that makes study 'more error-prone', while blocked practice feels easy.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says block practice lets the learner apply 'the same procedure again and again', which builds fluency rather than preventing it.
option_rationales.D: The passage never compares the time taken by blocked practice and rereading; both are described as methods that feel easy.

common_misconception: Reversing which method is error-prone during study.

correct_answer: (B) an unhelpful difficulty, since there is nothing learned for the effort of retrieval to consolidate.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'a test on something never learned teaches little except discouragement', and paragraph 2 explains that the benefit of testing comes from 'The effort of retrieving a half-forgotten fact'. With nothing learned, there is nothing to retrieve.

option_rationales.A: The passage never credits tests with this diagnostic value; paragraph 3 says such a test 'teaches little except discouragement'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 rejects the lesson 'that harder is always better' and says a difficulty helps 'only when the learner can, with effort, overcome it'.
option_rationales.D: Nothing supports this pairing; the passage treats spacing as useful because it calls on retrieval of learned material, which an untaught topic cannot supply.

common_misconception: Generalising paragraph 2 into the rule that testing always helps and missing the limit set in paragraph 3.

correct_answer: (A) sympathetic to the reasons for their choice while holding that the choice is mistaken.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says learners 'systematically prefer the methods that serve them worst' yet 'are not foolish to do so', because costs are felt now and benefits arrive later. The tone is understanding but critical.

option_rationales.B: The author grants that fluency usually tracks competence (paragraph 1) but says that for durable learning the rule is 'frequently misleading', so the methods are not endorsed.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'they are not foolish to do so', and adds that information alone is not enough to change practice, so scorn is the opposite of the author's tone.
option_rationales.D: Most of paragraph 4 concerns learners' own judgement; teachers are mentioned as facing 'a similar temptation', not as the sole concern.

common_misconception: Reading the criticism of the methods as contempt for the learners.

correct_answer: (D) A student revising for a mixed examination shuffles problems from last month's topics, so that each must first be identified before it is solved.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says useful difficulties can be overcome with effort and 'call on processes the learner will later need, such as retrieval, discrimination and reconstruction'. Shuffling familiar problems demands discrimination (paragraph 2: deciding which procedure applies), and last month's material is within reach.

option_rationales.A: This only slows things down, like the 'faint, awkward typeface' in paragraph 3; it calls on no process the student will later need.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says material 'pitched far beyond a student's grasp produces confusion rather than consolidation'; struggle for its own sake is not the point.
option_rationales.C: This remains blocked practice: it adds difficulty but never makes the student decide 'which procedure the problem calls for' (paragraph 2).

common_misconception: Treating any added difficulty as useful, especially the graded blocked practice, which feels demanding but lacks the discrimination step.

correct_answer: (B) practitioners whom long experience has made sure of their judgements, although those judgements are not reliably right.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says that in fields where feedback is slow and noisy 'long careers can produce confidence without accuracy': years of work make people sure of themselves without making their judgements correct.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the violinist 'hears a wrong note at once'; the violinist is the example of good feedback, not of misplaced confidence.
option_rationales.C: The phrase describes practitioners in fields with poor feedback, not researchers; the critique of hour counting comes in paragraph 2 and paragraph 4.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 attributes this state to 'long careers', not to beginners who have practised too little.

common_misconception: Attaching the phrase to the wrong group (beginners, researchers) instead of reading the sentence it sits in.

correct_answer: (C) an overstatement that stretches sound findings about practice into a promise they cannot keep.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says the research 'was right that expertise is built' but cannot 'deliver the promise sometimes made in its name, that anyone who puts in the hours will arrive at the same place'. The rule is a strong version of findings that hold in weaker form.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the rule is 'in that form, hard to sustain', so the author does not think it a fair summary.
option_rationales.B: This reverses paragraph 2, where practice 'accounts for more' in games and sports and 'for less' where outcomes are delayed.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says 'None of this restores the old picture of talent as a fixed endowment'; rejecting the rule is not a return to talent.

common_misconception: Assuming that rejecting the hours rule means endorsing talent.

correct_answer: (C) In one profession, members who learn quickly whether they erred improve more with experience than colleagues who learn the results only years later.
explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that 'what practice builds depends on what the environment can teach', meaning on quick and reliable feedback. A comparison within one profession, where only the speed of feedback differs, isolates that factor and supports the explanation.

option_rationales.A: This concerns the unexplained remainder within a field with good feedback; it does not test whether poor feedback is what limits practice elsewhere.
option_rationales.B: Starting age has nothing to do with the quality of feedback, which is the factor paragraph 3 uses to explain the difference between fields.
option_rationales.D: Higher earnings for seniority fit the remark about 'seniority' but say nothing about whether feedback governs how much practice improves skill.

common_misconception: Choosing an option that mentions a field from the passage (chess, finance, sport) without checking whether it bears on feedback.

correct_answer: (A) It grants that practice builds expertise but denies that equal hours bring equal results, without making talent decisive.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says the research 'was right that expertise is built' and right about the manner of practice, but cannot deliver the promise of equal outcomes for equal hours; its first sentence rules out a return to talent as 'a fixed endowment'.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 opens by saying that nothing in the argument 'restores the old picture of talent as a fixed endowment that settles everything'.
option_rationales.C: No advice is given; the paragraph only observes that some fields make demanding practice 'barely possible'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 denies that anyone who 'puts in the hours will arrive at the same place', so it confirms rather than reverses paragraph 3.

common_misconception: Reading the rejection of the hours promise as an endorsement of talent.

correct_answer: (B) are often not far from the estimates that adults give for the same activities.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says that in a calm setting adolescents' answers 'are often not very different from those of adults'.

option_rationales.A: The effect of instruction on estimates is never reported; paragraph 1 says only that information campaigns have had modest results.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 contrasts calm and social decisions, not estimates of danger; nothing says estimates improve among friends.
option_rationales.D: This is the 'familiar explanation' set out in paragraph 1, which paragraph 2 says rests on a premise 'weaker than it looks'.

common_misconception: Picking the ignorance view because it is stated in the passage, without noticing that the author disputes it.

correct_answer: (D) try to supply missing knowledge, when the difficulty lies largely in how knowledge is used in certain situations.
explanation: Paragraph 1 describes campaigns that 'Teach young people the facts'; paragraph 2 says the premise of ignorance 'is weaker than it looks' because what distinguishes adolescents is 'less what they know than what happens to that knowledge in particular situations'.

option_rationales.A: The passage never questions the accuracy of the information; its point is that the information is largely already known.
option_rationales.B: Distrust of the source is never mentioned; paragraph 2 locates the problem in 'what happens to that knowledge in particular situations'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says many adolescents 'reason about risk in hypothetical cases about as well as their parents do' and that 'Decisions taken alone and at leisure look quite mature', so a missing capacity is not the author's diagnosis; the problem is the situation.

common_misconception: Choosing the reasoning-capacity option, which sounds developmental, despite paragraph 2's statement about hypothetical reasoning.

correct_answer: (D) A school arranges for evening events to end with a supervised bus home, so that riding with a newly licensed classmate becomes the awkward option.
explanation: Paragraph 4 favours interventions that 'change the situations adolescents find themselves in' and that 'make the safe choice the socially easy one'. A supervised bus changes the situation and makes the safe choice the easy one in front of peers.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says adolescents already reason about risk 'about as well as their parents do'; the course adds knowledge rather than changing situations.
option_rationales.B: A pledge made alone works on decisions 'taken alone and at leisure', which paragraph 2 says already 'look quite mature'; it leaves the social situation unchanged.
option_rationales.C: This tries to change 'the beliefs they carry into' situations, the information-based approach the passage says has had modest results.

common_misconception: Choosing the pledge, which seems to address peer pressure, though it works only on calm, solitary decisions.

correct_answer: (C) The heightened response to reward in adolescence is limited to non-social rewards such as money or prizes.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says the reward systems that become more responsive are those that make 'rewards, and especially social rewards, feel intense', and that the gap shows most when 'peers raise the value of a daring act'. Limiting the effect to non-social rewards contradicts this.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 itself says 'plenty of teenagers who are surrounded by friends behave with conspicuous care', and 'adolescents differ widely'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says restraint and planning 'continue to mature into the early twenties', so the gap would be expected to narrow in that decade.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 warns that 'Brains do not determine behaviour on their own', which allows circumstances a share in the explanation.

common_misconception: Treating the hedges in paragraph 3 as contradictions of the account, when the author includes them as part of it.

correct_answer: (B) replacing the image of a language window that shuts at a fixed age with a picture of gradual age effects that differ by component.
explanation: Paragraph 1 states the thesis ('a slope rather than a window'), paragraph 2 adds the confound of exposure, paragraph 3 the differences between components, and paragraph 4 the cost of the window image. The correct answer covers both the slope and the component point.

option_rationales.A: This is one point within paragraph 3, used to support the case against a single critical period; it is too narrow to be the passage's concern.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says it is 'hard to tell how much of the outcome' exposure and age each explain, so naming exposure as the chief cause overstates the author's view.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 grants that the belief 'has some foundation' and that early learners end up closer to native-like command; the author denies only the fixed window.

common_misconception: Taking the confound in paragraph 2 as the author's whole explanation, or overstating the critique into a denial of any age effect.

correct_answer: (A) cannot by itself show how much of the gap between them is due to age rather than to conditions of learning.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says that in such comparisons 'differences in the quantity and character of exposure travel along with age, and it is hard to tell how much of the outcome each explains'. The comparison therefore cannot isolate the effect of age.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says 'some' immersed adults reach high levels; this is far weaker than equal success for all immersed adults, and 'proves' is too strong.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says only that it is 'hard to tell how much of the outcome each explains', which rules out attributing the whole gap to exposure.
option_rationales.D: Vocabulary and memory strategies are discussed in paragraph 3 and are not linked to the comparison of attainment in paragraph 2.

common_misconception: Converting 'hard to tell how much of the outcome each explains' into the stronger claim that exposure explains the whole gap.

correct_answer: (D) separate parts of language ability, each affected to a different degree by the age at which learning starts.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says accent is 'most sensitive to the age of first exposure', some grammar 'sensitive too', while vocabulary keeps growing; it concludes with 'different sensitivities, declining at different rates for different components'.

option_rationales.A: Interference between languages is never discussed; the phrase contrasts accent and grammar with vocabulary in their sensitivity to age.
option_rationales.B: The sensitivities belong to components of language 'declining at different rates', not to stages of childhood matched to languages.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 is about components of language (accent, grammar, vocabulary), not about differences in learners' feelings.

common_misconception: Attaching 'sensitivities' to learners rather than to components of language.

correct_answer: (B) Among learners matched for the amount and kind of daily exposure, attainment fell sharply at one particular age, with little decline before or after it.
explanation: The author holds that age effects form 'a slope rather than a window' and that exposure is confounded with age. A sharp drop at one age, with exposure held equal, is exactly the discontinuity the window theory predicts and removes the confound the author relies on.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says adults 'often learn the early stages of a new language faster than young children do', so this agrees with the author.
option_rationales.C: The author already grants in paragraph 3 that some aspects of grammar 'seem sensitive too'; a gradual, component-specific age effect fits this finding.
option_rationales.D: This supports paragraph 2, where immersed adults reach levels that the stricter window theories say 'should be out of reach'.

common_misconception: Choosing the grammar finding because it shows a lasting age effect, without seeing that the author concedes such effects and disputes only their shape.

correct_answer: (A) far larger on abstract classification and pattern detection than on vocabulary and arithmetic.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says the gains 'were largest on tasks that ask for abstract classification and for the detection of patterns in unfamiliar material, and much smaller on tasks that draw on stored knowledge, such as vocabulary and arithmetic'.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says scores rose 'in country after country'; no comparison of early and late schooling countries is made.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the gains 'were not spread evenly across the tests'.
option_rationales.D: This reverses paragraph 2, which says gains were 'much smaller on tasks that draw on stored knowledge'.

common_misconception: Reversing which tasks showed the larger gains.

correct_answer: (C) an answer can earn no credit on a test while still reflecting a sensible way of thinking about the world.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'The first answer earns credit; the second does not. Yet the second is not stupid', since it reflects a habit 'well suited' to a practical life. An uncredited answer can still be a sensible one.

option_rationales.A: Nothing in the passage describes a change in scoring rules; the change described is in the habits of test takers.
option_rationales.B: The passage draws no such recommendation; paragraph 4 asks for caution in interpreting comparisons, not for changes to scoring.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the practical answer reflects a 'habit', not an inability; nothing is said about what such people can do when asked to classify.

common_misconception: Turning the descriptive point into a recommendation about scoring.

correct_answer: (B) pose a dilemma whose two obvious resolutions both look unacceptable, which the rest of the passage tries to escape.
explanation: Paragraph 1 states that the rise 'presents an awkward dilemma': if the gains are real gains in intelligence, earlier generations were absurdly dull; if they are an artefact, the artefact is inexplicably large. Paragraph 2 opens 'The way out begins', confirming that the rest seeks an escape.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 treats the artefact explanation as one horn of the dilemma and says it is 'hard to see why the artefact should be so large'; it does not establish it.
option_rationales.C: Apart from noting that tests were renormed, paragraph 1 says nothing about methods of detection; its focus is the puzzle the rise creates.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 calls the conclusion that our grandparents were of low intelligence 'absurd on its face'.

common_misconception: Taking one horn of the dilemma for the author's claim.

correct_answer: (A) mark a genuine spread of one style of thinking, without amounting to a rise in general intellectual power.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says the century 'trained a particular style of thought' and that the gains are real 'since the habit genuinely spread, but they are not gains in a single underlying power'. The correct answer holds both halves of this position.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the tests 'remain good predictors of success in schools and workplaces', so this contradicts the passage.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says 'The gains are therefore real, since the habit genuinely spread'; the artefact horn is rejected.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the century 'did not make people more intelligent in some general sense', so any rise in general intelligence, even a smaller one, contradicts the author.

common_misconception: Accepting a hedged version of the 'more intelligent' horn because it sounds moderate.

correct_answer: (C) Scores on abstract tasks rose as fast among people with little schooling and manual jobs as among people whose education and work centred on symbols.
explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 attribute the gains to a habit spread by 'Mass schooling, work that deals in symbols rather than objects' and a culture of categories. If gains were equal among people with little schooling and manual work, the proposed cause would not explain them.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says the tests 'remain good predictors', and explains why; continued prediction is consistent with the explanation.
option_rationales.B: This agrees with paragraph 3, which denies that today's average person is 'a match for the most gifted minds of a century ago'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 already says gains on stored-knowledge tasks were 'much smaller', not absent, so a small rise in vocabulary fits the explanation.

common_misconception: Choosing the vocabulary option because it seems to blur the pattern in paragraph 2, without noticing that the passage says 'much smaller', not none.

correct_answer: (D) Ageing alters the balance among mental capacities, so whether it counts as decline depends on what a task demands.
explanation: Paragraph 4 states the author's view: 'ageing changes the mix of a person's capacities rather than lowering a single level, and ... whether the change amounts to a loss depends on the task'. Paragraphs 1 to 3 build toward this by qualifying the decline picture.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 calls this 'an equally simple narrative of wisdom' and says 'Older people are not uniformly wise', so it is a view the author rejects.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says 'Neither method gives a clean view'; and the point about methods is only one step toward the central claim in paragraph 4.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 concludes that 'some decline is real', and paragraph 4 says losses in speed 'have real consequences'; the author denies only the steep, uniform picture.

common_misconception: Taking the critique of the decline picture for a denial of decline, or the rejected wisdom narrative for the author's view.

correct_answer: (C) qualified interest: doubtful that it accounts for every loss, but valuing what it shows about interpretation.
explanation: Paragraph 3 reports the proposal, notes 'The proposal is contested, and it cannot explain away every loss', and then says 'It does, however, show' that the same observation can be read as deterioration or as a cost of accumulation.

option_rationales.A: The author judges both its limits ('cannot explain away every loss') and its value ('It does, however, show'), so the stance is not neutral.
option_rationales.B: The author goes on: 'It does, however, show' that a slower response can be read two ways, so the proposal is valued, not dismissed.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the proposal 'is contested, and it cannot explain away every loss', which rules out firm endorsement.

common_misconception: Seizing on the reservation and missing the 'however' that follows it.

correct_answer: (A) may understate the decline that occurs in the population at large, because those who remain in them tend to be healthier and more able.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says that 'those who stay in a long study are often healthier and more able than those who drop out'. If the remaining sample is healthier and abler, the decline it shows is likely to be smaller than the decline in everyone, so such studies may understate it.

option_rationales.B: They do remove that difference, but paragraph 2 adds that they 'carry biases of their own' and that 'Neither method gives a clean view', so the author withholds this ranking.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says such studies 'tend to show later and gentler declines than such snapshots suggest', which is not a confirmation of the familiar picture.
option_rationales.D: Waning interest is never mentioned, and the bias the passage does name, healthier and abler people staying in, would push the other way.

common_misconception: Choosing the 'more accurate' option because it is half right about schooling, while missing that the author refuses to rank the methods.

correct_answer: (B) A computer model of word retrieval, given ever larger vocabularies with its processing unchanged, slowed down in the way that older adults do.
explanation: The proposal is that slowing partly reflects 'a larger store': a mind that knows more words 'takes longer to find any one of them'. A model in which only vocabulary size changes, and retrieval slows as in ageing, isolates store size as a sufficient cause, which supports the proposal.

option_rationales.A: If slowing is equal where no store is searched, the store cannot be its cause; this weakens the proposal rather than strengthening it.
option_rationales.C: A larger vocabulary here brings no slowing, which counts against the proposal; it is relevant, but in the wrong direction.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 already reports this; it shows that the store is larger but not that a larger store causes slower responses, which is what the proposal claims.

common_misconception: Choosing the vocabulary finding because it fits the proposal's premise, without seeing that it does not connect store size to slowing.

correct_answer: (D) fails to recognise the serenity and sound judgement that age reliably brings to those who reach it.
explanation: Paragraph 4 rejects the 'narrative of wisdom' and says 'Older people are not uniformly wise', so the author does not fault the decline picture for missing a serenity that age reliably brings. The other three shortcomings are stated in paragraphs 2 and 3.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says a slower response 'can be read as a symptom of deterioration or as a cost of accumulation', which the familiar picture ignores.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says one-time comparisons confound age with 'less schooling, different work and less familiarity with the kind of test'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the familiar picture 'attends to only half of what changes', omitting knowledge that 'goes on accumulating'.

common_misconception: Assuming that because the author criticises the decline picture, the author must endorse its opposite.

correct_answer: (A) dispute the usual gloomy moral of the experiments, arguing that much yielding was sensible reliance on others as evidence, though pressure also played a part.
explanation: Paragraph 1 states the familiar gloomy moral, paragraphs 2 and 3 challenge it (most answers were correct; yielding often reflected 'treating others as evidence'), paragraph 4 concedes that 'Normative pressure ... was real' but only 'part of the picture', and paragraph 5 draws out the consequence for remedies. The correct answer captures both the challenge and the concession.

option_rationales.B: This reverses the author's emphasis: paragraph 3 makes informational influence central, and paragraph 4 treats normative pressure as 'only part of the picture'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 5 rejects exhorting people 'to be brave' and proposes better information instead; the option also takes the closing remark for the passage's whole purpose.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the room was 'deliberately arranged to defeat' a sound rule, but the author uses this to reinterpret the results, not to dismiss the experiments as uninformative.

common_misconception: Picking the option about social pressure because paragraph 4 discusses it at length, without noticing that the author treats it as only part of the explanation.

correct_answer: (C) indicate that some agreement with the majority reflected a wish to avoid embarrassment, not a change of belief.
explanation: Paragraph 4: private answers 'produced far less agreement with the majority, which suggests that some yielding was about avoiding embarrassment rather than about belief.' The correct answer restates this.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says a sizeable share 'never yielded at all' and nothing in the passage says this figure was exaggerated; the private-answer variations concern a different question.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says only that private answers produced 'far less agreement'; it does not claim that informational influence vanished, and the author's paragraph 3 argument implies it would not.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 draws the opposite lesson: the drop in agreement when answers were private points to embarrassment, not to genuine persuasion, and to speak of proof overstates any inference here.

common_misconception: Overreading the variation as showing that all yielding was social, or that the majority stopped counting as evidence.

correct_answer: (B) allowing what other people report to count as evidence about how things actually are.
explanation: Paragraph 3 ends: 'much of what looks like spineless deference is better described as informational influence: treating others as evidence.' The correct answer paraphrases this definition.

option_rationales.A: This describes what paragraph 4 calls 'Normative pressure, the wish to fit in', which the author explicitly distinguishes from informational influence.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 concerns a single participant weighing the reports of several others, not a confident person persuading a crowd.
option_rationales.D: The experimenter's instructions are never discussed; paragraph 3 defines the phrase as 'treating others as evidence'.

common_misconception: Confusing informational influence with the normative pressure described in the next paragraph.

correct_answer: (D) A review panel publishes the reasoning behind each member's vote and records every dissenting opinion alongside the final decision.
explanation: Paragraph 5 proposes 'making dissent visible' and 'designing institutions in which the reasons behind a majority view can be inspected rather than merely counted'. Publishing each member's reasoning and recording dissent does both.

option_rationales.A: Announcing only the majority's position strengthens the 'appearance of unanimity' and lets views be 'merely counted', the opposite of what paragraph 5 proposes.
option_rationales.B: This is the remedy the author sets aside in paragraph 5: 'If people conform because they are weak, the cure is to exhort them to be brave.'
option_rationales.C: Requiring unanimity suppresses visible dissent, whereas paragraph 5 wants dissent made visible so that a single honest voice breaks apparent unanimity.

common_misconception: Choosing the workshop on courage, which sounds like a sensible anti-conformity measure but is the remedy the author regards as misdirected.

correct_answer: (D) each witness reads the calm of the other onlookers as a sign that nothing serious is happening.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'each witness looks to the others to work out whether anything is really wrong, and the calm faces of people who are themselves only watching can persuade everyone that nothing is.'

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 attributes the assumption that 'someone better placed is already responding' to shared responsibility, not to ambiguity, and it mentions no authorities.
option_rationales.B: The passage says the reluctance comes from concluding that nothing is wrong, not from an unwillingness to help people whose situation is unclear.
option_rationales.C: Physical visibility is never mentioned; paragraph 2 locates the problem in what witnesses infer from 'the calm faces' of others.

common_misconception: Mixing up the two mechanisms in paragraph 2, diffused responsibility and ambiguity.

correct_answer: (B) Showing that each person helps less in a group does not by itself settle how likely a victim is to be helped.
explanation: Paragraph 3 separates two claims: individuals help less when others are present (shown), and victims are helped less (not shown). Because a crowd 'contains many potential helpers', the first does not settle the second.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the chance of help 'can remain high, and may rise' with crowd size; saying help is always more likely turns a possibility into a universal rule.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 accepts that the studies 'showed that a given individual is less likely to help when others are present'; it disputes only the step to the popular claim.
option_rationales.D: This contradicts the passage, which grants that each person in a crowd may be 'somewhat less willing' to help.

common_misconception: Choosing the option claiming victims are always more likely to be helped, which overstates the author's hedged 'can remain high, and may rise'.

correct_answer: (A) respectful of the mechanisms they uncovered but critical of the sweeping lesson popularly drawn from them.
explanation: Paragraph 4 opens 'None of this makes the original research worthless. The mechanisms it identified are real', while paragraph 3 and the end of paragraph 4 reject the popular claim. Respect for the research plus criticism of its popularisation is the correct answer.

option_rationales.B: The author does reach a view: the research is valuable but 'does not support' 'a sweeping verdict on human nature' (paragraph 4).
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says the newspaper account 'greatly exaggerated' the facts, and paragraph 3 criticises the popular reading, so there is reservation.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 calls the experiments 'more careful than the parable' and paragraph 4 says the mechanisms 'are real', so the author does not dismiss them.

common_misconception: Treating criticism of the parable as criticism of the experiments.

correct_answer: (C) show that the research offers practical guidance drawn from the mechanisms it found, not from the sweeping popular claim.
explanation: The advice targets exactly the two mechanisms of paragraph 2: telling one person what to do means 'responsibility is no longer shared and the situation is no longer ambiguous'. It illustrates the author's claim that the research is 'modest and useful'.

option_rationales.A: The advice is addressed to the person who needs help and concerns singling out one bystander; teaching crowds about the effect is never mentioned.
option_rationales.B: Nothing in the passage assigns blame to victims; the advice simply removes the shared responsibility and ambiguity described in paragraph 2.
option_rationales.D: The same paragraph says the research does not support 'a sweeping verdict on human nature'; the advice draws on the mechanisms, not on the popular version.

common_misconception: Reading the advice as a concession to the popular claim.

correct_answer: (A) preferred divisions that widened the difference between the two groups even when another division would have given their own group more.
explanation: Paragraph 1: 'Some even preferred allocations that maximised the gap between the groups over allocations that would have given their own group more in absolute terms.'

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says 'You never meet another member of your group; you do not know who they are', so no friendships could form.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 reports that favouritism shrinks when one's group will not know the allocations; it never says observation led people to favour the other group.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says participants gave 'a little more' to their own group, not that they gave nothing to the other group.

common_misconception: Inflating mild favouritism into outright exclusion.

correct_answer: (C) Participants favoured their own group just as strongly when assured that nobody would ever learn how they had allocated.
explanation: The reciprocity account rests on the finding that favouritism 'shrinks when participants are told that members of their group will not know how they allocated'. If favouritism stayed as strong under guaranteed anonymity, the expectation of reciprocity could not be what drives it.

option_rationales.A: This concerns how thin the basis for a group can be (paragraph 4), not whether favouritism depends on being known to one's group.
option_rationales.B: This echoes the favouritism-not-hostility point in paragraph 3, a separate argument; it says nothing about the expectation of reciprocity.
option_rationales.D: The size of the sums does not bear on whether favouritism depends on group members knowing one's choices, which is what the reciprocity account claims.

common_misconception: Choosing the penalties option because it comes from the same paragraph, without noticing it supports a different claim.

correct_answer: (D) set a limit on what the experiments can explain, separating the origins of group loyalty from the causes of bitter conflict.
explanation: The paragraph contrasts what the paradigm shows ('where the raw material of loyalty comes from') with what it 'does not show' ('what turns that material into enmity'). It marks the boundary of the evidence.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says the finding is not 'trivial' and the final sentence credits the paradigm with showing 'where the raw material of loyalty comes from'.
option_rationales.B: The final paragraph does not retract paragraph 4; it says only that the laboratory cannot explain why divisions 'become bitter', leaving the point about redrawing categories intact.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph lists 'histories, grievances and competing claims' as what real groups have, and it grants that the paradigm shows 'the raw material of loyalty'; it does not make competition the sole cause.

common_misconception: Reading the list of real-world factors as a rival causal theory rather than as a marker of what the laboratory leaves out.

correct_answer: (B) That arbitrary categories take hold so easily gives grounds for hope as well as for concern about relations between groups.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says the finding 'deserves to be taken seriously' (concern) and also that categories 'learned so easily are not fixed', so cross-cutting identities 'can be built by the same mechanism' (hope). The author rejects 'the fatalistic' lesson without dismissing the finding.

option_rationales.A: This is the 'dramatic' reading reported in paragraph 2, which the author says 'outruns the evidence'; the final paragraph adds that the laboratory cannot show what turns loyalty into enmity.
option_rationales.C: The reciprocity point concerns why participants favoured an arbitrary group; the author never extends it to real-world prejudice, and paragraph 5 says real divisions involve histories and grievances absent from the laboratory.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says it 'remains striking that so thin a basis for belonging should shape behaviour at all', so the author holds that such categories do affect behaviour.

common_misconception: Accepting the reported dramatic reading of paragraph 2 as the author's own view, or extending the reciprocity account beyond what the author claims.

correct_answer: (C) the feeling is real, but the selective set of people it reaches and excludes is what makes it harmful.
explanation: Paragraph 3 describes sympathy for 'a single person wronged' being turned into demands to punish 'the whole group'. The emotion is 'genuine'; the fault lies in how narrowly it is aimed and whom it excludes, echoing the 'narrow beam' of paragraph 2.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says nothing about intensity overwhelming the feeler; the problem it describes is sympathy for one victim being turned against 'the whole group'.
option_rationales.B: Duration is never discussed; 'range' in context refers to whom the sympathy reaches, a single victim, while others are targeted.
option_rationales.D: The same sentence says 'The emotion in such cases is genuine', which rules out pretence.

common_misconception: Taking 'range' to mean intensity or duration rather than scope of concern.

correct_answer: (B) does not require sharing a stranger's feelings, and so is not confined to people one can vividly imagine.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says compassion means 'caring about another's good without necessarily sharing the feeling' and 'can be extended to people one will never see'. Since paragraph 2 locates empathy's bias in its dependence on felt, identifiable individuals, compassion's independence from shared feeling is what lets it reach strangers.

option_rationales.A: The passage claims only that compassion 'can be extended to people one will never see'; claiming it is entirely free of bias, unlike every other form of concern, goes well beyond this.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 defines compassion as 'caring about another's good', which is a form of concern, not a feelingless principle; the author resists the idea that the alternative is 'bloodless'.
option_rationales.D: The passage never compares the intensity of the two; its point is that compassion 'does not exhaust the carer' and reaches people 'one will never see'.

common_misconception: Equating compassion with the cold principle the objection fears, or overstating its freedom from bias.

correct_answer: (A) weaken as the person who is suffering becomes more familiar to the one who feels it.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says empathy favours 'the familiar over the strange' and is most easily directed at people 'who are near us, who resemble us'. A tendency to weaken with familiarity is the reverse of what the passage says, so it is the exception.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 lists 'the present over the future' among the biases empathy reliably produces.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 describes exactly this: sympathy 'turned into demands for punishment of the whole group'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the plight of one child 'can move us more than a report of thousands', so this is attributed to empathy.

common_misconception: Missing that the correct answer reverses the 'familiar over the strange' bias.

correct_answer: (D) The most intensely empathic people turn out also to give the most generously and impartially to distant populations they will never see.
explanation: The central claim is that empathy, being a 'narrow beam', is a poor guide when allocating help 'across many people' or towards 'those we do not know'. If high empathy went with generous, impartial giving to unseen populations, the alleged bias would not appear and the claim would be undercut.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 already grants that feeling with another person is valuable in close relationships such as 'the consulting room', so this is consistent with the author's narrower claim.
option_rationales.B: This illustrates the insensitivity to number described in paragraph 2 and therefore strengthens the author's case.
option_rationales.C: This fits paragraph 4's claim that compassion 'does not exhaust the carer' and so supports, rather than weakens, the author.

common_misconception: Choosing the doctors option because it praises empathy, without noticing that the author already concedes its value in close relationships.

correct_answer: (A) carries news of a person's conduct to people who were not present and never witnessed it.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'Gossip ... is the channel through which a person's conduct becomes known to people who never saw it.'

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 presents gossip as a way of spreading information to those who did not watch; immediate punishment by witnesses is never mentioned.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 explains kin and neighbour kindness without reputation; gossip in paragraph 2 concerns strangers and absent third parties.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says observers must track motives and context, and gossip is described as an exchange of 'judgements', not a substitute for them.

common_misconception: Attributing to gossip a function from another part of the passage.

correct_answer: (C) cheats would gain from the rule, since anyone who refused to help them would be marked down for doing so.
explanation: Paragraph 3: 'If they do, anyone who withholds help from cheats will be punished for it, and cheating becomes safer.' The correct answer restates the consequence.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the opposite: cooperation is 'far more stable under the second, more demanding standard', the one that does not count such refusals against people.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 attaches this demanding bookkeeping to the second standard, under which refusals to cheats are not counted against the refuser.
option_rationales.D: Nothing in the passage connects the choice of standard to whether people gossip; this is outside the argument.

common_misconception: Assigning the demands of the second standard to the first, since both are described in consecutive sentences.

correct_answer: (B) a plausible defence that nonetheless changes the type of explanation from calculation to disposition.
explanation: Paragraph 4: 'That reply is plausible, but it shifts the explanation from calculation to disposition, and it should be acknowledged as a shift.'

option_rationales.A: The author calls the reply 'plausible'; the criticism is only that the shift it involves 'should be acknowledged as a shift'.
option_rationales.C: The reply concerns why generosity persists in anonymity; the author draws no conclusion about the design of the watching-eyes studies.
option_rationales.D: Immediately after the reply the author settles for 'a narrower and more defensible claim', so the reply is not taken to restore the broad claim.

common_misconception: Choosing the option that calls the reply an implausible excuse because the author qualifies the reply, missing that the qualification grants its plausibility.

correct_answer: (D) Concern about being talked about is a major support of cooperation among strangers, though it cannot explain all generosity and needs accurate talk.
explanation: Paragraph 4 closes: 'What survives is a narrower and more defensible claim: that the expectation of being talked about is one of the main forces that make large-scale cooperation possible, and that it works only as well as the talk is accurate.' The correct answer keeps both the claim and its limits.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says models find cooperation 'far more stable' under the demanding standard, and paragraph 2 says gossip lets reputation work beyond a village.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 begins 'It would be too much to say that reputation explains all cooperation among strangers', which rules out the claim that reputation fully explains it.
option_rationales.C: The dispositional reply is offered by 'A defender of the reputational account'; the author does not rank dispositions above reputation, and still calls reputation 'one of the main forces'.

common_misconception: Picking the dispositional option, which takes a defender's reply for the author's conclusion, or the option claiming a full explanation, which ignores the qualification.

correct_answer: (C) offers no support for the view that correcting a false belief is likely to do more harm than good.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says that 'Only the second', reversal, 'would justify the conclusion that correcting is counterproductive'. Unchanged confidence is resistance, which is 'common and unremarkable', so it gives no support to that conclusion.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 reports average movement towards accuracy and imperfect updating; one person's resistance is compatible with that finding.
option_rationales.B: The passage says people update 'though often less than they should', and that resistance after 'a single encounter' is 'unremarkable'; calling people perfectly unresponsive is extreme.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 defines this as resistance, not reversal; backfire would require the person to become 'more convinced of the falsehood'.

common_misconception: Treating any failure of a correction as a backfire, which is exactly the confusion paragraph 3 diagnoses.

correct_answer: (A) Repeat the correction over several weeks and explain what actually caused the reports, rather than simply denying the rumour.
explanation: Paragraph 4 calls for 'corrections that are repeated, that offer an alternative explanation rather than a bare denial'. Repetition over weeks addresses fading, and explaining the real cause supplies the alternative explanation.

option_rationales.B: This assumes reversal among believers, which paragraph 2 says 'appears to be rare'; the passage reports that people on average move towards the accurate view.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 notes that the effects of correction 'often fade over weeks' and recommends corrections 'that are repeated', so a single denial falls short.
option_rationales.D: This is the 'discouraging moral' of the backfire idea in paragraph 1, which the author rejects: the limits of correction 'do not call for silence'.

common_misconception: Choosing silence or targeting only doubters, both of which rest on the backfire assumption the author argues against.

correct_answer: (B) turning the passage's distinction on the history of the finding itself, suggesting that its correction meets resistance but not reversal.
explanation: Paragraph 5 calls the episode 'a small lesson about the life of findings as well as about belief' and says that correcting a mistaken finding 'meets the same ordinary resistance, though not reversal, that greets any correction', applying paragraph 3's distinction reflexively.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the correction of the finding meets 'resistance, though not reversal', which applies the author's distinction rather than conceding that backfire is real.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph does not restate paragraph 2's evidence; it draws a broader moral about 'the life of findings'.
option_rationales.D: No evidence or claim about deliberate exaggeration appears; the paragraph speaks only of how striking results 'travel much faster' than checking.

common_misconception: Reading the persistence of the finding as a concession that backfire occurs.

correct_answer: (D) Several early reports of backfire counted as a backfire any case in which participants' beliefs simply failed to move towards the correction.
explanation: The claim is that the backfire idea treated mere failure to update (resistance) as becoming 'more convinced of the falsehood' (reversal). If early reports labelled non-movement as backfire, that confusion is directly documented.

option_rationales.A: This explains why later findings may be more reliable (paragraph 2), but says nothing about whether the early idea mixed up resistance and reversal.
option_rationales.B: Fading is a separate limit of correction discussed in paragraph 4; it does not bear on how backfire was defined or detected.
option_rationales.C: This might help explain resistance, but it does not show that resistance was being mistaken for reversal, which is the specific claim.
