option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says such efforts leave the conditions of tenancy 'largely untouched', so the author does not accept that home has been extended to all.

common_misconception: Choosing an option that supplies a factual reason, when the passage's explanation is conceptual.

correct_answer: (C) the parent's place among their kin has shifted, not that the parent has become a different individual.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'the new name announces not that the individual has changed but that their position in a web of kin has changed'. The correct answer restates this.

option_rationales.A: Property and inheritance are never mentioned; paragraph 2 says the name marks a change in 'position in a web of kin'.
option_rationales.B: The passage links the new name to the birth of a child, not to reaching an age or to any grant of rights.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the personal name 'has not been forbidden'; using it is only 'mildly rude' in some communities.

common_misconception: Reading 'outranked' or 'mildly rude' in paragraph 3 as a formal ban on the old name.

correct_answer: (B) a lapse of manners rather than a breach of any rule, since the old name is out of place but not banned.
explanation: The analogy makes the old name inappropriate rather than forbidden: it 'has simply been outranked by a title that carries more social information'. Using it is a social awkwardness, which the passage calls 'mildly rude'.

option_rationales.A: The passage presents the old name as out of place, not as a privilege of intimates; the judge analogy points to awkwardness, not closeness.
option_rationales.C: This reverses the analogy: the nickname is out of place precisely in court, the formal setting.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 calls it 'mildly rude'; nothing suggests punishment, so the option exaggerates.

common_misconception: Over-reading the analogy as a rule enforced by punishment.

correct_answer: (A) displaced in everyday use by a title that carries greater social weight.
explanation: The sentence contrasts being 'forbidden' with being 'outranked by a title that carries more social information'. The old name survives but gives way in use to the more informative title.

option_rationales.B: The name 'has not been forbidden' and can still be used, if rudely, so it has not been forgotten.
option_rationales.C: No legal or ceremonial procedure is described; the change concerns how people are addressed.
option_rationales.D: The ranking is between two ways of addressing the same person, not a moral comparison with the children's names.

common_misconception: Taking 'outranked' to mean abolished or erased.

correct_answer: (C) Naming parents through their children expresses a view of persons as made by their place among kin, differing from fixed naming in emphasis.
explanation: Paragraph 2 gives the central contrast (identity owned first versus identity given by relationship), paragraph 3 extends it, and paragraph 4 qualifies it as 'one of emphasis rather than of kind' while insisting 'the emphasis matters'. The correct answer holds both the claim and the qualification.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says surnames announce a lineage, that is ancestry, and calls the contrast one of emphasis, not a disguised identity of the two.
option_rationales.B: The hardship on the childless is a concession in paragraph 4; the author draws no verdict that one system is less humane.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 grants 'something in this' but calls it the less interesting point; the passage's claim concerns how the person is understood.

common_misconception: Choosing the 'children are prized' reading that the author mentions only to move past it.

correct_answer: (D) what the person doing the work could have earned in paid employment in that hour.
explanation: Paragraph 2: opportunity cost 'asks what the person doing the work could have earned in paid employment during those hours'.

option_rationales.A: This is the replacement-cost method described in paragraph 2, not the opportunity-cost method.
option_rationales.B: Pricing by a bought equivalent is the logic of replacement cost; the restaurant meal in paragraph 1 illustrates what accounts count.
option_rationales.C: Time-use surveys supply the hours; paragraph 2 says turning hours into money then 'requires a choice' of method.

common_misconception: Confusing the two methods, which are defined in consecutive sentences.

correct_answer: (B) show that the two methods can disagree about the value of particular work, not merely about totals.
explanation: The example follows the statement that the methods 'can rank the same work differently': the same hour is valued highly by opportunity cost (a surgeon's earnings) and modestly by replacement cost (a childminder's wage).

option_rationales.A: The author does not prefer either method; paragraph 4 says 'Both methods' share the same limit.
option_rationales.C: How much time surgeons spend on childcare is never discussed; the example concerns how one hour is valued.
option_rationales.D: Early statisticians appear in paragraph 1; the surgeon example comes after the methods are defined and compares them.

common_misconception: Reading the example as a claim about surgeons rather than about methods.

correct_answer: (C) leaving such care out of the accounts is itself a contestable choice and not a refusal to choose.
explanation: Paragraph 3 rejects the idea that zero is 'the neutral one': since conventions must be chosen anyway, choosing zero is one more valuation, and a poor one. Omission is therefore a choice open to challenge.

option_rationales.A: The author defends estimating but never chooses between the two methods, so this prescription goes beyond the passage.
option_rationales.B: The passage says estimates have improved policy debate; it does not reject the accounts as a guide.
option_rationales.D: The author calls the critics' conclusion 'too quick' and says zero is 'the least accurate available', so methods are not equally arbitrary.

common_misconception: Choosing the option that reports the critics' view, which the author rejects.

correct_answer: (A) Elderly people cared for by both paid workers and their own children often value the children's care for reasons unrelated to the tasks.
explanation: Paragraph 4 argues that part of family care is valuable because 'it is they who provide it', which no market price can capture. Evidence that recipients value relatives' care for reasons beyond the tasks performed directly supports that reason.

option_rationales.B: This concerns how families reallocate tasks; it does not bear on care that has value because of who provides it.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 already grants that 'Much of it can be' handed over; this adds nothing about the element that cannot be bought.
option_rationales.D: Rising wages would change the size of a replacement-cost estimate but say nothing about what a price cannot capture.

common_misconception: Picking an option about care and money that is on topic but does not touch the author's specific reason.

correct_answer: (B) what the goods secure is the attachment of the couple's future children to the husband's lineage.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'what passes with the goods is not the woman herself but the affiliation of her future children to the husband's lineage, which is why ... the goods must be returned if the marriage ends before any children are born'.

option_rationales.A: Wedding expenses are never mentioned; the return is tied to what the goods secure, the children's affiliation.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the goods are usually 'not kept by the bride's father as profit', so there is no profit to refund.
option_rationales.D: Administrators appear only as observers who misdescribed the custom; the passage never says they imposed rules on it.

common_misconception: Supplying an outside explanation (refunded profit, costs) instead of the one the passage gives.

correct_answer: (D) bridewealth sets up lasting connections among groups, which is the reverse of what a sale does.
explanation: Right after the chain, the author writes: 'A purchase ends a relationship between buyer and seller; this transfer begins several.' The chain is offered as proof that bridewealth creates ties, the opposite of a market sale.

option_rationales.A: The chain links a daughter's marriage to her brother's, but the passage draws no comparison of how much families cared about either.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the chain links 'households that may never meet', which this contradicts.
option_rationales.C: Nothing suggests the cattle were worthless; they are valuable enough to secure another marriage, so the option is unsupported and extreme.

common_misconception: Drawing a conclusion about family preferences that the example does not support.

correct_answer: (B) qualified acceptance: their judgement is granted for such cases without the older verdict being revived.
explanation: The author concedes that in cash-based, narrowly held transfers the payment 'can begin to behave much more like a price' and that the critics 'are not simply repeating the old error', while insisting that the lesson is not that 'the travellers were wrong and the custom is innocent' in general but that meaning depends on context.

option_rationales.A: The author limits the market reading to settings where 'the web thins'; paragraphs 2 and 3 reject it for the older form.
option_rationales.C: The author explicitly credits the critics in paragraph 4, so this is not neutrality.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says these critics 'are not simply repeating the old error', which rules out dismissal.

common_misconception: Missing the negation in 'not simply repeating the old error' and reading the author as dismissive.

correct_answer: (C) the bride herself could take back the goods for her own use if her husband's family mistreated her.
explanation: The passage gives the bride's family, not the bride, a stake in the marriage: the family 'may have to gather them again in order to return them' and has reason 'to intervene'. Nowhere does the bride reclaim the goods for her own use, so this is the one difference the passage does not present.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says 'A purchase ends a relationship between buyer and seller; this transfer begins several.'
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the goods are 'distributed among a wide circle of her kin' rather than 'kept by the bride's father as profit'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the transfer gives 'the bride's family a continuing stake' and 'reason ... to intervene when it goes badly'.

common_misconception: Choosing the 'continuing stake' option because it sounds like a consequence rather than a difference, or rejecting the correct answer because it resembles the family's stake in paragraph 3.

correct_answer: (D) show that medieval images followed conventions and so are not plain records of how children were seen.
explanation: The example follows 'Artistic conventions are not photographs': haloes were never seen, so medieval art did not simply depict what it saw, and the small-adult portrayal of children cannot prove an absence of the idea of childhood.

option_rationales.A: The saints are an example of a non-realistic convention; nothing links them to how parents viewed children.
option_rationales.B: No change of style is described; the example is used to discredit the 'argument from paintings'.
option_rationales.C: The passage makes no claim about how much artists cared for different subjects; the saints illustrate convention, not preference.

common_misconception: Treating a supporting image as a claim about religion.

correct_answer: (A) rescuing a defensible core from an influential thesis much of whose evidence has been overturned.
explanation: Paragraph 2 records what 'has not survived', paragraph 3 says 'it would be a mistake to conclude that nothing changed' and identifies the institutional change, and paragraph 4 reframes the debate. The passage salvages part of the thesis.

option_rationales.B: This is the critics' finding, summarised in paragraph 2; the passage goes on to say the thesis still captures a real change.
option_rationales.C: The author criticises one inference from paintings, not the use of paintings as evidence in general.
option_rationales.D: The author accepts that 'Childhood as a feeling may be ancient', so the original strong claim is not defended.

common_misconception: Choosing the critics' conclusion, which is only one stage of the argument.

correct_answer: (D) settled one question while leaving open the one on which the thesis is still illuminating.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says the critics 'established that medieval people knew children were different and loved them' but 'did not establish that childhood occupied the same place in social life'; paragraph 4 says the two sides were 'talking past each other' and that the second question is more fruitful.

option_rationales.A: The author accepts their findings from these sources; no objection to the sources is made.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 dates the spread of age-graded schooling to the early modern period; the passage never credits the critics with any such finding.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says they 'assembled a large body of material' showing that parents grieved, so this contradicts the passage.

common_misconception: Inferring that because the critics were right on feeling, they were right on everything.

correct_answer: (A) Records from many medieval towns show most ordinary children attending age-sorted schools and barred by local rule from adult work until their teens.
explanation: The claim is about institutions: age-graded schooling and separation from adult work spread in the early modern period. Widespread medieval evidence of exactly such institutions would show that this form of childhood was not 'far more recent'.

option_rationales.B: This supports the critics' point about feeling, which the author already accepts; it says nothing about age-graded institutions.
option_rationales.C: This concerns painting conventions, which paragraph 2 treats as unreliable evidence; it says nothing about whether age-graded institutions existed before the early modern period.
option_rationales.D: The author speaks of a 'gradual spread' of institutions, so continued child labour in the period is consistent with the claim.

common_misconception: Choosing the sermon option because it contradicts the original thesis, without noticing that the author's claim is about institutions, not feeling.

correct_answer: (C) dividing the number of people above a set age by the number in the conventional working-age band.
explanation: Paragraph 1: the ratio 'divides the number of people above a fixed age, usually sixty-five, by the number of people of working age, conventionally fifteen to sixty-four'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 defines the ratio by age bands alone; the author's complaint in paragraph 2 is precisely that it ignores who is actually employed.
option_rationales.B: Unpaid care is discussed as something the ratio overlooks; it plays no part in how the ratio is calculated.
option_rationales.D: This describes the prospective measure that 'Some demographers have proposed' in paragraph 3, not the ratio itself.

common_misconception: Confusing the ratio with the alternative measure or with the author's proposed corrections.

correct_answer: (B) treats as pure dependants some people whose work makes it possible for others to earn.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says grandparents' childcare 'allows both parents to hold jobs', yet 'on the ratio's accounting, those grandparents appear only as a cost'. The example shows the ratio counting contributors as dependants.

option_rationales.A: The ratio makes no assumption about parents' productivity; the passage criticises how it classifies the grandparents.
option_rationales.C: The passage says nothing about what grandparents prefer; the point is how their existing work is counted.
option_rationales.D: Pensions saved by working grandparents are not discussed; the grandparents in the example provide unpaid childcare, not earnings.

common_misconception: Reading the example as a claim about grandparents' preferences or pensions.

correct_answer: (A) projecting actual rates of paid and unpaid work at each age and the number likely to need intensive care in very late life.
explanation: The author objects to equating age with dependence (paragraph 2) and to a fixed threshold (paragraph 3), and wants concern directed to 'very late life, in which it is most acute' (paragraph 4). A forecast built on actual activity and on late-life care needs answers all three.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'None of this means that ageing is costless', so this reverses the author's concession.
option_rationales.C: A margin keeps the faulty measure; the author's objection is to 'calibration', which a uniform margin does not correct.
option_rationales.D: This answers only the second equation; it still counts 'heads by birthday', ignores who actually works and does nothing to locate the costs of very late life.

common_misconception: Choosing the raised threshold, which fixes one of the author's two objections but keeps counting by birthday.

correct_answer: (B) how accurately the size of the problem and the point where it bites are gauged.
explanation: The next sentence explains the objection: the ratio will 'exaggerate the problem in its general form and ... obscure it in the specific form, very late life'. Calibration is the accuracy with which the scale and location of the problem are measured.

option_rationales.A: Indexing pensions is a sense the word can have elsewhere, but the passage never discusses pension levels.
option_rationales.C: Timing of a response is not discussed; the next sentence explains calibration as exaggerating one form of the problem and obscuring another.
option_rationales.D: The division of responsibility is not the subject of paragraph 4, which concerns what the measure gets wrong.

common_misconception: Taking a familiar technical sense of the word (adjusting payments) instead of the sense fixed by the following sentence.

correct_answer: (C) fictive, because it does not rest on birth or descent.
explanation: Paragraph 1 says the older vocabulary called 'fictive' all relations 'that did not ... rest on blood'. A milk tie is not a tie of birth, so it would have been fictive; paragraph 2 objects to exactly that.

option_rationales.A: The older vocabulary counted as 'real' only ties 'resting on birth and descent'; the bar on marriage is the author's evidence against that vocabulary.
option_rationales.B: The older scheme equated biology with birth and blood; nothing suggests it treated nursing as biological kinship.
option_rationales.D: Metaphor is not one of the two categories of the older scheme, and the author denies that the milk tie is 'a metaphor for kinship'.

common_misconception: Confusing the author's view of the milk tie with how the older vocabulary would have classed it.

correct_answer: (D) limit the scope of the argument and show that its point applies within Western kinship too.
explanation: Paragraph 3 opens 'This is not an argument that biology is irrelevant' and says 'The point is narrower', then adds 'Nor is the West an exception', using adoption, remarriage and donation as Western cases. It qualifies the thesis and extends it.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph narrows the claim but keeps it; it does not withdraw the charge made in paragraph 2.
option_rationales.B: Donated eggs and sperm are cited to show people choosing between birth and care, not to declare biology obsolete.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph calls birth 'one of the most powerful ways', not the most important everywhere, and stresses variation.

common_misconception: Mistaking a qualification for a retraction.

correct_answer: (A) inheriting a share of the same land from a common ancestor.
explanation: Paragraph 2 names food from the same land, a shared house and shared nursing. Land appears only as the source of food; inheriting land from a common ancestor is never given as a way of becoming kin, and inheritance from an ancestor would in any case rest on descent.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 lists 'eating food grown on the same land' as a way of becoming kin.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 lists 'living in the same house' as a way of becoming kin.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 lists being 'nursed at the same breast' and gives the rule on children nursed by the same woman.

common_misconception: Matching the word 'land' to the first item in paragraph 2 without noticing the change from eating its food to inheriting it.

correct_answer: (D) A man raised from infancy by his stepfather comes to regard him, and not the father he never met, as the parent whose funeral rites he must perform.
explanation: The author says kinship can be made through care and shared life, and that people must decide 'whether a tie of birth or a tie of care should prevail when the two come apart' (paragraph 3). The stepson treats years of care as the tie that confers the duties of a son, which is kinship made by conduct.

option_rationales.A: This is kinship discovered through birth alone; nothing is done to make or sustain the tie, so it shows only the 'born into' half.
option_rationales.B: The placement is made on the basis of birth; the tie has not yet been formed through shared living, so it does not illustrate kinship made by doing.
option_rationales.C: The family applies the biological rule the author criticises; the example shows kinship withheld on grounds of birth, not made through conduct.

common_misconception: Choosing the court placement or the genetic discovery because they involve a family relationship, without asking whether the tie is made by conduct.

correct_answer: (B) argue that calendar-based generation labels misplace the causes of difference, while granting a narrower, event-anchored notion of generation.
explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 give two reasons the labels mislead (confounded effects, arbitrary boundaries), paragraph 4 concedes a 'serious idea' anchored to events, and paragraph 5 explains the labels' persistence and cost. The correct answer captures the critique together with the concession.

option_rationales.A: Why the labels persist is the subject of paragraph 5 only; it is one part of a larger critique, so the option is too narrow.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 compares variation within and between cohorts; the passage never ranks age and period against class and region.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says separating the effects requires 'some assumption from outside the data', not that detection is impossible, and paragraph 4 says cohort effects 'have been found'.

common_misconception: Overstating paragraph 2's method problem into a claim of impossibility.

correct_answer: (C) cannot by itself show whether the difference reflects age or a lasting imprint left on each group by its birth cohort.
explanation: In one year, period is held constant, so the observed difference must be due to age or cohort, and in a single cross-section age and birth cohort move together exactly. Paragraph 2 says no observations 'can by itself pull them apart; some assumption from outside the data is always required'.

option_rationales.A: The obstacle is arithmetic ('once any two are known the third is fixed'), so a larger sample of the same design cannot remove it.
option_rationales.B: When all observations come from one year, the period is the same for both groups, so a period effect cannot explain a difference between them.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 offers the job-changing example only to illustrate what an age effect is; it insists that 'No set of observations can by itself pull them apart'.

common_misconception: Treating the illustrative example in paragraph 2 as a finding, or thinking that more data cures an identification problem.

correct_answer: (B) Attitudes shift sharply among people born within a year or two of the usual dividing line between two named generations but change little within each span.
explanation: Paragraph 3 objects that boundaries are conventional, that people a day apart are split while people fourteen years apart are joined, and that within-cohort differences exceed between-cohort ones. A sharp change exactly at the conventional line, with little change inside spans, would show the boundaries marking real breaks.

option_rationales.A: This supports the event-anchored cohort effects granted in paragraph 4; it says nothing about whether the conventional boundaries track real breaks.
option_rationales.C: This is the within-cohort variation that paragraph 3 uses against the labels; it strengthens the objection.
option_rationales.D: This is the disagreement paragraph 3 itself reports, so it supports the objection rather than weakening it.

common_misconception: Choosing the war example because it shows that cohort effects exist, without noticing that the objection concerns where boundaries fall.

correct_answer: (A) respectful but restrictive, accepting it as real provided it is not stretched into a character shared by a whole cohort.
explanation: Paragraph 4 grants that 'Such effects have been found, and they are not trivial', then limits them: they are tied to events, uneven within a cohort, and 'rarely produce a single character that an entire cohort shares'.

option_rationales.B: The idea is the passage's main concession and is used to define what a defensible notion of generation would be, so it is not set aside.
option_rationales.C: The author says such effects are 'anchored to events rather than to calendars', so they do not vindicate calendar labels.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 calls it 'a serious idea buried under the marketing' and says such effects 'are not trivial', which rules out dismissal.

common_misconception: Reading the concession as an endorsement of the labels.

correct_answer: (C) A difference between two cohorts observed at the same age in different decades must be a cohort effect, with no further assumption needed.
explanation: Comparing two cohorts at the same age holds age constant, but they are observed in different decades, so the difference could be a period effect. Paragraph 2 says the three effects cannot be separated by observations alone: 'some assumption from outside the data is always required'. The author would therefore reject the claim that no further assumption is needed.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 says this converts an economic question into one of character, which 'has no obvious policy answer', so the author would agree.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says genuine effects are 'anchored to events rather than to calendars', so the author would agree.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says such effects 'mark some members of a cohort far more deeply than others', so the author would agree.

common_misconception: Thinking that holding age constant isolates the cohort effect, forgetting that the period then differs.

correct_answer: (D) the father dies and his sons set up separate hearths of their own.
explanation: Paragraph 2: the household 'often divides when the father dies and the brothers set up separate hearths'.

option_rationales.A: Division of property among daughters is not described as a cause of partition; paragraph 5 mentions inheritance only as a contested question.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says this is when the household 'becomes joint', not when it divides.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says migration brings 'dispersal', which 'is not the same thing as dissolution'.

common_misconception: Confusing the stage at which a household becomes joint with the stage at which it divides.

correct_answer: (B) a count made on one day can find mostly nuclear households even where joint living is a near-universal stage of life.
explanation: The thought experiment ends in the conclusion drawn in the next sentence: 'A high proportion of nuclear households, then, is not by itself evidence that the joint family is disappearing.' It shows how a snapshot can mislead about a cycle.

option_rationales.A: The passage says nuclear households are a phase that 'may in turn become joint', so it does not call them more stable.
option_rationales.C: The population is explicitly hypothetical ('In a population in which every family followed this cycle exactly'); it is a thought experiment, not a claim about real families.
option_rationales.D: The passage blames the method of counting at a single moment, not any deliberate bias on the part of officials.

common_misconception: Treating a hypothetical population as a description of real families.

correct_answer: (A) the shared obligations and joint decisions that bind relatives even when they live apart.
explanation: Paragraph 4 lists what survives dispersal: money sent to parents, decisions 'still taken together', a son abroad 'bound by his family's expectations'. That is the jointness a residence-based census misses.

option_rationales.B: This is the residential definition that, the sentence says, a census uses and that 'will miss' the jointness meant.
option_rationales.C: Property is one subject of joint decisions in paragraph 4, but legal co-ownership is narrower than the obligations described.
option_rationales.D: Authority within the family is discussed in paragraph 5 as something being renegotiated, not as what jointness means here.

common_misconception: Choosing the residential definition because it is the usual meaning of joint family.

correct_answer: (C) Studies following the same families for several decades find that most of their members never lived in a household with more than one married couple.
explanation: Paragraph 2 argues that snapshot counts mislead because people pass through joint phases over a lifetime. If following families over time showed that most people never lived jointly, the life-cycle explanation would fail and a high nuclear share would again count as evidence of decline.

option_rationales.A: This supports paragraph 4's point about jointness across distance; it does not touch the life-cycle argument of paragraph 2.
option_rationales.B: This changes the timing of partition within the cycle but leaves the cycle, and hence the snapshot argument, intact.
option_rationales.D: The author predicts exactly this result from the cycle, so it is consistent with the argument and does not weaken it.

common_misconception: Choosing the single-day count because it sounds like evidence for the decline story, without seeing that the author has already explained it.

correct_answer: (D) Whether the joint family is declining depends partly on whether it is defined by co-residence or by shared obligation.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says a census defining jointness 'by shared residence' will record a dispersed but bound family as 'several nuclear ones'. So the verdict on decline turns partly on the definition used, which the author would accept.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 says it would be 'equally mistaken' to 'declare the joint family unchanged', so the author rejects this.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 5 calls these changes 'a transformation of jointness' rather than 'its end', so they do not vindicate the decline story.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says household form 'is not simply read off' the economy, which denies a simple link, not every effect.

common_misconception: Choosing the authority option because paragraph 5 concedes real change, or swinging to the claim that nothing has changed.

correct_answer: (C) explaining superstition as a response to uncontrollable stakes and proposing that it be judged by what it displaces.
explanation: Paragraph 1 rejects the ignorance view, paragraphs 2 and 3 explain superstition as a response to high stakes that lie partly beyond control, and paragraph 4 sets the criterion: it 'deserves to be judged by what it crowds out'. The correct answer covers both the explanation and the evaluative criterion.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says superstition is 'neither a quaint error to be laughed at nor a hidden wisdom to be celebrated', so this reverses the author's balance.
option_rationales.B: This is the view paragraph 1 rejects: superstition 'does not distribute itself the way ignorance does'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says such professionals are 'often among the most attached' to rituals, which is offered only to unsettle the ignorance view; nothing is proved about their being more superstitious than everyone else, and danger is not the stated cause.

common_misconception: Picking the option about professionals because paragraph 1 dwells on them, when that example only serves to clear away the ignorance view.

correct_answer: (D) used no protective magic in the sheltered lagoon but surrounded open-sea voyages with elaborate rites.
explanation: Paragraph 2 states that these communities 'use no protective magic when they work in a sheltered lagoon' yet 'surround voyages into the open sea with elaborate rites'.

option_rationales.A: The passage says nothing about the rites being abandoned; it contrasts two kinds of fishing done by the same people.
option_rationales.B: This reverses the passage: the lagoon is 'sheltered' and skill 'reliably brings a catch' there, which is why no magic is used.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says they 'use no protective magic' in the lagoon; only their exposure to chance changes, not their beliefs, and the rites follow the exposure.

common_misconception: Misreading 'the same beliefs about the world' as meaning the same practices in both settings.

correct_answer: (A) gives her a fixed action at the point where further deliberation could only unsettle her play.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says the routine marks 'a boundary between deliberation and execution' and 'protects the execution from second thoughts'; it is an outlet for anxiety 'when no further useful action is available'.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the ritual fills only 'the space that preparation cannot reach', so it does not replace preparation.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the ritual supplies 'not a causal lever over the outcome'; physical improvement of the serve is never claimed.
option_rationales.D: The author says she is 'not, in any serious sense, trying to bend the laws of physics', which rules this out directly.

common_misconception: Assuming the routine must work causally on the serve itself.

correct_answer: (B) A farmer leaves a dry field unirrigated because he trusts a rite performed at sowing to bring enough rain.
explanation: Paragraph 4 places the line 'where the ritual stops occupying the residue of chance and begins to displace action that would genuinely improve the odds'. Irrigation would improve the odds, and the rite displaces it. In the other three cases the useful action has already been taken.

option_rationales.A: Because the checks are complete, the gesture comes after all useful action; it does not displace anything that would improve the odds.
option_rationales.C: The preparation is done and the pendant occupies only the leftover uncertainty; it displaces no useful action, so it stays on the acceptable side of the line.
option_rationales.D: Opening nights are given in paragraph 2 as a case where the ritual fills space preparation cannot reach; nothing useful is crowded out.

common_misconception: Choosing any ritual that looks irrational, instead of applying the author's specific criterion of displacement.

correct_answer: (B) settle in advance how relatives, neighbours and the bereaved household should conduct themselves after a death.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says the fixed days 'settle a set of practical questions' about visiting, speaking and resuming work, and paragraph 3 sums up: 'Its main work was coordination.'

option_rationales.A: This is one custom mentioned in paragraph 1, and paragraph 4 treats it as policing; it is not given as the main work of the fixed days.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says 'The fixed days rarely claimed to measure how long sorrow lasts', which denies this directly.
option_rationales.D: Spending and supervision by elders are never mentioned; the passage speaks only of conduct and coordination.

common_misconception: Taking a vivid custom from paragraph 1 for the general function the author assigns.

correct_answer: (C) the effort of working out, unaided, how to behave and what to do while newly bereaved.
explanation: The phrase follows the list of questions (when to visit, what to say, when to resume work) that 'A prescribed sequence answers' in advance. Without the sequence, the bereaved would have to decide these matters themselves while 'exhausted'.

option_rationales.A: Pretended feeling is not the issue in paragraph 2; the phrase concerns not knowing how to act.
option_rationales.B: The phrase is about the bereaved person's own behaviour at the time, not about creating traditions for others.
option_rationales.D: The surrounding questions are about when to visit, what to say and when to resume work, not practical arrangements for the funeral.

common_misconception: Reading 'inventing' as creating new rituals rather than improvising one's behaviour.

correct_answer: (A) people who want to support the bereaved are often held back by not knowing what is expected of them.
explanation: Paragraph 3 describes friends who 'hesitate' and colleagues who 'say nothing for fear of saying the wrong thing', because 'nobody else knows what part to play'. Paragraph 4 adds that abandoning shared forms 'removes the cues that let others accompany' grief.

option_rationales.B: Nothing in the passage says that schedules prolonged sorrow or that grief has become shorter; this is outside its scope.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the result 'has not obviously been freer grief'; the author grants loneliness, not greater authenticity.
option_rationales.D: The passage describes the absence of scripts, not new rigid rules; this contradicts paragraph 3.

common_misconception: Accepting the half-true option that grief is lonelier, without noticing that its other half (more authentic) is denied.

correct_answer: (D) qualified appreciation of their coordinating role, together with criticism of the coercion some of them involved.
explanation: The author defends the customs' coordinating function (paragraphs 2 and 3) while conceding that some 'bore down hardest on those with least power' and policed widows (paragraph 4). Appreciation with a stated reservation is the attitude.

option_rationales.A: The author takes a clear position: the objection 'misreads what the calendar was for', and a replacement should keep the coordinating function.
option_rationales.B: This is the modern objection reported in paragraph 1, which the author says 'contains a truth' but largely rejects.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 opens 'This is not an argument for restoring every old rule', which rules out a wish for full restoration.

common_misconception: Mistaking the objection the author reports in paragraph 1 for the author's own view.

correct_answer: (A) show why the transitional phase of such rites has drawn more attention than the other two.
explanation: The sentence before the list says the middle phase has attracted the most attention 'for good reason', and the list begins 'It is there that most of the strange features of such rites are concentrated'. The list supplies that reason.

option_rationales.B: The list gives typical features; nothing claims that all cultures share every one of them, which would be an extreme reading.
option_rationales.C: The author never condemns the practices; paragraph 2 goes on to explain their function.
option_rationales.D: No ceremonies of incorporation are described, so there is nothing for the list to be contrasted with.

common_misconception: Reading a moral judgement into a descriptive list.

correct_answer: (C) helps to create bonds among novices that are not organised by the standing or wealth of their families.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says levelling makes sons of rich and poor families 'indistinguishable', and that shared hardship then creates 'cohorts whose loyalty cuts across lineage and wealth'. Levelling is the precondition for those cross-cutting ties.

option_rationales.A: The author presents the stripping as the 'function' of these features, against the 'waiting room' reading, so it is not an accident.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the novices are indistinguishable only 'for a time'; nothing suggests family rank is erased for good.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the opposite: people 'deprived of their usual footing' become more 'receptive to instruction'.

common_misconception: Ignoring the qualifier 'for a time' and treating the levelling as permanent.

correct_answer: (D) an open-ended freedom in which novices themselves decided when their transition was complete.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says the elders 'decided when it was over' and that the openness praised by modern admirers is exactly what the traditional threshold did not have. This option describes the modern image, not the traditional phase.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says 'Elders set its length, prescribed what novices could eat and say, and decided when it was over', so this is attributed.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says stripping names, clothing and possessions 'removes the markers by which they were previously ranked', so this is attributed.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says novices become 'receptive to instruction, since people deprived of their usual footing listen differently', so this is attributed.

common_misconception: Carrying the modern celebration of liminality as 'freedom, creativity and play' back into the traditional rite.

correct_answer: (B) Young people passing through open-ended, unmarked transitions are found to form lasting ties and take on new roles just as well as novices in bounded rites do.
explanation: The conclusion is that liminality was productive not because of its openness but because of 'the certainty that the openness would end'. If open-ended transitions with no exit produced the same goods (ties, new roles), the bounded frame would not be what made the difference.

option_rationales.A: This matches the author's description in paragraph 4 of the threshold 'without its discipline, its companions' and so supports the conclusion.
option_rationales.C: A long phase is still a bounded one, ended by elders; the length of the frame does not touch the claim that the frame is what mattered.
option_rationales.D: This shows elders controlling the threshold, which fits the author's picture of a 'firm frame' and does nothing to weaken it.

common_misconception: Choosing an option about modern young people because it is on topic, without checking whether it supports or undermines the conclusion.

correct_answer: (D) Pilgrims have chosen to bring back some of the effort, for instance by walking the last part of the way.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says the effortful element 'has instead been reintroduced by choice', with pilgrims leaving their vehicles 'to walk the final stretch, sometimes barefoot, sometimes on their knees'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 mentions this only as what 'One might have predicted'; it then says the effort 'has instead been reintroduced by choice'.
option_rationales.B: No requirement by shrine authorities is mentioned; paragraph 3 says the effort is reintroduced 'by choice'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 describes pilgrims adding hardship back, which is the opposite of valuing arrival alone.

common_misconception: Taking the prediction the author mentions and rejects for what actually happened.

correct_answer: (C) the same bodily hardship can carry different meanings depending on the goal towards which it is directed.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says the hiker's blisters are an inconvenience while 'the same blisters' become an offering for the pilgrim, and that 'What converts them is the fixed point towards which they are directed'.

option_rationales.A: The passage speaks of 'the same blisters'; the difference it draws is one of meaning, not of severity.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says just before the example that 'The hardships of the road are not valuable in the abstract', which contradicts this.
option_rationales.D: This reverses the passage, which says that for the hiker blisters are 'an inconvenience'; only the pilgrim's become 'an offering'.

common_misconception: Assuming the difference must be one of physical severity rather than meaning.

correct_answer: (A) The effort of the road and the fixed destination give each other their significance in pilgrimage, so neither can be understood on its own.
explanation: Paragraph 2 states the thesis: both familiar views 'detach two elements that draw their meaning from each other'. Paragraph 3 supports it with the reintroduction of effort, and paragraph 4 with the point that the destination's being fixed 'lends the road its gravity'.

option_rationales.B: This is the second misunderstanding set out in paragraph 1, which the author says detaches the walking from the destination.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the effort has been 'condensed rather than abandoned', and nothing says only the whole route will do.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 opens by denying this: such a walker is not 'deceived about what he finds', and the change 'can be real'.

common_misconception: Choosing one of the two views the author describes as misunderstandings.

correct_answer: (B) the walk may change him genuinely, though it lacks the gravity that a fixed and unchangeable destination helps to give a journey.
explanation: Paragraph 4 concedes that such walks 'do change people' but says the walker gives something up 'when the destination becomes optional': the pilgrim's inability to change destinations 'lends the road its gravity'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says 'the change can be real without being religious', which this contradicts.
option_rationales.C: This is the second view in paragraph 1, which the author rejects; paragraph 4 says such a journey is 'a different thing' from the pilgrim's.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says a visitor who arrives 'on a whim' sees what the pilgrim sees without the pilgrim's experience; the destination must be fixed from the start.

common_misconception: Choosing the shrine option because it adds a destination, missing that the passage requires the destination to be fixed and binding beforehand.

correct_answer: (B) an insistence by some outside authority that the site be formally assigned to one tradition.
explanation: The same sentence explains the phrase: 'when some authority, a government department, a heritage body or a movement seeking to purify practice, insists that the site be registered, restored or claimed as belonging to one tradition alone'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the communities are not 'much troubled by the discrepancy'; the demand comes from 'some authority', not from the communities' wish to agree.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 contrasts the demand with 'the slow pressure of difference', so a gradual build-up is exactly what the phrase does not mean.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says custodians are not asked and do not ask about belief; the phrase is glossed in paragraph 3 as registering or claiming the site for one tradition.

common_misconception: Reading 'definition' as explanation of meaning rather than official assignment of identity.

correct_answer: (A) It supplies the observations of how sharing actually works on which the author's rejection of both stories rests.
explanation: Paragraph 2 reports what 'Close observation' finds: parallel use, different names for the saint, custodians who do not ask about belief. Paragraph 3 then begins 'This is why the harmony story ... puts the emphasis in the wrong place' and goes on to reject the truce story as well.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the communities are not 'much troubled by the discrepancy'; it describes stable sharing, not decline.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says observation 'rarely finds a single, blended faith', and paragraph 3 says the harmony story 'puts the emphasis in the wrong place'; it is rejected, not accepted with qualifications.
option_rationales.D: Custodians in paragraph 2 'accept offerings from all'; the possibility of one side enlarging its claim is raised only in paragraph 4.

common_misconception: Assuming that because paragraph 2 describes real sharing it must support the harmony story.

correct_answer: (C) Two clubs meet in the same hall on different evenings, each calling it by its own name, and the caretaker never asks which club owns it.
explanation: The author's model is parallel use (different evenings, like different days), different names for the same thing, a custodian who does not ask, and the decisive question 'whose shrine it really is' left unposed (paragraph 2). The correct answer reproduces all of these.

option_rationales.A: The author says the arrangement 'does not depend on people believing the same thing'; prior agreement on purpose is the opposite model.
option_rationales.B: Settling ownership is the 'demand for definition' that paragraph 3 says threatens sharing, not the basis of it.
option_rationales.D: A merger with a common constitution is the 'single, blended faith' model that paragraph 2 says observation rarely finds.

common_misconception: Choosing an option with harmony or a formal settlement, both of which the author says misdescribe sharing.

correct_answer: (D) the vagueness at shared shrines is actively sustained, for instance by custodians not asking about belief, and is not simply a lack of clarity.
explanation: An achievement is something done, and the author calls the ambiguity 'carefully maintained'. Paragraph 2 shows how it is maintained: custodians 'refrain from asking visitors what they believe' and 'certain questions are never posed'. The correct answer links these two paragraphs.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says each group keeps 'a different name and a different story'; there is no common interpretation, agreed or otherwise.
option_rationales.B: The author says only that coexistence 'need not wait for agreement'; ranking ambiguity above agreement everywhere is an extreme reading.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 names government departments and heritage bodies as sources of the threat, not as protectors of the ambiguity.

common_misconception: Treating ambiguity as the absence of something, and so missing the sense of active maintenance the word 'achievement' carries.

correct_answer: (D) argue that the secularisation debate went astray by treating several independent claims as a single thesis.
explanation: Paragraph 2 states that 'Both the confidence and the recantation' treated 'as one hypothesis what was really a bundle of several'. Paragraph 3 tests each strand separately, and paragraph 4 concludes that 'the debate has been conducted at the wrong level of generality'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the privatisation thesis 'has fared worse still, since religious voices are plainly present in public debate', which contradicts this.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'It would be too quick to declare the older thesis vindicated', so the author explicitly declines this conclusion.
option_rationales.C: The revival is the starting point in paragraph 1, but the passage never explains its causes; it analyses what the revival does and does not refute.

common_misconception: Choosing the vindication option because paragraph 3 defends differentiation, without reading the refusal in paragraph 4.

correct_answer: (A) consistent with the differentiation strand of the thesis while failing to fit the decline strand.
explanation: Paragraph 2 defines differentiation as institutions such as law and medicine operating 'no longer answerable to religious authority', and decline as 'a fall in belief, membership and practice'. High attendance with independent courts and hospitals fits the first and contradicts the second; paragraph 2 calls this combination 'common'.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says 'that combination is in fact common', and nothing in the passage predicts it will break apart.
option_rationales.C: The case says nothing about whether religion is present in public argument, which is what privatisation concerns; the inference has no basis.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the strands are 'logically independent'; such a society refutes decline but fits differentiation, so not every form is refuted.

common_misconception: Running the strands together, which is the very error the passage diagnoses.

correct_answer: (C) In several countries resurgent movements won influence mainly by restoring clerical authority over courts and schools, not by competing within independent institutions.
explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that resurgent movements act 'as one set of claimants among many within institutions they do not control'. If resurgence typically worked by putting institutions back under religious authority, it would undo differentiation rather than presuppose it, which directly counters the claim.

option_rationales.A: This is further evidence that such movements act as 'one set of claimants among many', which supports the claim.
option_rationales.B: This bears on the decline strand, which the author already says 'has fared poorly as a universal law'; it says nothing about how resurgent movements operate.
option_rationales.D: Lobbying is one of the behaviours paragraph 3 cites as acting within differentiated institutions, so this fits the author's claim rather than weakening it.

common_misconception: Choosing the decline option because it seems to bear on secularisation, when the claim at issue concerns differentiation only.

correct_answer: (B) critical of their recantation for sharing the confusion behind their earlier confidence, without endorsing their original prediction.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'Both the confidence and the recantation' rested on treating several claims as one, so the author faults the recantation. Paragraph 4 also says the decline prediction was wrong and the thesis is not 'vindicated', so the author does not side with the original view either.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the recantation rested on an error, and paragraph 3 says differentiation 'has held up remarkably well', so the author does not think the thesis was refuted as a whole.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says the general question has 'no single answer' but that narrower questions are ones 'the evidence can actually settle'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the theory 'predicted the fading of faith and got that prediction wrong in much of the world', so the author does not think the original prediction was correct.

common_misconception: Inferring that because the author criticises the recantation, the author must think the original thesis was right.

correct_answer: (B) has been cited by supporters of each of the two dominant explanations as evidence for their view.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'Supporters of each view can point to cases': funding 'suggests they found them useful' (the safety valve) and banning 'suggests they found them dangerous' (the subversive view).

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says banning suggests rulers 'found them dangerous', and funding suggests they found them 'useful'; neither implies no significance.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says riots occurred only 'on a few occasions'; nothing ties them to long toleration.
option_rationales.D: The passage contrasts different responses by rulers; it says nothing about ordinary people opposing the festivals.

common_misconception: Reading the funding and banning as evidence for a single conclusion.

correct_answer: (C) the economic and political conditions surrounding the festival in the year that it turned violent.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'The difference lay not in the ritual but in its circumstances: a bad harvest, a disputed tax, a quarrel between factions of the elite'. Inversion 'takes' its charge 'from the situation into which it is performed'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the same festival, 'with the same masks and the same songs', could be harmless or rebellious; the forms do not explain the difference.
option_rationales.B: The author rejects the idea that a festival's meaning is 'fixed by its form', so there is no such fixed type to identify.
option_rationales.D: Funding appears in paragraph 2 only as evidence cited by one theory; paragraph 3 locates the cause in 'circumstances' such as harvests and taxes.

common_misconception: Looking for the cause in the ritual itself, which is the assumption the author attacks.

correct_answer: (D) attack one of the two explanations on a ground distinct from the objection raised against both in paragraph 3.
explanation: Paragraph 3 criticises both theories for assuming that meaning is 'fixed by its form'. Paragraph 4 announces 'a further weakness' of the safety valve theory only: its hydraulic image of resentment has no observed basis. It is a second, independent objection aimed at one theory.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 begins its account afresh 'from a simpler observation'; paragraph 4 is about the steam image and does not set up that account.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says only that participants 'may feel more entitled'; its point is that no one has observed the mechanism, not that grievances generally grew.
option_rationales.C: Riots are not mentioned in paragraph 4, and paragraph 3 has already rejected the second explanation along with the first.

common_misconception: Treating paragraph 4 as a bridge to paragraph 5, or as support for the rival theory, instead of as a second objection to one theory.

correct_answer: (A) Town records show that formal complaints against local officials rose rather than fell in the weeks after festivals mocking those officials.
explanation: Paragraph 4 argues that resentment does not behave like steam: participants 'do not obviously feel less aggrieved afterwards' and may feel 'more entitled to their grievance'. Complaints rising after the festival is direct evidence that grievance was not discharged.

option_rationales.B: This is the kind of case paragraph 2 says safety valve supporters cite; it supports that theory rather than the author's criticism of it.
option_rationales.C: The later fate of the songs says nothing about whether resentment is released like steam, so it is irrelevant to the criticism.
option_rationales.D: This concerns why authorities banned festivals, not whether mocking masters leaves people less aggrieved afterwards.

common_misconception: Choosing an option about riots or bans because it sounds like evidence against the safety valve.

correct_answer: (B) Because inversion displays the hierarchy in a way that can be read as confirming or exposing it, the surrounding situation must decide which reading prevails.
explanation: Paragraph 5 says inversion teaches the order 'in that sense' but also shows ranking to be 'a convention rather than a fact of nature', and that which lesson is learned 'depends, again, on what else is happening'. The word 'again' points back to paragraph 3: the charge comes from circumstances, and paragraph 5 explains why the form can carry either charge.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 says 'the lesson cuts both ways'; this keeps only the conservative lesson and contradicts the claim that the festival has no fixed charge.
option_rationales.C: 'The mock bishop presupposes a real one' means the parody depends on the existence of the hierarchy, not on the bishop's participation; this is a distortion.
option_rationales.D: This keeps only the subversive lesson; paragraph 5 says which lesson is learned 'depends, again, on what else is happening'.

common_misconception: Fastening on one of the two lessons in paragraph 5 and turning it into a fixed effect.

correct_answer: (C) belonging to the group in name while lacking any real commitment to it.
explanation: The sentence contrasts someone willing to bear years of hardship with someone 'only nominally attached'; the preceding sentences describe people who 'take the benefits of membership without bearing its burdens'. Nominal attachment is membership in name only.

option_rationales.A: No trial period is mentioned; the phrase describes the kind of member that demanding rituals screen out.
option_rationales.B: Nothing in paragraph 2 concerns family names; the contrast is between real and merely apparent commitment.
option_rationales.D: This reverses the sense: the free rider is formally a member who takes the 'benefits of membership', but is not committed.

common_misconception: Reading 'nominally' literally as having to do with names.

correct_answer: (D) belonging becomes less valuable once uncommitted people can enter more easily and draw on its benefits.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says demanding rituals 'screen' out free riders so that members 'can extend trust', and that when demands fall 'the value of belonging falls along with its cost'. Lower costs let in the free riders the screen used to exclude, which reduces the value of membership.

option_rationales.A: The demands have been lowered, so the remaining costs fall rather than rise; this distorts the passage.
option_rationales.B: Nothing in paragraph 2 refers to outsiders' views of doctrine; the explanation offered concerns the value of belonging.
option_rationales.C: The signalling account treats costs as screens, not as enjoyable in themselves; this explanation is outside the theory.

common_misconception: Supplying a plausible psychological reason not contained in the signalling account.

correct_answer: (A) its inability to explain why groups that relax their demands sometimes lose members.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'The theory also explains' the pattern of groups losing members when they lower their demands; this is a success of the account, not a limitation. The other three are the three gaps listed in paragraphs 3 and 4.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 gives this as the first gap: the theory explains why a ritual is costly 'not why it should take the particular form it does'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 gives this as the third and 'most important' gap: cost 'helps to manufacture' commitment.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 gives this as the second gap: a rite performed on an infant 'cannot be a signal of the child's own' commitment.

common_misconception: Remembering that the loss of members is discussed but forgetting that the theory is credited with explaining it.

correct_answer: (C) A volunteer who joined a relief group half-heartedly finds, after months of exhausting night shifts, that she is now deeply loyal to it.
explanation: The third gap is that the practice can change the performer, producing 'the conviction it was supposed to display' (paragraph 4). The volunteer's commitment grows out of the costly practice instead of preceding it.

option_rationales.A: Refusing an equally costly substitute illustrates the first gap in paragraph 3, about the particular form of a rite.
option_rationales.B: A practice imposed on an infant that signals the parents' commitment illustrates the second gap in paragraph 3.
option_rationales.D: This illustrates the signalling account itself (paragraph 2), not any gap in it.

common_misconception: Matching the club example to the third gap because it involves cost, without checking which gap each case illustrates.

correct_answer: (B) what people report about being changed by demanding practices is broadly accurate rather than a later rationalisation.
explanation: Paragraph 4 bases the claim on what people 'commonly report' and introduces it conditionally: 'If that is so, cost does not only reveal commitment but helps to manufacture it.' The conclusion therefore requires that those reports be broadly true.

option_rationales.A: The author criticises the theory for treating ritual only as 'a message addressed to observers'; the claim does not need performers to be aiming at observers.
option_rationales.C: Children's rites belong to the second gap, and nothing in paragraph 4 compares the strength of commitment produced in children and in adults.
option_rationales.D: If this were assumed the signalling account would fail outright, yet paragraph 5 says the objections do not overturn it; the claim does not depend on it.

common_misconception: Overlooking the conditional 'If that is so', which shows exactly what the claim rests on.

correct_answer: (D) illustrate how choices that make sense for each employer combine into an outcome that helps nobody.
explanation: The image follows directly on 'Each employer is behaving sensibly' and 'the sum of these sensible choices'. When everyone stands on tiptoe, each person's move makes sense, but 'no one sees better than before, and everyone is more tired': raising the bar for all buys no advantage for anyone and only adds cost.

option_rationales.A: This reads 'more tired' literally; the image is about the collective result of everyone raising the bar, not about the fatigue of students.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says 'Each employer is behaving sensibly' on its own account; there is no agreement or collusion among employers anywhere in the passage.
option_rationales.C: The passage says the degree is 'the cheapest filter available' and once selected a more persistent group, so it does carry some information; the image concerns the collective result.

common_misconception: Taking the image literally, or reading collusion into what the passage presents as separate sensible choices.

correct_answer: (A) was picking out a small group who tended, on average, to be more persistent and better connected.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'When few people held degrees, an employer who asked for one was selecting a small group who were, on average, more persistent and better connected than the rest.'

option_rationales.B: Asking for a master's is what employers did later, once degrees had become common; it does not describe the period when few people held degrees.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 explains the selection in terms of persistence and connections, not task training, and paragraph 3 says much of what graduates studied 'is barely used in the job'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 describes exclusion as a result of the rising bar, a requirement 'introduced in the name of competence'; the passage never says exclusion was intended.

common_misconception: Confusing the early stage with the later stage of the process, or reading intention into an effect.

correct_answer: (C) A rise in the education a job demands does not by itself show that the job has become harder.
explanation: Paragraph 1 says the explanation that work has become more demanding 'is offered far more often than it is checked', and paragraph 2 offers a rival account in which requirements rise because degrees stop separating applicants. So a rising requirement does not by itself show the work is harder.

option_rationales.A: The passage proposes no regulation; paragraph 4 mentions employers who test applicants directly, but as a development that raises a question, not as a law the author recommends.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 concedes that 'Some occupations really have changed beyond recognition' and says only that the change in many jobs is 'often modest', which is far weaker than saying most jobs are exactly the same.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says education 'has goods that no labour market can measure', so the author does not reduce its value to a labour-market signal.

common_misconception: Turning the author's 'often modest' into 'no change at all', or crediting the author with a prescription.

correct_answer: (A) In a firm that began requiring degrees for clerks, graduates did the job's tasks markedly better, and the gap was traced to their coursework.
explanation: The account in paragraph 2 treats the degree 'less as a certificate of skill than as a ticket in a queue', valued for 'the signal rather than the substance' (paragraph 3). Evidence that graduates do the job better because of what they learned shows the degree certifying real skill, which cuts directly against the account.

option_rationales.B: This supports the account, which says the degree is 'the cheapest filter available' to each employer.
option_rationales.C: More people seeking degrees is what the queue account predicts, as each tries to keep a place in line; it does not challenge the account.
option_rationales.D: This fits paragraph 3's claim that the rising bar rewards 'the capacity to pay for time'; it does nothing to show that the degree certifies skill.

common_misconception: Choosing an option that is about degrees and access but is consistent with, or even supports, the signalling account.

correct_answer: (D) free time falling at the same hours for everyone became a market that businesses could plan to serve.
explanation: The phrase is explained by the next sentence: football matches, excursion trains and seaside resorts 'arranged themselves around Saturday afternoon and Sunday'. Because everyone was free at the same time, businesses could sell leisure to that shared block.

option_rationales.A: The passage says leisure came to be paid for, not that it became unaffordable; it calls guaranteed free time 'a real gain' for most working people.
option_rationales.B: The passage never mentions overtime; the sentence that follows lists football matches, excursion trains and resorts, which sell leisure to workers rather than buy their time.
option_rationales.C: The sellers in paragraph 3 are leisure businesses, and what changes is that leisure becomes 'something one went out and paid for'; workers are the buyers, not the sellers.

common_misconception: Reading 'sold' as a sale of labour time rather than a sale of leisure to workers.

correct_answer: (B) Workers who could be relied upon to arrive, in a fit state, at the start of the week.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'employers won a workforce that turned up, sober, on Monday morning.' Employers had wanted predictable hours, and this is what the compromise gave them.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says leisure was organised by football, trains and resorts, not by employers, and gives employers no control over Sundays.
option_rationales.C: Wages are never mentioned in the passage; the employers' gain is stated as predictability, not savings on pay.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says workers 'wanted fewer hours' and gained guaranteed rest; nothing suggests hours were added elsewhere in exchange.

common_misconception: Supplying a plausible economic gain (hours, wages) that the passage does not state.

correct_answer: (B) appreciative of what it won for workers, while noting how it reshaped the nature of leisure.
explanation: Paragraph 3 calls guaranteed free time 'a real gain' won against resistance, yet adds that 'the weekend also changed what free time was', turning it into a scheduled block that could be sold to. The attitude is appreciation with a critical observation.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says free time 'was won against resistance', and paragraph 2 presents a struggle and a compromise, not employer generosity.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says plainly that 'The lesson is not that the old irregular rhythm was better', noting its ties to poverty and overwork.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 opens by saying it would be 'wrong to see the outcome merely as a defeat dressed up as a victory'.

common_misconception: Picking up the critical note in paragraph 3 and overstating it into dismissal.

correct_answer: (D) Musicians who rested whenever bookings dried up join an orchestra with a fixed August holiday, and travel firms begin selling August trips to its players.
explanation: The passage describes two linked shifts: irregular, self-chosen rest becomes guaranteed rest fixed for everyone (paragraph 2), and that shared block becomes something businesses sell to (paragraph 3). The orchestra case reproduces both: guaranteed, standardised holiday replaces rest taken when bookings ran out, and a market forms around the fixed period.

option_rationales.A: This concerns pay alone, whereas the passage stresses that the struggle over hours was 'also a struggle over the shape of time'.
option_rationales.B: This provides a place for leisure but changes neither who decides when free time falls nor its regularity, which is the heart of the passage's change.
option_rationales.C: This moves from fixed to discretionary time, the reverse of the passage's change from rest taken 'at the worker's discretion' to 'a fixed block'.

common_misconception: Choosing any case that involves leisure or workers' gains without both the standardisation of time and the market that forms around it.

correct_answer: (C) examples of how a house was laid out so that the work of servants went unseen.
explanation: Paragraph 1 introduces the staircases and bells right after saying that 'the best servant was the one who was least noticed'; the staircases mean maids 'need never meet the family', and the bells let a summons be answered without anyone seeing 'who answered it'.

option_rationales.A: The passage makes no comparison between large and small households, and it treats the features as concealment rather than harshness.
option_rationales.B: Cost and efficiency are never discussed; paragraph 1 presents these features as means of keeping servants out of sight.
option_rationales.D: The passage says nothing about family members avoiding one another; the staircases kept maids from meeting 'the family', and the bells hid 'who answered'.

common_misconception: Inferring a purpose (efficiency, privacy) that the surrounding sentences do not give.

correct_answer: (A) treats as a nuisance what is often simply the customer's meeting with the person doing the work.
explanation: The sentence says designers speak of removing friction 'as though the friction in question were not, very often, the encounter with another person who is doing the work'. The phrase is revealing because it recasts contact with the worker as an inconvenience, echoing the old wish 'to receive service without meeting the server' (paragraph 4).

option_rationales.B: The author claims a durable wish, not conscious imitation; nothing suggests designers have the Victorian household in mind.
option_rationales.C: This takes 'friction' as a technical glitch; the author's 'as though' clause says the friction is, very often, a human encounter.
option_rationales.D: Workers' physical burden is not discussed; 'friction' in the passage refers to the encounter between customer and worker.

common_misconception: Reading the author's point as a claim about designers' intentions or about technical faults.

correct_answer: (D) Couriers and cleaners today work under essentially the same conditions as Victorian servants, though under a different name.
explanation: Paragraph 4 warns that 'The comparison must not be pressed too far': modern workers are not bound to one household, keep hours that end and have legal protections a scullery maid lacked, so 'to call such workers servants is to erase real gains'. The claim of essentially the same conditions contradicts this.

option_rationales.A: Supported: paragraph 1 says 'snobbery explains less than it seems to' and that invisibility was 'one of the things the household was for'.
option_rationales.B: Supported: paragraph 2 says 'The ease was manufactured by a great deal of labour, and the labour had to be hidden for the ease to be believed'.
option_rationales.C: Supported: paragraph 4 says the means 'are now available to far more people than ever owned a back staircase'.

common_misconception: Taking the passage's comparison between old and new service as an identity claim, missing the qualification in paragraph 4.

correct_answer: (C) Hiding the labour behind comfort once helped a class seem exempt from necessity, and the wish behind that concealment outlives the old form of service.
explanation: Paragraph 2 argues that hiding labour let a class 'appear exempt from necessity', and paragraphs 3 and 4 argue that 'the wish to receive service without meeting the server' survives in new forms, even though modern workers have real gains. The correct answer holds both halves.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says 'snobbery explains less than it seems to'; the author's explanation is that concealment produced the appearance of ease and so produced hierarchy.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says 'it is easy to assume that its logic went with it' and then argues the opposite, that the logic survives by other means.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says that calling such workers servants 'is to erase real gains'; the author draws a qualified parallel, not an identity.

common_misconception: Choosing the option that echoes the passage's comparison most strongly, or the familiar snobbery explanation the author sets aside.

correct_answer: (A) who sets the terms on which a worker's feelings are displayed, and for whose benefit.
explanation: Paragraph 3 contrasts 'the presence of emotion at work' with 'its ownership', picking up paragraph 2's distinction between feeling a worker manages 'according to her own judgement' and feeling whose display is 'specified, monitored and sold by someone else', where 'the employer, not the worker, sets its terms'.

option_rationales.B: This takes 'ownership' literally; the passage never discusses recordings or legal rights over them.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says a scripted greeting 'can be delivered with real goodwill', so sincerity is a separate matter from who controls the display.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the distinction 'was never between jobs that involve feeling and jobs that do not', and paragraph 3 contrasts ownership with mere presence.

common_misconception: Equating ownership with sincerity, or with the amount of emotion involved.

correct_answer: (B) no emotional labourer in the strict sense, provided nobody else scripts or monitors how his courtesy is displayed.
explanation: Paragraph 2 puts the line between feeling managed 'according to her own judgement' and feeling 'specified, monitored and sold by someone else'. The surgeon's calm 'is left to her; nobody scripts it'. The self-managing builder resembles the surgeon, so he falls outside the strict concept unless someone else controls his display.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says a builder who loses his temper 'will not keep' his clients, so feeling clearly matters to his work; the author's criterion is control, not relevance.
option_rationales.C: This is the critics' reductio, which the author answers: the distinction 'was never between jobs that involve feeling and jobs that do not'.
option_rationales.D: Losing clients shows only that emotion matters to his work; on the author's test what counts is whether someone else specifies and sells the display.

common_misconception: Accepting the critics' broad criterion, or treating the commercial consequences of emotion as the test.

correct_answer: (A) In one chain of shops, staff whose greetings were scripted and scored were more exhausted than staff serving the same customers as they saw fit.
