option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 implies the best customers genuinely did not want the new thing at first; it was other buyers, 'never well served', who took it up.

common_misconception: Inventing a hidden motive or a price story instead of following the mechanism the passage gives.

correct_answer: (D) raise an objection to the account and turn it into further support for the author's conclusion.
explanation: Paragraph 3 begins 'It may be objected', states the hindsight objection, calls it 'fair', and then says 'it strengthens rather than weakens the point', because if good managers cannot foresee which markets will matter, vigilance cannot be the remedy.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 contains no example of a surviving firm; separate units are discussed in paragraph 4.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 concedes that the account involves hindsight, not that complacency explains most cases; the author continues to reject complacency.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says an incumbent that chased all such technologies 'would have squandered its resources', which is the opposite of this advice.

common_misconception: Confusing the content of the objection with the author's own recommendation.

correct_answer: (A) its engineers lack the technical skills needed to work with the newer and simpler design.
explanation: Paragraph 2 lists three correct judgements: customers say no, margins are thin, the market is too small. A lack of technical skill is never mentioned; indeed the passage insists managers were capable and 'doing, carefully and well, exactly what they had been trained to do'.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the market is 'too small to move a company of its scale', so this too is given as a reason.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says 'The incumbent asks its customers whether they want the new thing, and they say no', so this is a stated reason.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says 'It examines the margins, and they are thin', so this is one of the reasons given.

common_misconception: Assuming incompetence of some kind, which the passage explicitly denies.

correct_answer: (B) A large firm's criteria for funding projects reflect its size and costs, so a smaller unit with its own measures can value what the parent dismisses.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says the separate unit has 'its own costs and its own measures of success, small enough that a small market can still excite it', and that it escapes 'the scrutiny of the rules' that would have rejected it. This works only if the rejection stems from criteria tied to the parent's size and costs, rather than from the technology itself or from managers' alertness.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says good managers 'cannot tell in advance' which small markets will matter, and the remedy is offered precisely because such prediction is not possible.
option_rationales.C: The author concedes that separate units 'can be starved or smothered by the parent' and calls the remedy 'no guarantee', so the argument does not assume this.
option_rationales.D: The author denies that the problem is one of alertness ('not a failure to look'), so the remedy cannot rest on the unit's managers being more vigilant.

common_misconception: Choosing the alertness option, which restates the complacency view the author rejects.

correct_answer: (A) showing that the effect of chief executives on results is commonly overstated, and that the overstatement is costly.
explanation: Paragraph 1 identifies 'a systematic error about how much any one leader actually controls', paragraphs 2 and 3 show how other forces drive results, and paragraph 4 says the error 'lies in degree, not in kind' and describes its costs to boards.

option_rationales.B: The journalists' preference is explained only briefly in paragraph 1 as the starting point; the passage goes on to argue about leaders' real influence and its consequences.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'None of this means that leaders are irrelevant' and names situations in which they 'can matter a great deal', so this overstates the author's claim.
option_rationales.D: The passage criticises boards that hunt for saviours but makes no rule about internal promotion; it suggests only spending 'less on heroes'.

common_misconception: Taking the claim of exaggeration for a claim that leaders do not matter at all.

correct_answer: (D) exaggerating how much leaders matter, rather than in believing that they matter at all.
explanation: The sentence comes right after the concession that leaders 'can matter a great deal' in some situations. The author thus accepts that leaders have influence (the 'kind' is right) and objects only to how much influence is assumed (the 'degree').

option_rationales.A: The passage says leaders are both credited and blamed for movements they did not cause, with no contrast between small and large changes.
option_rationales.B: Frequency of decisions is not discussed; the sentence follows a concession that leaders can matter and limits the error to its size.
option_rationales.C: The passage never distinguishes right and wrong kinds of leader; 'kind' here refers to whether leaders matter, not to types of leader.

common_misconception: Reading 'kind' as types of leaders or decisions instead of as the question whether leaders matter at all.

correct_answer: (B) the comparisons that would reveal how much success owes to circumstances are seldom made, because unremarkable success draws little attention.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says that the celebrated leader's firm will be credited for 'what was largely a rising market carrying both firms upward', and that such comparisons 'are rarely made' because the second firm 'has no story to tell'. The implication is that the evidence needed to correct the error is missing because steady, undramatic success is not reported.

option_rationales.A: The passage makes no such comparison of performance; its hypothetical firms both prosper, and it draws no general conclusion about which type does better.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says 'Both firms prosper', so there is no suggestion that the second firm did worse.
option_rationales.D: Nothing suggests deliberate suppression; the passage explains the neglect by the absence of a dramatic narrative, not by any motive to protect anyone.

common_misconception: Assuming that the second firm must have done worse, or that the neglect is intentional.

correct_answer: (C) A new head teacher is praised for rising examination results that stem from teaching reforms her predecessor introduced years earlier.
explanation: Paragraph 2 notes that many products a firm sells 'were conceived years earlier, under managers who have since left', yet results are credited to the current leader. The head teacher praised for her predecessor's reforms is a direct parallel: an individual is credited with an outcome produced by earlier decisions.

option_rationales.A: Sharing credit accurately is not an error of attribution; if anything it avoids the error the passage describes.
option_rationales.B: Here credit follows a fair comparison under similar conditions, which is exactly what paragraph 3 says is usually missing; there is no misattribution.
option_rationales.D: This blames circumstances for what a person caused, the reverse of the passage's error, which credits or blames people for what circumstances caused.

common_misconception: Choosing the flooding case because it also involves wrong attribution, without noticing that its direction is reversed.

correct_answer: (A) Managers, out of kindness or to avoid awkward conversations, rate nearly everyone above average, so the ratings convey nothing.
explanation: Paragraph 1 states the defenders' case: 'Left to themselves, managers tend to rate almost everyone above average, partly out of kindness and partly to avoid difficult conversations, and a scale on which everyone scores highly conveys no information at all.'

option_rationales.B: Joint work is raised in paragraph 2 as part of the author's objection, not as a problem that defenders of the system say it solves.
option_rationales.C: Favouritism towards friends is not mentioned; paragraph 1 describes generous rating of almost everyone, not of particular people.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 is about managers' ratings of staff, not employees' views of themselves, though awkward conversations are mentioned as a motive for managers.

common_misconception: Attributing to the defenders a point the author makes against them.

correct_answer: (C) find it harder to keep and attract able people, since some of its good members must still be rated poorly.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says forcing a distribution on a team of good people 'manufactures distinctions', and paragraph 3 says able people 'learn to avoid strong teams, since a good performer is safer among weaker colleagues'. Together these imply that a strong team would lose or fail to attract able members.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 argues that ranking makes 'helping a colleague' a cost, which points away from greater cooperation, not towards it.
option_rationales.B: No exemption is mentioned; the passage's point is that the system forces a distribution even on a small team 'assembled precisely because all its members are good'.
option_rationales.D: The passage presents ranking among excellent colleagues as manufacturing distinctions 'the work itself does not support', not as a spur to better work.

common_misconception: Supplying a general belief about competition that the passage does not endorse.

correct_answer: (B) Where forced ranking is used, the rank of each employee depends chiefly on colleagues' accounts of how much that person helped them.
explanation: The author's claim in paragraph 3 rests on the premise that 'If my rating depends on being ranked above my colleagues, then helping a colleague is a cost to me'. If ranks were determined mainly by how much one helped others, helping would raise one's rank, and the mechanism the author describes would run the other way.

option_rationales.A: This shows that cooperation is valuable, which the author would accept; it says nothing about whether ranking makes people less willing to cooperate.
option_rationales.C: Discomfort in appraisal meetings concerns managers' experience of the system, not employees' incentives to cooperate with colleagues.
option_rationales.D: What happens to departing employees has no bearing on whether those who remain are discouraged from helping one another.

common_misconception: Choosing the option about the value of shared ideas, which is on topic and favourable to cooperation but does not touch the incentive the author describes.

correct_answer: (D) fair-minded, presenting the case as reasonable before examining what it takes for granted.
explanation: Paragraph 1 says 'Its defenders make a reasonable case' and sets it out without mockery; paragraph 2 begins 'The difficulty is that the system assumes far more than it appears to', moving to examine its assumptions. The treatment is fair before it is critical.

option_rationales.A: No hidden motives are attributed to defenders; the author engages with their argument on its merits in paragraphs 2 and 3.
option_rationales.B: The author calls it 'a reasonable case' and, in paragraph 4, accepts that a single round of ranking may expose real problems; the case is not dismissed.
option_rationales.C: The author ends by warning against a 'permanent regime' of ranking, so the defenders' conclusion is not adopted.

common_misconception: Inferring from the author's overall criticism that the opposing case must have been dismissed.

correct_answer: (D) illustrate how a working standard can shift through decisions that are each sensible, without anyone choosing to change it.
explanation: Paragraph 1 claims that organisations 'walk towards' catastrophe 'by steps that each seemed reasonable at the time'. The plant illustrates exactly this: each night's decision is defensible, yet 'the limit has quietly moved' and 'No one decided to change it'.

option_rationales.A: Whether the written limit was too low is never assessed; the point is that the working limit moved without a decision, whatever its merits.
option_rationales.B: The engineers judge 'correctly as it turns out' that the vessel is safe; the example concerns reasonable decisions, not carelessness or indifference to safety.
option_rationales.C: The example is offered against the culprit-finding approach of paragraph 1; its lesson is that 'No one decided to change it'.

common_misconception: Reading the example as a story of negligence, which is the very interpretation the passage opposes.

correct_answer: (B) running above the limit has become so habitual that insiders no longer perceive it as a departure from the rules.
explanation: Paragraph 3 ends: the question 'sounds naive, because everyone inside knows that it always has'. Repeated deviation has become normal practice, so a question about it appears to show ignorance rather than insight.

option_rationales.A: The passage says nothing about the outsider's expertise; the question sounds naive because of what insiders have grown used to.
option_rationales.C: The phrase 'everyone inside knows that it always has' indicates a long-standing habit, not a brief episode of a few nights.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says 'the written figure still stands in the manual'; no official revision has taken place.

common_misconception: Assuming that the outsider must be ignorant, rather than that the insiders have adjusted their sense of normal.

correct_answer: (C) a change that accumulates without ever being decided leaves no one accountable for having made it.
explanation: The final sentence contrasts a departure that is 'noticed, argued over and formally adopted', which 'is a decision', with one that 'simply accumulates'. A decision has an author who can be held to it; drift, having no decider, has no one who answers for it. This echoes paragraph 2: 'No one decided to change it.'

option_rationales.A: Irreversibility is not the point; the contrast with 'a decision' that is 'argued over and formally adopted' concerns responsibility, not permanence.
option_rationales.B: The phrase is about the absence of any decision-maker, not about a failure to report; nothing in the passage concerns reporting lines.
option_rationales.D: No refusal to explain is described; the passage implies that no single person made the change, so there is nothing for anyone to answer for.

common_misconception: Reading 'answers to no one' as defiance by individuals rather than as the absence of anyone responsible.

correct_answer: (A) The deviations most likely to end in disaster are those large enough to attract attention at the moment they are made.
explanation: The author locates the danger in deviations that pass unnoticed: in paragraph 2 the excess is 'small' and the limit moves 'quietly', and paragraph 4 says the danger lies in 'deviation that is never recognised as such'. The statement that ties danger to conspicuous deviations reverses this, so it is the one the author would reject.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 calls mistaken the inference 'that a risk which has not yet produced harm has thereby been shown to be small', so the author would agree.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'much good practice begins as a sensible exception', so the author would agree.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says such findings 'are rarely false, but they are often beside the point', so the author would agree.

common_misconception: Rejecting the statement about beneficial departures because the passage is about disasters, missing the concession in paragraph 4.

correct_answer: (D) Much spare capacity serves real if irregular purposes, so slack should be held deliberately and judged by its use rather than cut wholesale as waste.
explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 show two functions of slack (absorbing shocks, permitting unplanned experiments), paragraph 4 concedes that some slack is waste and says the usual question is 'badly posed', and paragraph 5 concludes that slack should be held 'deliberately' and judged by 'what the slack is for'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 says 'The aim is neither to maximise slack nor to abolish it', so a policy of keeping as much as possible contradicts the author.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says of these savings that 'the savings are real'; the author's objection is that the programmes miss what slack was doing, not that the savings are false.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'Some slack is indeed waste', not most, and this concession is a qualification of the thesis rather than the thesis itself.

common_misconception: Picking the option that defends slack most strongly, which overshoots the author's balanced conclusion.

correct_answer: (C) is cheaper to run on ordinary days but stops altogether when a single supplier fails.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'A supply chain that holds no spare stock is cheaper to run on every ordinary day, and on the day a single supplier fails it halts entirely'.

option_rationales.A: This describes the hospital ward staffed to average occupancy, not the supply chain, and the chain's stated weakness is supplier failure, not a rise in demand.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says it 'halts entirely' when a supplier fails, because 'there is nothing between the failure and the factory floor'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the opposite about cost: such a chain 'is cheaper to run on every ordinary day'.

common_misconception: Transferring the hospital example's details to the supply chain.

correct_answer: (B) slack cannot sensibly be assessed as a single amount, since reserves serving a purpose and reserves sheltering comfort call for opposite treatment.
explanation: The sentence that follows explains the phrase: asking 'how much slack an organisation has' treats 'a heterogeneous quantity as if it were uniform'. Paragraph 4 has just shown that slack may shelter 'invention' or 'comfort', and paragraph 5 proposes asking instead 'what the slack is for'. The fault in the question is that it lumps together reserves that should be kept and reserves that should be cut.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 attributes self-interest to some defenders of slack, not to its critics; no motive is ascribed to the critics at all.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'Some slack is indeed waste' and that the critics 'are therefore not simply wrong', so the author does not deny that some slack is waste.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 5 recommends reserves 'whose size is reviewed and whose use is reported', which presupposes measurement and accounting rather than abandoning them.

common_misconception: Choosing the option that says the critics are simply wrong, overlooking 'not simply wrong'.

correct_answer: (A) In several firms, the most profitable products began as projects staff pursued with time or money not assigned to any plan.
explanation: Paragraph 3 claims that new products and methods 'often began in precisely the margins that a thorough efficiency drive would have closed'. Evidence that the most profitable products began as unplanned projects using unassigned time or money directly supports this.

option_rationales.B: Job satisfaction is not the claim; paragraph 3 argues that new products and methods originate in unclaimed time, which enjoyment does not establish.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 already grants that 'Most of these experiments come to nothing'; repeating this does not show that the valuable innovations come from such margins.
option_rationales.D: This concerns the savings discussed in paragraph 1 and, if anything, suggests slack was unneeded; it says nothing about experiments or innovation.

common_misconception: Choosing the option about failed experiments because it matches a sentence in paragraph 3, without noticing that it adds no support to the conclusion.

correct_answer: (B) the worth of a reserve held against rare events cannot be seen by looking only at periods in which no such event occurs.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says the value of a margin held against an unpredictable shock 'appears only in the period that the efficiency audit treats as an exception'. An umbrella judged on dry days looks useless for the same reason: its use lies in the days that such a judgement leaves out.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 accepts that the savings from removing slack 'are real', and paragraph 5 wants reserves reviewed and 'trimmed' when they outlive their purpose, so cost still counts.
option_rationales.C: The comparison concerns shocks only and ranks nothing; paragraph 3 calls the second circumstance, room for experiment, 'perhaps more important'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the reserve is held 'against an event whose timing could not be known', so the comparison concerns unpredictable events, not frequent and foreseeable ones.

common_misconception: Reading the comparison as a ranking of the two functions of slack, or as a rejection of all attention to cost.

correct_answer: (D) such firms leave little documentation and attract neither researchers nor opportunities for interviews.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'The graveyard of failed firms is not consulted because it cannot easily be visited: failed companies leave few records, attract no researchers and give no interviews.'

option_rationales.A: Unwillingness is not mentioned; paragraph 2 says failed firms 'give no interviews' because they no longer exist to give them, not because managers refuse.
option_rationales.B: The passage suggests the opposite: failed firms may have shared the very practices of the winners, which is why ignoring them matters.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 explains why the books sell, but paragraph 2 gives the reason failures are not studied as a matter of access to evidence, not readers' tastes.

common_misconception: Supplying a plausible human motive instead of the reason the passage states.

correct_answer: (C) It grants that a proposed remedy improves the method, then shows that it leaves one objection standing and fails to address another.
explanation: Paragraph 4 states the defenders' answer (matched comparison), acknowledges it as 'a real improvement', then says it 'does not remove the second difficulty' and does not 'settle a third', the unfalsifiable explanation of later decline.

option_rationales.A: The author calls the comparison 'a real improvement' but does not withdraw anything; the paragraph's purpose is to show what the remedy does not fix.
option_rationales.B: The matched comparison is the defenders' answer, not the author's method, and it adds less successful firms rather than replacing the winners.
option_rationales.D: The author does not claim the companies were poorly run; the point about their later stumbles concerns how such failures are explained, not how the firms were managed.

common_misconception: Treating the acknowledgement as a full retreat, or treating the defenders' remedy as the author's proposal.

correct_answer: (A) the explanation cannot be tested, because the abandonment of the principles is inferred from the very failure it is meant to explain.
explanation: The final sentences of paragraph 4 describe a theory that explains success by 'the presence of certain practices, and ... failure by their supposed absence'. The word 'supposed' shows that the absence is assumed after the failure, so no outcome could count against the theory: it 'has arranged never to be wrong'.

option_rationales.B: The author does not say the explanation is false; the objection is that it is immune to refutation, which is different from being shown to be wrong.
option_rationales.C: No such confirmation is suggested; the passage says matched comparison does not 'settle' this third difficulty at all.
option_rationales.D: The passage never suggests that the principles were misapplied in the wrong markets; this introduces an explanation of its own.

common_misconception: Equating an explanation that cannot be refuted with one that is false.

correct_answer: (C) it rests on too few companies for any of its conclusions to reach statistical significance.
explanation: The passage raises three criticisms: selection of winners only (paragraph 2), descriptions shaped by known outcomes (paragraph 3) and an unfalsifiable account of decline (paragraph 4). The number of companies studied is never criticised; the selection objection concerns which firms are studied, not how many.

option_rationales.A: This is the third difficulty in paragraph 4: such a theory 'has arranged never to be wrong'.
option_rationales.B: This is the selection objection of paragraph 2: the method 'has no way of knowing how many companies followed the same practices and failed'.
option_rationales.D: This is the objection of paragraph 3: traits are 'described after the fact, by people who already know the result'.

common_misconception: Confusing the selection problem with a problem of sample size, since both sound like statistical objections.

correct_answer: (D) A study of every firm founded in one industry in a given decade, survivors and failures alike, rating cultures from interviews held after each fate was known.
explanation: The first difficulty (paragraph 2) is studying only winners; including failures avoids it. The second (paragraph 3) is that traits are 'described after the fact, by people who already know the result'. Only the correct answer includes all firms while still relying on descriptions made after outcomes were known.

option_rationales.A: Studying only the most profitable firms keeps the selection problem of paragraph 2, while surveys taken before results avoid the second difficulty; this is the reverse pattern.
option_rationales.B: Studying only survivors falls into the first difficulty, so this study does not avoid it, although it is also open to the second.
option_rationales.C: Including all firms avoids the first difficulty, and surveys made before outcomes were known avoid the second as well, so this study is not open to the second.

common_misconception: Mixing up which difficulty concerns the choice of firms and which concerns the timing of descriptions.

correct_answer: (B) reject the idea that work is a fixed quantity while granting that technological change still harms particular workers.
explanation: Paragraph 1 names the fallacy, paragraph 2 shows why the quantity of work is not fixed, paragraph 3 applies this to work-sharing schemes, and paragraph 4 concedes that change can 'ruin particular lives and places'. The purpose is to correct the fixed-work belief while keeping the concession.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 is one application of the argument, and it does not say firms refuse to hire; it says a firm 'may simply produce less'. The option is too narrow and distorts the reason.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 calls the anxiety understandable but never recommends slowing technology; it asks that policy be judged by what it does for those harmed.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the new jobs 'are rarely the jobs that were lost' and appear in other places and trades, so the claim about the same trades contradicts the passage.

common_misconception: Picking the application in paragraph 3, or turning the concession into a call to resist technology.

correct_answer: (A) losses tend to arrive as single identifiable events, while gains are spread thinly over many trades and places.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'A closed mill is a single event with an address; the thousand small expansions that follow are scattered across an economy'. Concentrated losses are noticed, dispersed gains are not.

option_rationales.B: The passage attributes no motive to the press; paragraph 2 says the expansions are 'reported, if at all, as ordinary growth', which is about how they appear, not about deliberate neglect.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 never compares the pay of new and old jobs; the option adds a claim that the passage does not make.
option_rationales.D: The 'generation' in paragraph 4 is how long transitions can take for workers; paragraph 2 explains visibility by concentration versus dispersion, not by delay and forgetting.

common_misconception: Borrowing the 'generation' from paragraph 4 and attaching it to the wrong claim.

correct_answer: (D) A town should refuse a permit for a second cinema, since its filmgoers would merely be split between two halls and no new jobs could result.
explanation: The fallacy, defined in paragraph 1, assumes a set amount to be shared out, so that any addition simply takes from someone else. The cinema argument assumes a fixed number of filmgoers to be divided, ignoring that a second hall might increase total attendance, just as cheaper cloth increased the number of shirts bought.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says new jobs 'are rarely the jobs that were lost', so this is consistent with the passage rather than an example of the fallacy.
option_rationales.B: This is the reasoning the passage endorses in paragraph 2: a lower price raises demand and frees money for other spending.
option_rationales.C: This matches the concession in paragraph 4 that transitions are slow and costly; it involves no assumption of a fixed amount of work.

common_misconception: Choosing an option that mentions job losses or slow transitions, which sounds pessimistic but does not assume a fixed total.

correct_answer: (C) an argument about the total amount of work can be correct and still say nothing to the people who lose out.
explanation: The weaver appears in the sentence saying the fallacy 'concerns the total amount of work, not its distribution' and that a correct argument about totals 'is cold comfort' to him. He shows the gap between aggregate truth and individual loss.

option_rationales.A: The same paragraph says 'technology does not abolish work in aggregate', so this reverses the author's view.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 criticises both schemes as resting on the same error; the passage never prefers one to the other.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the argument about totals is 'correct'; the weaver shows its limits, not that the premise is right for some age group.

common_misconception: Reading the concession as a retraction of the main argument.

correct_answer: (B) the set of protections and obligations that come together with the legal status of being an employee.
explanation: Paragraph 1 says an employee accepts direction 'in exchange for a wage and a bundle of protections', and paragraph 2 lists 'fixed shifts, minimum hours and the rest of the employment bundle'. The phrase means the package of terms that comes with employee status.

option_rationales.A: The bundle is a set of terms 'designed around a fixed schedule and a single employer', not the workers themselves.
option_rationales.C: Fares and passengers belong to paragraph 1's description of platform control; the bundle is what employment law attaches to a status.
option_rationales.D: The phrase names what would be 'imposed' on platform work, such as 'fixed shifts, minimum hours', not a worker's income from several apps.

common_misconception: Taking 'bundle' literally as a collection of earnings or jobs.

correct_answer: (A) each accurate about a feature of platform work that the other response neglects.
explanation: Paragraph 2 states that 'Each side is right about what the other ignores': the first sees the platform's control, the second sees that the employment bundle fits flexible work badly. Paragraph 3 then identifies their shared mistake, which shows the author thinks each is partly right.

option_rationales.B: The author credits each side with one truth and ranks neither; nothing in the passage favours the first response.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 argues that some protections 'depend on nothing that a flexible schedule makes impossible', which is a way of reconciling the two concerns.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says 'Each side is right about what the other ignores', so calling both simply mistaken overstates the author's criticism.

common_misconception: Treating the shared mistake identified in paragraph 3 as a verdict that both responses are wholly wrong.

correct_answer: (B) A minimum rate for time worked could be enforced only if platforms fixed in advance the hours a worker counts as available, ending free log-ins.
explanation: The claim is that protections such as a minimum rate for time actually worked are compatible with flexible scheduling. If enforcing that rate required fixing hours in advance, the protection would after all depend on ending flexibility, which directly undercuts the claim.

option_rationales.A: The author already grants in paragraph 3 that such holidays 'are harder to translate'; the claim under test concerns the other protections.
option_rationales.C: This bears on the danger noted in paragraph 4, not on whether the named protections can coexist with a flexible schedule.
option_rationales.D: This concerns workers' wishes, not whether the protections are compatible with flexibility, so it leaves the claim untouched.

common_misconception: Choosing the paid-holiday option because it shows a protection is hard to provide, missing that the author has already conceded that case.

correct_answer: (D) acknowledge the risks of the author's proposal while explaining why it remains preferable to the binary.
explanation: Paragraph 4 opens 'Unbundling has dangers of its own', names two, and then says the case for unbundling 'is therefore not that it is free of risk, but that the binary has already failed'. It concedes and then defends.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph describes what 'could' happen and what firms are invited to do; it reports nothing that has occurred.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph warns that a third category 'could become a convenient place' to move employees; it does not recommend one or withdraw the proposal.
option_rationales.C: The responses are set out in paragraph 2, and nothing in the passage reports any decision by courts.

common_misconception: Reading the warnings as a change of position or as reports of fact.

correct_answer: (C) they would otherwise move to other occupations, where wages have risen along with productivity.
explanation: Paragraph 1: 'The musicians' pay must rise too, or they would drift into other work', following the statement that manufacturing wages have risen with productivity.

option_rationales.A: The passage denies that the halls have become 'inefficient' and gives no figures for their running costs.
option_rationales.B: Audience expectations are never mentioned; paragraph 1 says 'nothing about the quartet has changed'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says the opposite: the quartet still needs four players and 'roughly forty minutes', and no innovation has shortened it.

common_misconception: Assuming the musicians' productivity has changed.

correct_answer: (A) show that raising output per worker in such services can change the service rather than supply it more cheaply.
explanation: The sentence before says that 'attempts to compress that time often degrade what is delivered', and the class example shows it: the larger class is cheaper per pupil 'but it is not the same product at a lower price'.

option_rationales.B: The point of the paragraph is that productivity in such sectors 'lags'; the comparison explains why it cannot simply be raised.
option_rationales.C: The comparison works against the suspicion of waste mentioned at the end of paragraph 2, so this reverses its purpose.
option_rationales.D: The passage makes no recommendation about class size; the comparison illustrates why compressing time 'often' degrades the service.

common_misconception: Reading an illustration of a mechanism as a policy recommendation.

correct_answer: (B) fits the pattern of the cost disease but does not by itself show that none of the increase is waste.
explanation: Paragraph 2 places nursing and similar work under the cost disease, so rising relative costs are expected. Paragraph 4 adds that 'some cost growth in services is unavoidable' does not mean 'all of it is', so the rise alone cannot rule out waste. The correct answer holds both points.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 argues that a richer society can afford services 'even at their higher relative price'; the passage nowhere calls for rationing.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 warns that the argument 'should not be stretched into a blanket excuse'; the cost disease is consistent with the rise but does not rule out waste.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says administrative growth 'can' occur, not that it must explain any rise; paragraph 2 says such sectors' costs rise under the cost disease.

common_misconception: Choosing the option that says the cost disease must explain the rise, which keeps paragraph 2 but drops the limit in paragraph 4.

correct_answer: (C) manufacturing productivity may one day stop growing, which would remove the cause of the cost disease.
explanation: Paragraph 4 names three limits: unavoidable growth does not excuse administrative bloat, the price falls hardest on those left out of the gain, and tax-funded budgets may cut services early. The passage never considers manufacturing productivity ceasing to grow.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says such budgets 'may cut services long before the arithmetic says they must', so this limit is stated.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the higher price 'falls hardest on those whose incomes have not shared in the general gain'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says administrative layers 'can multiply' and that 'the cost disease offers them no defence', so this limit is in the passage.

common_misconception: Accepting a plausible economic idea because it involves the mechanism described in paragraph 1.

correct_answer: (A) arguing that the common debate about remote work overlooks how it affects the way juniors learn their jobs.
explanation: Paragraph 1 says the usual question 'says little about how anyone becomes competent', paragraphs 2 and 3 show what juniors lose and why the loss is hidden, and paragraph 4 says firms must build learning 'on purpose'.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says that for many experienced professionals the answer to the productivity question 'appears to be yes', so this reverses the passage.
option_rationales.C: Efficiency of calls for routine matters is not discussed; calls appear only to show that remote contact is planned.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 begins 'This is not an argument for ordering everyone back to their desks', so the prescription contradicts the author.

common_misconception: Turning the author's concern into a call to end remote work.

correct_answer: (D) that learning relies on unplanned exposure, while contact in remote work is mostly scheduled.
explanation: Paragraph 3: such learning 'depends on unplanned exposure and remote work is organised around planned contact'.

option_rationales.A: The passage says some questions feel 'too trivial', not too complicated, to put in an email; complexity is not the reason given.
option_rationales.B: Saved commuting hours are mentioned only as a gain for experienced staff in paragraph 1; nothing is said about how juniors use them.
option_rationales.C: Seniors' willingness is never discussed; paragraph 3 blames the planned nature of remote contact, not reluctance.

common_misconception: Inventing a motive for seniors or borrowing a detail from paragraph 1.

correct_answer: (C) judged the move by a measure that could not register what their newest recruits were losing.
explanation: The partners see 'no fall in billable work', while the passage says of what juniors miss that 'None of this appears in any measure of output'. Their yardstick could not show the loss.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says 'almost none of it is deliberately taught', which is the opposite of formal training.
option_rationales.B: The passage says only that billable work did not fall in the first year; it reports nothing about later output.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the loss is something 'they cannot see', so the partners are not described as knowing about it.

common_misconception: Reading 'cannot see' as 'chose to ignore'.

correct_answer: (D) Staff who joined remote firms as recruits took longer, years afterwards, to be trusted with difficult client work than earlier cohorts had.
explanation: Paragraph 3 predicts that the cost 'shows up years later, as a cohort of mid-career staff who are slower to exercise judgement'. Evidence that remote-era recruits were later slower to be trusted with hard work matches that prediction directly.

option_rationales.A: This fits the partners' first-year impression in paragraph 2 but says nothing about a cost appearing years later.
option_rationales.B: This supports the point in paragraph 4 that offices do not guarantee learning, not the claim that remote work imposes a delayed cost.
option_rationales.C: Satisfaction of experienced staff is irrelevant to whether juniors suffer a later cost; it concerns the group the author sets aside.

common_misconception: Choosing the shut-doors option because it comes from the passage, without noticing it supports a different claim.

correct_answer: (B) the tasks people find easy would also be the easy ones for a machine to master.
explanation: Paragraph 1: 'They took easy to mean what people find easy and hard to mean what people find hard'.

option_rationales.A: The evolutionary account is the passage's own explanation in paragraph 2, and it implies the opposite of what the researchers assumed, since they judged by what 'people find easy'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says they assumed such a machine 'would soon be able to fold laundry', so this reverses their assumption; it is closer to what actually happened.
option_rationales.D: That measure is the passage's own suggestion in paragraph 2; the researchers instead equated difficulty with what 'people find hard'.

common_misconception: Confusing the researchers' expectation with what actually happened.

correct_answer: (A) requiring relatively little effort or computation to reproduce in a machine.
explanation: The sentence contrasts faculties that are 'cheap ones to mechanise' with those that are 'expensive'. Given the board-game and grasping examples, the contrast is between what is easy and what is hard to build into machines.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says explicit reasoning is 'effortful' for people; the word describes how easily machines reproduce a faculty, not how easily people learn it.
option_rationales.C: Pay enters only in paragraph 4, and there it concerns skills that are hard to mechanise; in paragraph 1 'cheap' describes the cost of mechanising.
option_rationales.D: The passage calls these faculties 'higher', so it does not treat them as worthless; the word concerns machines, not value to people.

common_misconception: Reading 'cheap' as a remark about wages because the passage later discusses pay.

correct_answer: (A) Restoring antique chairs, each built differently and damaged in its own way, for private collectors.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says the cleaner is hard to replace because she works in rooms 'never arranged twice in the same way' and handles 'objects of every shape and texture'. Restoring varied, individually damaged chairs has the same features, while the other three jobs follow written rules.

option_rationales.B: This follows 'rules that can be written down', like the reconciliation in paragraph 3, which the passage says a machine finds easier.
option_rationales.C: Allocation by a fixed set of rules is a written procedure, so on paragraph 3's reasoning it is easier to mechanise than physical work in varied settings.
option_rationales.D: A fixed formula is exactly the kind of explicit procedure the passage treats as easy to mechanise.

common_misconception: Judging by how skilled or prestigious a job seems rather than by whether it follows explicit rules.

correct_answer: (C) Since care work resists automation, care workers can expect higher pay as machines take over clerical tasks.
explanation: Paragraph 4's second caution says 'being hard to automate is not the same as being well rewarded', because abundant skills keep wages low 'whatever a robot can or cannot do'. Expecting care workers' pay to rise because their work resists machines is the inference the author rejects.

option_rationales.A: This is the point of paragraphs 2 and 3: our 'sense of difficulty' is not a good guide to what machines find hard.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the paradox 'describes a stage of technology' and that it 'would be rash to assume the boundary will stay where it is'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says a machine finds reconciling accounts 'far easier to take over' and that forecasts 'may therefore have the direction partly backwards', so the author accepts this.

common_misconception: Accepting this conclusion because it seems to follow from paragraph 3, without reading the caution in paragraph 4.

correct_answer: (B) acceptance of it as an account of one real effect, joined to rejection of it as a full account.
explanation: The author grants that unions have a cartel face that can predominate (paragraph 3) but calls measuring them only by the premium 'a category error' (paragraph 4). The view is accepted as partial and rejected as complete.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 calls judging unions by the wage premium alone 'a category error', which is a clear stance, not neutrality.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the cartel face is real and can be 'what remains', so the author does not dismiss the view as baseless.
option_rationales.D: The author argues that the view leaves out a possible gain from voice, not that it understates the losses.

common_misconception: Mistaking strong criticism of the textbook's completeness for a denial that it describes anything real.

correct_answer: (D) impose a higher wage bill while yielding little of the information that might have offset it.
explanation: Paragraph 3: where management treats the procedure as an adversary, 'voice tends to harden into obstruction, and the cartel face is what remains'. The cartel face is the wage premium of paragraph 1, and the offsetting benefit of voice in paragraph 2 is lost.

option_rationales.A: The passage compares quitting with and without voice in paragraph 2 but never says an adversarial setting raises departures above the non-union level.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 attributes productivity gains to management that treats the procedure 'as an early warning'; in the adversarial case only 'the cartel face' remains.
option_rationales.C: Nothing suggests the union stops bargaining; the cartel face, which is the wage premium, is precisely 'what remains'.

common_misconception: Assuming that some productivity gain from voice survives in every setting.

correct_answer: (B) In firms without unions, workers who complain about safety or supervision are no more likely than silent colleagues to be dismissed or passed over.
explanation: Paragraph 2 rests on the premise that, without a union, an individual who complains 'marks herself as troublesome', so leaving is 'often the only safe course'. If complainers suffered no penalty, individual voice would be safe and a union would not be needed to convert departures into information.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 already allows that some managers treat the procedure as an adversary; this is consistent with the argument.
option_rationales.C: Both the cartel view and the voice view expect a wage premium, so this finding leaves paragraph 2 untouched.
option_rationales.D: This supports paragraph 2's claim that firms which hear complaints 'may lose fewer trained workers', so it strengthens rather than undermines.

common_misconception: Choosing an option about wages or managers' attitudes, which concerns other paragraphs, instead of attacking the premise of paragraph 2.

correct_answer: (A) confine the conclusion to a claim about how unions should be judged rather than a verdict on their worth.
explanation: After arguing that the wage premium is the wrong single measure, the author states that this does not show unions are good for firms, and that it shows 'only that the question cannot be answered by looking at the price of labour alone'. The sentence narrows the claim.

option_rationales.B: The next sentence repeats that the question 'cannot be answered by looking at the price of labour alone', which rules out the textbook view as complete.
option_rationales.C: No evidence is introduced; the sentence limits what has been shown, and paragraph 3 says the evidence is 'mixed'.
option_rationales.D: The sentence says only that the argument has not shown unions to be good for firms; paragraph 3's claim that voice 'can' raise productivity still stands.

common_misconception: Reading a limiting statement as a reversal of the author's argument.

correct_answer: (C) the structure of jobs, rather than workers' free choices, has decided how productivity gains are divided.
explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that 'the hours we observe tell us what jobs offer, not what workers want', and paragraph 5 concludes that 'The division has in fact been made largely by the structure of jobs'.

option_rationales.A: This is the 'related account' the author reports in paragraph 2 and then criticises for treating hours as freely chosen.
option_rationales.B: The passage never says governments stopped legislating; 'rules on hours' appear in paragraph 5 only as one way the structure could be altered.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says productivity 'kept rising'; paragraph 5 locates the forecasters' mistake in how labour markets work, not in productivity estimates.

common_misconception: Choosing the status account because it is described in detail, without noticing that the author rejects its premise.

correct_answer: (D) some costs of employing a worker, such as recruitment and training, arise per person rather than per hour.
explanation: Paragraph 3: 'A firm that pays a fixed cost for each person it hires, in recruitment, training, benefits and supervision, has good reason to prefer fewer people working longer'.

option_rationales.A: Turnover among short-hours workers is never mentioned; the reason in paragraph 3 is a fixed cost per hire.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says long hours are a signal that firms reward with promotion, not something professionals demand from firms.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says nothing about productivity per hour; the reason given is the 'fixed cost for each person it hires'.

common_misconception: Reversing the direction of the signalling point that comes in the next sentence.

correct_answer: (C) illustrate that a trade of income for time that a worker wants may be unavailable or heavily penalised.
explanation: The lawyer would 'gladly trade a fifth of her salary for a fifth of her week' but may find the trade 'not on offer at all, or that it costs her far more than a fifth of her career'. This supports the claim that observed hours reflect what jobs offer.

option_rationales.A: The trade 'may' be 'not on offer at all, or' very costly; the passage does not claim part-time work has disappeared everywhere.
option_rationales.B: The quality of legal work is never discussed; long hours are described as 'a signal of commitment', not as a cause of better work.
option_rationales.D: The lawyer 'would gladly trade' salary for time, so the example shows the opposite preference, frustrated by the job.

common_misconception: Taking the lawyer's long hours as evidence of her preference, which is the premise the paragraph attacks.

correct_answer: (A) Where workers gained a legal right to cut their hours at proportionally lower pay, with no effect on promotion, very few used it.
explanation: The author's claim is that workers who want shorter hours cannot get them. If a genuine, penalty-free option to work less were offered and hardly anyone took it, observed hours would after all reflect what workers want, which directly weakens the claim.

option_rationales.B: This shows actual hours departing from desired hours, which is consistent with the author's view and appears in paragraph 4.
option_rationales.C: A gap between preferred and actual hours supports the author's claim that observed hours do not reveal what workers want.
option_rationales.D: Rising fixed costs per hire strengthen the author's explanation of why firms prefer fewer people working longer.

common_misconception: Choosing an option from the passage's own evidence, which supports rather than weakens the claim.

correct_answer: (B) compatible with longer weeks for some groups of workers and too few hours for others.
explanation: Paragraph 4: 'An average that holds steady can conceal one group working too much and another too little', following the example of professionals with longer weeks and lower-paid workers with too few hours.

option_rationales.A: The author denies that observed hours reveal preferences, and paragraph 4 says an average 'can conceal' opposite movements.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 5 says whether people would work less is 'an open question', so the author makes no such prediction.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 names a limitation of the institutional account, but nothing about a steady average refutes it.

common_misconception: Treating an average as information about every worker or about preferences.

correct_answer: (D) present an earlier explanation whose prediction is contradicted by the pattern reported in paragraph 2.
explanation: Paragraph 1 sets out the skill story and notes its 'defect of predicting a smooth gradient'. Paragraph 2 opens 'found instead was a hollowing out', which contradicts that prediction.

option_rationales.A: Producing graduates is the remedy the skill story offered; the author reports it, and paragraph 2 shows the story missed the pattern.
option_rationales.B: The author describes the skill story as having 'the defect of predicting a smooth gradient', so it is not the author's own account.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 describes the skill story, not the task view, and paragraphs 3 to 5 criticise the task view, so it is not defended without reservation.

common_misconception: Taking a view the author reports for the author's own.

correct_answer: (D) may rest on little more than the fact that the task has not yet been automated.
explanation: Paragraph 3: whether a task 'counts as routine is usually settled by asking whether it has in fact been automated', so using the label to predict automation is circular. A task called non-routine may simply be one that has not been automated so far.

option_rationales.A: The author criticises exactly this kind of relabelling 'after the event'; the passage does not endorse it.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says tasks 'once thought to demand judgement' are now candidates for automation, so judgement offers no permanent protection.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the task view 'explains a pattern the skill view could not', including growth at the bottom.

common_misconception: Choosing the relabelling option, which describes the practice the author criticises as if the author accepted it.

correct_answer: (C) Two insurers buy identical claims software; one cuts its claims clerks, while the other, whose tax rules favour keeping staff, trains them to settle complex claims.
explanation: Paragraph 4 argues that 'which tasks are automated is a decision made by firms' that depends partly on the tax system, and that 'The same software can be deployed to remove a clerk or to let her handle cases that once needed a specialist'. The insurers show the same technology used in opposite ways under different incentives.

option_rationales.A: This illustrates the skill story of paragraph 1, which paragraph 4 treats as sharing the task story's mistake.
option_rationales.B: This illustrates the circularity objection of paragraph 3, a different difficulty from the one raised in paragraph 4.
option_rationales.D: This illustrates the remark in paragraph 5 that some tasks 'really are cheaper to mechanise', not the point that firms choose how to use the same technology.

common_misconception: Choosing the typing pool because it involves automation, though it illustrates the limit stated in paragraph 5.

correct_answer: (A) how many years of schooling the workers in a task have typically completed.
explanation: Paragraph 4 names three influences: relative cost, tax treatment and managers' view of workers. Schooling belongs to the skill story of paragraph 1 and is not offered as an influence on the firm's decision.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the decision 'depends on what machines cost relative to people'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 lists 'how the tax system treats investment in equipment compared with spending on wages'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 lists 'whether managers regard workers as a cost to be reduced or a capacity to be developed'.

common_misconception: Recalling that schooling is discussed in the passage and assuming it must be among the listed factors.

correct_answer: (B) Changing how equipment is taxed could alter how far the middle of the wage scale shrinks, though not every task is equally easy to mechanise.
explanation: Paragraph 4 names the tax treatment of equipment as one influence on which tasks are automated, so a change in it could alter the extent of hollowing out. Paragraph 5 adds that 'Some tasks really are cheaper to mechanise than others', which the qualification in the correct answer preserves.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 begins 'None of this makes the task view wrong' and speaks of technology 'filtered through institutions', not institutions alone.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 5 warns against replacing one determinism 'with another in which every outcome is a choice', and paragraph 4 says polarisation is only 'partly' a matter of incentives.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 calls the category 'less solid than it appears', not useless, and paragraph 5 says some tasks 'really are cheaper to mechanise'.

common_misconception: Choosing the option that turns the author's 'partly' into 'rather than', the overcorrection paragraph 5 warns against.

correct_answer: (C) challenge the belief that a gold-backed currency protected people, while granting the concern for trustworthy money behind it.
explanation: Paragraph 1 states the belief, paragraphs 2 and 3 argue that gold discipline transferred risk to debtors and did not really bind governments, and paragraph 4 concedes that the underlying wish for trust is 'a legitimate demand' while saying institutions serve it better. The correct answer captures both the critique and the concession.

option_rationales.A: The passage gives no history of adoption or replacement; it evaluates the standard's effects and the case its admirers make for it.
option_rationales.B: This reverses the author's view: paragraph 4 says a rule no one made is one 'no one can sensibly adjust', and recommends accountable institutions instead.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 mentions the 1930s only to say that early leavers 'tended to recover earlier'; the passage makes no claim about what caused the depression, and the point is one piece of evidence, not the purpose.

common_misconception: Picking the 1930s detail as the main point, or misreading the closing sentences as praise for fixed rules.

correct_answer: (A) how quickly metal was mined and how it moved between countries, factors largely unrelated to what trade needed.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'the quantity of money depended on the pace of mining and on the flow of metal between countries, neither of which had much to do with the needs of trade.'

option_rationales.B: Savers' behaviour is never described as setting the quantity of money; the passage mentions savers only as the people the standard was supposed to protect.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the determinants had little 'to do with the needs of trade', which is the opposite of this option.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 names mining and flows of metal as the determinants; the discretion governments had (paragraph 3) concerned suspending convertibility and the official price, not setting the money supply at will.

common_misconception: Choosing the option about government issue because paragraph 1 says governments 'cannot issue what they do not hold'.

correct_answer: (B) illustrate how falling prices raise the real burden of a debt that is fixed in money terms.
explanation: The sentence before the example says that 'falling prices are hard on anyone who owes money'; the farmer's harvest fetches less while his debt stays the same, which illustrates that point and supports the conclusion that debtors bore the cost.

option_rationales.A: The passage says nothing about farmers being careless or about merchants; the farmer suffers because prices fell while 'the sum he owed stayed exactly the same'.
option_rationales.C: The harvest is said to have 'fetched less', a fall in price, not in quantity; the passage never says harvests shrank.
option_rationales.D: No deliberate scheme by creditors is described; the passage says only that debtors 'bore much of the cost', which is an effect, not a plot.

common_misconception: Reading the example as a claim about the size of harvests or about the motives of lenders.

correct_answer: (D) the impersonality that makes gold seem trustworthy is also what makes it unable to respond to changing conditions.
explanation: The passage presents the absence of a human author as gold's appeal ('the comfort of a rule that no one made') and, in the same breath, as its defect: no one can 'sensibly adjust' it. The same feature produces both, which is what the correct answer says.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says governments did alter the official price of gold, and the 'rule that no one made' refers to the supply set by geology, not to a decision by officials.
option_rationales.B: The author prefers institutions 'whose conduct can be observed, questioned and corrected', so the passage favours human judgement under scrutiny rather than condemning it.
option_rationales.C: The author does not accuse supporters of dishonesty; the sentence grants that gold 'offers the comfort' of an unmade rule and then names the cost of that very feature.

common_misconception: Taking the closing sentence as an attack on supporters, or as a general distrust of human judgement.

correct_answer: (C) the customers most likely to claim are staying in the pool while safer customers leave it.
explanation: Paragraph 2: the safe find the premium expensive and 'some of them leave'; the insurer, 'seeing claims rise relative to premiums, raises the price'. The pool is left with those more likely to claim.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 presents screening as a way to close the information gap; the passage never says that its cost drives premiums up.
option_rationales.B: Compulsion is offered in paragraph 3 as a remedy for unravelling, not as a cause of the price rises described in paragraph 2.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says unravelling 'can happen even though no one has lied to anyone'; concealment is not the mechanism described.

common_misconception: Assuming that adverse selection requires dishonesty by buyers.

correct_answer: (B) a premium matching one's own expected cost leaves nothing of the bad luck shared with other people.
explanation: Insurance is valuable because the lucky help pay for the unlucky. If the premium equals the expected cost of one's own condition, the buyer is simply paying for his own treatment in advance, so the risk is not pooled. Paragraph 3 makes the point that 'a pool sorted precisely by risk is no longer sharing much risk at all'.

option_rationales.A: No law is mentioned; the passage is describing an economic effect of sorting, not a legal violation.
option_rationales.C: The person is 'quoted a premium', so cover is offered; the point is that the price removes its value, not that it is refused.
option_rationales.D: The passage speaks of the premium being close to the expected cost, not of exclusions; the policy would pay, but the buyer would have prepaid nearly all of it.

common_misconception: Reading 'no insurance' literally as a refusal to sell.

correct_answer: (A) A voluntary repair plan for old cars loses its owners of well-kept cars after each price rise, until only owners of failing cars stay enrolled.
explanation: Unravelling (paragraph 2) is a cycle: safe buyers leave, the price rises, the next safest leave, until only the riskiest remain. The correct answer reproduces that cycle without any dishonesty; the other options describe fraud, compulsion and risk pricing respectively.

option_rationales.B: This describes the compulsory remedy in paragraph 3, which keeps the pool mixed; it is the opposite of a pool shrinking.
option_rationales.C: Deliberate damage concealed from the insurer is dishonesty, whereas paragraph 2 stresses that unravelling 'can happen even though no one has lied to anyone'; the mechanism is the exit of safe buyers.
option_rationales.D: This is the first remedy, sorting by risk, which paragraph 3 says erodes pooling; it is not the spiral of exits and price rises that defines unravelling.

common_misconception: Confusing unravelling with the remedies described in paragraph 3, or with fraud.

correct_answer: (D) conditionally accepting: fair for risks people take on by choice, but troubling for risks imposed by birth or chance.
explanation: Paragraph 4 draws a line: for risks 'people largely take on by choice' pricing by risk 'seems fair enough', while for risks that 'arrive at birth or by pure chance' it looks like 'penalising people twice'. The attitude depends on the kind of risk.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says pricing by risk 'seems fair enough' for chosen risks, and paragraph 3 notes compulsion is not free either, so the author opposes neither remedy outright.
option_rationales.B: The author does take a view, calling it fair for chosen risks and like 'penalising people twice' for risks of birth or chance.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 rejects treating the choice as 'a technical matter for actuaries' and calls sorting by inborn risk penalising people twice.

common_misconception: Treating the author's sympathy for those born with costly conditions as total opposition to risk pricing.

correct_answer: (C) depositors acting sensibly on a rumour bring about the very trouble that the rumour had wrongly alleged.
explanation: Paragraph 1: each depositor is better off withdrawing first, so a run is rational 'whether or not the rumour is true', and 'once enough people run, the rumour becomes true'. Hurried loan sales create the losses, so it fails 'because it was believed to be' unsound.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 stipulates that the loans 'are prudent and its borrowers will repay'; the failure happens despite this.
option_rationales.B: The passage says it is 'rational to run whether or not the rumour is true', so the depositors are not acting irrationally.
option_rationales.D: Deposit insurance is introduced only in paragraph 2, and paragraph 1 describes no risk-taking; the institution is sound throughout.

common_misconception: Equating a panic with irrational behaviour, when the passage stresses that each withdrawal is individually rational.

correct_answer: (B) a guarantee that is believed removes the motive to run, so the promised payment rarely has to be made.
explanation: Paragraph 2 explains the phrase in the same sentence: insurance is 'a promise that, by being believed, makes its own fulfilment unnecessary'. Because no one runs, 'the guarantee is seldom called upon', so it seems to deliver stability at almost no cost.

option_rationales.A: Premiums are not discussed; the 'lunch' is free because the promise prevents the runs it insures against, not because depositors pay nothing.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 presents the optimistic view before any objection; the hidden cost of recklessness is the critics' point in paragraph 3, not the meaning of the phrase.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says nothing about who pays for the scheme; the point concerns the guarantee seldom being called upon.

common_misconception: Importing the objection of paragraph 3 into the meaning of a phrase that states the case for insurance.

correct_answer: (D) Before guarantees existed, depositors steadily moved money away from banks with weaker loan books, well before any panic, and these banks then lent more cautiously.
explanation: The author's reply rests on the claim that ordinary depositors 'were never skilled readers of loan books' and so supplied only indiscriminate panic. Evidence that they once discriminated quietly and effectively between weak and strong banks attacks that premise directly, implying that guarantees do remove genuine scrutiny.

option_rationales.A: This confirms the premise of the objection, which the author grants; the author's reply is that such watching was never valuable, so showing that insured depositors do not watch leaves it intact.
option_rationales.B: When limits were raised says nothing about whether depositors once supplied useful scrutiny, which is the premise of the author's reply; the option is on topic but bears on neither side.
option_rationales.C: This supports the author: it confirms that depositor discipline was 'indiscriminate, striking prudent and imprudent banks without distinction'.

common_misconception: Choosing the survey of inattentive depositors, which sounds damaging to deposit insurance but only restates the objection the author has already granted.

correct_answer: (A) unwise, because it would remove the incentive of large creditors who are among the few equipped to scrutinise banks.
explanation: Paragraph 4 assigns scrutiny to supervisors and to 'the large uninsured creditors whose money remains at stake', and says the limit on cover 'decides who still has a reason to care'. Unlimited cover would leave those creditors with no stake.

option_rationales.B: The author thinks ordinary depositors were 'never skilled readers of loan books', so requiring them to read the books is no remedy on the author's view.
option_rationales.C: The author says 'the limit on cover matters a great deal, since it decides who still has a reason to care'; removing the limit ignores this warning.
option_rationales.D: The author's worry is not about small depositors, whose attention the author thinks was worthless, but about the 'large uninsured creditors whose money remains at stake'.

common_misconception: Assuming that because the author defends deposit insurance the author would favour more of it without limit.

correct_answer: (C) in both cases resources pass from the public to the authority that collects or issues the money.
explanation: Paragraph 1: 'In one respect the analogy with taxation is exact: resources move from the public to the issuer of money'.

option_rationales.A: The point about who bears the burden is made in paragraph 2 by critics; it is not the respect in which paragraph 1 calls the analogy exact.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says of the inflation tax that 'no collector calls', so this is a respect in which the two differ.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says of the inflation tax that 'No law is passed', and paragraph 2 contrasts it with taxes that must be voted upon.

common_misconception: Picking the distributional point from paragraph 2 because it is the critics' main complaint.

correct_answer: (B) It sets limits on the inflation-tax idea by noting cases in which inflation involves neither intention nor much gain.
explanation: Paragraph 3 opens with 'The analogy misleads, however, when it is pressed too far' and gives two limits: some inflation is unchosen, and with interest-bearing deposits the gain from mild inflation is small. Paragraph 4 then restores the idea for the cases where it applies, so paragraph 3 qualifies rather than refutes.

option_rationales.A: The historical comparison is made in paragraph 1; paragraph 3 qualifies the analogy rather than tracing its history.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says 'much inflation' has such causes, not all of it, and paragraph 4 goes on to endorse the idea where inflation is high and persistent.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 makes the opposite point about deposits: because their interest rises with inflation, the state's revenue from mild inflation 'is modest'.

common_misconception: Treating a qualification as an outright rejection.

correct_answer: (A) is collected mainly from people with large incomes, who are able to move their wealth abroad.
explanation: Paragraph 2 gives three complaints: the inflation tax is hidden and unvoted, it hits cash savers and fixed incomes, and it benefits debtors including the state. Nowhere does the passage say it falls on people with large incomes; it says the reverse, that it falls on 'those least able to protect themselves'.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says it 'benefits anyone whose debts shrink in real value', and that the state is often among the largest debtors.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 names exactly these households as 'least able to protect themselves', so this reason is given.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says a tax on incomes 'must be proposed, debated and voted upon' while the inflation tax does not; this is a reason the critics give.

common_misconception: Overlooking that the correct answer reverses the passage's claim about who bears the burden.

correct_answer: (D) Whether a period of inflation deserves to be called a tax depends on examining who gained from it, not only on how much prices rose.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says the concept is best treated as 'a tool of diagnosis rather than as a verdict reached in advance' and that the right question is 'who gains?'. The correct answer states this: the label depends on an inquiry into gain, which paragraph 3 shows is not settled by the bare fact of rising prices.

option_rationales.A: The author says the language is 'accurate description' when inflation is high and persistent and the state is a heavy debtor, so the idea still applies today.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says calling inflation a tax attributes 'intention' where there may be none; inflation from a failed harvest also shrinks state debt, yet the author would not call it a tax.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says that for inflation that 'arrives from abroad' the language of taxation 'obscures more than it reveals'; the author would reject this description.

common_misconception: Choosing the option about government debt, which echoes paragraph 2 but ignores paragraph 3's insistence on intention.

correct_answer: (D) people expect the loosening and raise wages and prices beforehand, which cancels its effect on output.
explanation: Paragraph 1: 'Because the public comes to anticipate this, it builds the expected inflation into wages and prices in advance, so that the boost to output never materialises'.

option_rationales.A: The passage says only that 'only the inflation remains', not that output ends up lower than before; the option adds a net loss that is not stated.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 describes what happens when governments control money; independence is offered as the remedy, not as the reason the boost fails.
option_rationales.C: No reversal or electoral punishment is mentioned; the passage says the boost 'never materialises' because it was anticipated.

common_misconception: Supposing that the remedy of independence is part of the mechanism it is meant to cure.

correct_answer: (B) A city council sets a target for reducing road deaths, and a safety agency decides how to meet it and must explain any shortfall publicly.
explanation: Paragraph 3: 'A legislature can fix the target ... and require the central bank to explain in public whenever it misses; that body then decides how to reach the target'. The correct answer keeps exactly that division: elected body sets the end, agency chooses the means, with public explanation of misses.

option_rationales.A: Here the elected body keeps the instruments too, so there is no delegation of means and no commitment device of the kind paragraph 3 describes.
option_rationales.C: Balancing several goals is the situation paragraph 4 warns about, in which the agency's choices become political; it is not the paragraph 3 settlement.
option_rationales.D: This delegates goals as well as instruments, which is precisely the independence of goals that paragraph 3 distinguishes from the settlement.

common_misconception: Choosing the multi-goal option, which mirrors paragraph 4 rather than paragraph 3.

correct_answer: (A) Delegating only the means of monetary policy can reconcile credibility with democracy, though the reconciliation weakens as mandates widen.
explanation: The passage reports two views, reconciles them in paragraph 3 by separating independence in the 'choice of instruments' from independence in the 'choice of goals', and in paragraph 4 says the settlement 'is stable, however, only while the mandate remains narrow'. The correct answer holds both the resolution and its limit.

option_rationales.B: This is the case reported in paragraph 1, and the author goes on to accept the democratic objection in part, so it is not the passage's conclusion.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 argues that wider mandates weaken the case for being 'left alone', not that trust has actually been lost; the option also omits the passage's main resolution.
option_rationales.D: This is the democratic objection of paragraph 2, which the author calls 'partly right' and then largely answers with the distinction between goals and instruments.

common_misconception: Mistaking one of the two reported positions for the author's own conclusion.

correct_answer: (C) A central bank told to support employment as well as stable prices has a weaker case against elected oversight than one with only a price target.
explanation: Paragraph 4: when central banks are asked to pursue extra goals such as employment, trading them off 'is itself a political judgement', and 'The more a central bank is asked to do, the weaker its claim to be left alone'. A bank with the wider mandate therefore has a weaker claim to be left alone, that is, a weaker case against oversight by elected bodies, than one confined to a price target.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says independence 'removes the temptation'; an appointed body does not face voters, so the passage implies the reverse.
option_rationales.B: The author says the arrangement 'answers much of the democratic objection', not all of it, and paragraph 4 shows how the objection returns as mandates grow.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says the gain from independence lies 'in credibility rather than in any superior cleverness', and paragraph 4 treats wider goals as a problem, not a sign of skill.

common_misconception: Choosing the option that overstates 'answers much of the democratic objection' into answering all of it.

correct_answer: (A) the usual moral view of debt is one-sided, since lenders who are paid to bear risk share responsibility for loans that fail.
explanation: Paragraph 2 states the thesis ('assigns the whole of the responsibility to one side of what is a two-sided contract'), paragraph 3 draws out consequences, and paragraph 4 concludes that 'obligation runs in both directions' and calls for a moral language recognising both duties.
