option_rationales.C: A charge that stopped imports would be the 'wall' the author contrasts with a lever; the lever works by changing other governments' choices, not by blocking trade.

common_misconception: Picking the high-charge option, which treats the charge as a barrier, the very idea the author sets aside.

correct_answer: (B) would think the charge of protectionism justified against a border charge lacking the design features just listed.
explanation: The final sentence concerns a charge that 'does none of these things', and says it will be read 'not unreasonably' as protectionism. The author thus grants the critics' reading in that case, while the previous sentence shows a well-designed charge might be accepted.

option_rationales.A: The author mentions retaliation only as a possible outcome that depends on design; no judgement that retaliation would be right is made.
option_rationales.C: 'Not unreasonably' means the reading is reasonable; this option reverses the phrase.
option_rationales.D: The preceding sentence says a well-designed charge 'has a chance of being accepted as what it claims to be', so the author limits the judgement to badly designed ones.

common_misconception: Extending the author's concession to every border adjustment.

correct_answer: (B) correct a widespread habit of treating heritability as a measure of how unchangeable a trait is.
explanation: Paragraph 1 names the error of hearing heritability as 'a claim about destiny', paragraphs 2 and 3 show why the reading fails, and paragraph 4 concludes that 'The fault lies not with the statistic but with the habit of reading it as a measure of fixity'. The passage exists to correct that habit.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says only that a gap between groups 'need not be' genetic; the passage never asserts that actual human group differences are environmental, so this overstates and widens its claim.
option_rationales.C: Breeding is mentioned in a single clause of paragraph 4 as an example of proper use; it is a detail, not the purpose of the passage.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says 'None of this makes heritability useless' and gives breeders and researchers as legitimate users, so the option reverses the author's view.

common_misconception: Choosing the option about group differences, which magnifies one paragraph into a sweeping empirical claim.

correct_answer: (A) the environmental differences among the children would have been removed, leaving mainly genetic ones.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says heritability would rise 'because the environmental differences had been taken away', so the differences that remain are largely genetic.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the rise would happen 'not because genes had become more powerful', which directly rejects this explanation.
option_rationales.C: The passage never discusses resemblance to parents; the explanation it gives is the removal of environmental differences.
option_rationales.D: Precision of measurement is not mentioned anywhere; the rise is explained by what varies in the group, not by how it is measured.

common_misconception: Picking the 'stronger genes' option, which the passage explicitly rules out.

correct_answer: (C) a trait built by a genetic programme can still show low heritability.
explanation: The example follows 'Second, a trait can be built almost entirely by genes and still show low heritability': fingers are built by a genomic programme, yet the variation in their number is 'mainly environmental'.

option_rationales.A: The passage says injury explains variation in finger number only; it makes no claim about most human traits, so the option overgeneralises.
option_rationales.B: The passage compares no such dependability; the example concerns what heritability measures, not which influence is more reliable.
option_rationales.D: That is the first consequence in paragraph 2, illustrated by identical upbringing; the finger example introduces the 'Second' consequence, which is a different point.

common_misconception: Attaching the example to the first consequence in the same paragraph.

correct_answer: (D) The gap between the towns could be produced entirely by differences between their schools or homes.
explanation: The towns correspond to the two plots in paragraph 3: within each, variation can be largely genetic, while the difference between them may be due 'entirely to the soil', here the schools or homes.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says a highly heritable trait 'may still be changed by changing the environment', so reading heritability as fixity is the error the passage attacks.
option_rationales.B: This is exactly the inference paragraph 3 calls 'the most consequential error'; high heritability within groups is compatible with a gap that 'has no genetic basis at all'.
option_rationales.C: The seed example in paragraph 3 shows that high heritability within each plot and a large gap between plots can coexist, so nothing here is contradictory.

common_misconception: Treating within-group heritability as evidence about the cause of a between-group gap.

correct_answer: (B) soon stops telling the receiver anything about the animal that sends it.
explanation: Paragraph 2 ends: 'A cheap signal could be produced by anyone, and a signal that anyone can produce soon carries no information.'

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 argues the reverse: the cost is 'the very thing that keeps the signal reliable', so cheapness is no ground for preference.
option_rationales.C: The antelope leap is offered in paragraph 3 as a display that 'could not be produced' by an unfit animal, the opposite of a signal anyone can produce.
option_rationales.D: The passage says nothing of cheap signals being replaced by more beautiful ones; it says only that they 'carry no information'.

common_misconception: Connecting the antelope example to cheap signals because both appear near the middle of the passage.

correct_answer: (A) the burden that an extravagant ornament places on the animal that carries it.
explanation: Paragraph 1 calls the peacock's tail 'an embarrassment' for a view of selection as an 'editor of waste', because it is heavy and dangerous. Paragraph 2 makes that very costliness the reason the signal is reliable.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says Darwin did propose an explanation, female preference; the embarrassment is the cost of the tail, not a gap in Darwin's work.
option_rationales.C: The passage describes the tail as 'awkward in flight', not the courtship as awkward; the embarrassment is the tail's cost to survival.
option_rationales.D: Female difficulty in judging males is never called an embarrassment; the word in paragraph 1 refers to the heavy, conspicuous tail.

common_misconception: Reading 'embarrassment' as a personal failure of Darwin's rather than as the costly trait.

correct_answer: (D) a display reveals quality only if weaker animals find it harder to bear than stronger ones do.
explanation: The preceding clause says a signal works when it is 'more expensive for weak individuals than for strong ones'. If the cost fell equally, every animal could bear it to the same degree and the display would not distinguish strong from weak.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says what matters 'is not that a signal is expensive in absolute terms', so tying reliability to sheer expense reverses the point.
option_rationales.B: The passage makes no claim about how costs are distributed among most real ornaments; the remark is about what would follow if costs were equal.
option_rationales.C: The remark concerns signals of equal cost, not the mere presence of ornaments; males with ornaments may still differ in how well they bear them.

common_misconception: Choosing the 'more expensive is more reliable' option, which keeps the theme of cost but misses the point about unequal cost.

correct_answer: (C) appreciative of what it explains while insistent that it does not explain everything.
explanation: The author presents the idea favourably in paragraphs 2 and 3, then limits it in paragraph 4: it 'explains why many displays can be trusted, not why every display exists'.

option_rationales.A: The author judges the idea explicitly, both in its favour and in the qualification 'not why every display exists', so the stance is not neutral.
option_rationales.B: The author calls it 'influential', extends it to antelope and says it 'explains why many displays can be trusted'; nothing suggests it lacks support.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says it would be 'a mistake ... to treat costliness as the whole story' and gives a rival mechanism, so the author is not unreserved.

common_misconception: Picking 'unreserved' after reading only the middle paragraphs.

correct_answer: (D) show that fitness can be a real property of an organism even when outcomes fail to display it.
explanation: Paragraph 2 calls fitness 'a disposition that holds whether or not it is ever displayed'. The glass that never breaks and the moth that dies by accident both show that a single outcome does not refute the disposition.

option_rationales.A: This reads the analogy literally; the glass is compared to the moth only in that both have dispositions that may go undisplayed.
option_rationales.B: The passage says fitness can be established 'independently', by measuring predation, before any outcome; the option reverses the point of the analogy.
option_rationales.C: The passage allows that chance can override fitness in particular cases, but it never ranks chance above traits in general.

common_misconception: Taking the analogy literally or as a claim about the power of chance.

correct_answer: (A) evidence that fitness and the actual record of reproduction are not the same thing.
explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that drift would be 'unintelligible' if fitness meant survival, because there would be 'no gap between expectation and outcome for chance to fill'. Drift therefore shows the gap between fitness and the reproductive record.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says biologists count offspring 'because propensities are hard to observe directly'; drift is not given as the reason.
option_rationales.C: The author says the distinction 'explains why biologists speak of drift', so drift supports rather than troubles the propensity view.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says only that in small populations 'the lucky can outbreed the fit'; that chance can override selection does not mean selection ceases to operate.

common_misconception: Overextending 'the lucky can outbreed the fit' into the claim that selection is absent.

correct_answer: (B) For most traits, the only available way to tell which variant raises expected reproduction is to see which variant has in fact left more offspring.
explanation: The reply depends on fitness being identifiable 'independently', by analysing traits as in the moth example. If, for most traits, fitness could be identified only through which variant reproduced more, the propensity would collapse back into the record and the complaint would regain force.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 cites failed predictions as proof that the theory is not a tautology, so this finding supports the author's reply.
option_rationales.C: The author expects this: paragraph 3 says 'the lucky can outbreed the fit' and treats such gaps as support for the propensity view, so it does not weaken the reply.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 already concedes that biologists 'often measure fitness by counting offspring' and argues that this is evidence for a disposition, not its definition.

common_misconception: Picking a fact that sounds damaging (unfit outbreeding fit, offspring counting, failed predictions) without checking that the author has already absorbed it.

correct_answer: (C) Predictions derived from natural selection have so far been confirmed whenever they were tested.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says predictions 'are tested constantly, and some fail', and treats those failures as the mark of a non-tautological theory. A claim that every prediction has been confirmed contradicts the passage.

option_rationales.A: Supported: paragraph 4 says 'careless writing can slide from the measurement to the definition'.
option_rationales.B: Supported: paragraph 2 says the dark moth's advantage can be established 'independently, by measuring how often birds find each kind of moth'.
option_rationales.D: Supported: paragraph 3 says 'in small populations the lucky can outbreed the fit'.

common_misconception: Assuming that an author defending a theory must claim its predictions always succeed.

correct_answer: (C) Termites, which lack that pattern of inheritance, have also evolved sterile castes.
explanation: Paragraph 3 lists three problems for the argument, the first being that 'Termites, whose inheritance has no such peculiarity, have sterile castes too'.

option_rationales.A: This is the puzzle in paragraph 1 that troubled Darwin; it is not one of the objections listed against the later argument.
option_rationales.B: This is the starting point of the argument in paragraph 3, so it cannot be evidence against it.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 offers this in support of the general kinship principle, not as evidence against the argument from inheritance.

common_misconception: Picking a statement that appears in the passage but plays a different role.

correct_answer: (D) sterile workers differ from other helpful relatives in how far they help, not in the kind of explanation they need.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says sterility 'is not an anomaly to be explained away' but lies on a continuum, so the same calculation of benefit, relatedness and cost that explains ordinary helping explains sterility, which is simply its limit.

option_rationales.A: A continuum concerns degree, not chronology; the passage says nothing about which form of helping appeared first.
option_rationales.B: The phrase places sterility at one end of a range of helping, which implies that milder helping exists elsewhere; the option restricts helping to sterile species.
option_rationales.C: The passage treats sterility as a strategy favoured when helping pays more, not as damage caused by the work of helping, so the option reverses the relation.

common_misconception: Reading 'continuum' as a sequence in time, or reversing cause and effect.

correct_answer: (A) present an appealing refinement of the kinship argument and then show why it proved inadequate.
explanation: Paragraph 3 introduces the 'almost too neat' argument from inheritance, notes it 'was widely taught', and then says 'It has not survived well', giving three objections.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'The lesson is not that kinship is irrelevant' and that the principle 'remains the best account', so the general argument survives.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 criticises the argument from peculiar inheritance, a later refinement; Darwin's family idea is developed in paragraph 2, not rejected.
option_rationales.D: Ecological conditions are introduced only in paragraph 4, and there they are combined with kinship rather than set against it.

common_misconception: Confusing the rejection of the refinement with rejection of kinship explanations as a whole.

correct_answer: (B) Two insect species with similar relatedness among nestmates might differ in whether sterile castes evolve, because of differences in their surroundings.
explanation: Paragraph 4 makes relatedness 'only one term in the calculation' and says ecological conditions raise the benefit of helping. Holding relatedness equal, different conditions could therefore lead to different outcomes.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says the general kinship principle 'remains the best account' of why workers can forgo reproduction, so this understates its role.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says ecological conditions 'can tip the balance even where relatedness is modest', so the author would reject this.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 cites multiple mating only as diluting relatedness and weakening one argument; it never says sterile castes then become impossible.

common_misconception: Treating the dilution of relatedness as fatal to sterile castes, which keeps the rejected argument's logic.

correct_answer: (D) a switch can alter a single structure while leaving the others in which the gene acts untouched.
explanation: Paragraph 3: 'a change to the gene itself would tend to disrupt many structures at once, whereas a change to one of its switches can alter a single structure and leave the rest alone'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says the toolkit genes themselves are shared 'across almost the entire animal kingdom', so the contrast is false.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says it is switch changes that alter when and where genes act 'without any change in the proteins', so this reverses the roles.
option_rationales.C: The passage says nothing about how often switch changes arise; its reason concerns the range of structures each change affects.

common_misconception: Reversing which change leaves the protein intact.

correct_answer: (B) a common design for the structures that the developmental genes bring into being.
explanation: Paragraph 4 contrasts the shared toolkit with a shared plan and then restates the point: common genes show 'a deep common ancestry of the control system, not a common design for what is controlled'.

option_rationales.A: The passage does not discuss the order in which organs appear; it glosses the idea as 'a common design for what is controlled'.
option_rationales.C: Nothing in the passage concerns purpose or direction in evolution; 'plan' refers to the design of the organs themselves.
option_rationales.D: That describes the toolkit, which the author accepts is shared; the sentence contrasts 'the shared toolkit' with 'a shared plan', so the two cannot mean the same thing.

common_misconception: Equating 'plan' with the toolkit itself, the very thing the sentence distinguishes it from.

correct_answer: (A) Concluding that the hearts of two distant animals must be built alike because the same gene starts heart formation in both.
explanation: The opposite error is 'assuming that similar genes imply similar forms'. Inferring the same heart construction from a shared starting gene is exactly that, just as a shared eye switch does not make fly and mouse eyes 'the same organ'.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 itself says the structures downstream of the switch 'were assembled separately', so the author holds this view rather than calling it an error.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says 'there is much truth in that' and explains why, so the author accepts this conclusion rather than treating it as a mistake.
option_rationales.D: This is the older error, that 'different forms require different genes'; the opposite error runs from similar genes to similar forms.

common_misconception: Choosing the older error because it is also called wrong in the same sentence.

correct_answer: (C) An expectation is overturned by a discovery, whose lesson is then accepted in part and guarded against overextension.
explanation: Paragraph 1 states the expectation and the surprise, paragraph 2 gives the eye evidence, paragraph 3 accepts the rewiring lesson ('much truth in that'), and paragraph 4 warns against the 'opposite error'.

option_rationales.A: No practical or medical uses are mentioned, and the final paragraph limits an inference rather than dismissing objections.
option_rationales.B: The passage does not stage two rival theories; it reports how one expectation was overturned and then qualifies the lesson drawn from that.
option_rationales.D: The passage does not reject a series of solutions or leave its question open; it grants that switch rewiring has 'much truth in' it and states a clear conclusion.

common_misconception: Seeing the older view and the newer enthusiasm as two rival theories weighed evenly.

correct_answer: (B) depend on a narrow range of foods, occupy small areas or breed slowly.
explanation: Paragraph 1: in ordinary times 'species with narrow diets, small ranges or slow breeding are more likely to vanish when conditions shift'.

option_rationales.A: The passage gives the marginal mammals as survivors of a mass extinction, not as typical victims of ordinary extinction.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 lists small size and dormancy as traits that mattered in the end-Cretaceous catastrophe, not as the factors at work in ordinary times.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says flourishing groups can be swept away in mass extinctions; it does not say this happens in ordinary times.

common_misconception: Carrying the catastrophe traits of paragraph 2 back to ordinary times.

correct_answer: (C) had not arisen as adaptations to the kind of crisis in which they turned out to be decisive.
explanation: The sentence before the word explains it: 'Such traits had not been selected for their value in a catastrophe of this kind, which no living lineage had experienced.' They were accidents relative to the crisis, not useless or random in effect.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says mass extinctions are not 'pure lotteries' and that survival in them 'is selective', so the option contradicts the author.
option_rationales.B: The passage says the traits were already present and 'had not been selected for their value in a catastrophe'; it never says they appeared after the impact.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says these traits 'determined survival in the aftermath', so they plainly gave an advantage.

common_misconception: Reading 'accidents' as meaning that survival was a lottery.

correct_answer: (A) Large mammals with specialised diets also died out at the end of the Cretaceous, while small mammals with varied diets survived.
explanation: The claim is that mammals survived because they 'passed through a narrow gate', not because they were superior. If being a mammal did not protect large specialised mammals, while the crisis traits of paragraph 2 did, survival tracked those traits rather than any general mammalian superiority.

option_rationales.B: This hints at a general superiority of mammals, the very reading paragraph 3 says their success does not support, so it does not strengthen the claim.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 already says a marginal group 'inherits an emptied world'; rapid diversification says nothing about whether their survival reflected superiority.
option_rationales.D: This suggests the dinosaurs were failing before the crisis, which supports the 'tournament' picture the author rejects and so weakens the claim.

common_misconception: Choosing the diversification option, which is consistent with the passage but neutral on the claim.

correct_answer: (D) Because the traits that mattered in mass extinctions were accidents, the survivors of those events were not selected at all.
explanation: Paragraph 4 insists that 'Survival in them is selective; it simply selects for different things.' The traits were accidents only in that they had not evolved for catastrophes; selection still acted on them, so the correct answer contradicts the author.

option_rationales.A: The author accepts this: it restates the last sentence, which calls for knowing 'how well they fitted their world' and 'which rare disasters' occurred.
option_rationales.B: The author accepts this: paragraph 4 says the survivors 'went on to diversify through ordinary selection once the crisis had passed'.
option_rationales.C: The author accepts this: paragraph 3 says a flourishing group 'would probably have continued to flourish under normal conditions' and yet was swept away.

common_misconception: Taking 'accidents' to mean that no selection took place.

correct_answer: (D) can speed up chemical reactions as well as carry information.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'RNA, it turned out, can not only carry information but also catalyse reactions', which is why a world in which RNA did both jobs would dissolve the chicken-and-egg problem.

option_rationales.A: The passage says information is stored in nucleic acids and calls RNA a relative of DNA; it does not say RNA stores most instructions, and that is not the discovery reported.
option_rationales.B: No such ability is reported; paragraph 3 says RNA building blocks are 'prone to fall apart in water', and paragraph 4 speaks only of 'modest accuracy'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the reverse: RNA's building blocks are 'hard to make without the help of enzymes'; simple ingredients describe reaction networks.

common_misconception: Choosing an option that attributes the metabolism camp's ingredients to RNA.

correct_answer: (B) the claim that a network without heredity has no means of building up improvements.
explanation: Paragraph 2 ends with the replicator camp's 'deeper argument' that a network 'cannot accumulate improvements, because there is nothing to record which variants did better'. The reply that heredity 'need not wait for a dedicated molecule' answers precisely that.

option_rationales.A: The discovery supports the RNA world, but the inheritance point addresses heredity, not the evidence of the protein-building machinery.
option_rationales.C: That difficulty is the metabolism camp's own objection to the RNA world in paragraph 3, so they are not responding to it.
option_rationales.D: That setting belongs to the metabolism camp's own account in paragraph 1; they would not be answering it.

common_misconception: Matching the reply to the nearest preceding point (the chemistry problem) instead of to the argument it answers.

correct_answer: (A) the absence of any earlier chemistry to supply materials and energy.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says metabolism theorists explain 'where the materials and energy for any such molecule came from'. The replicator camp's weakest claim is that replicators could form without such a setting, that is, 'in a chemical vacuum'.

option_rationales.B: The phrase concerns where materials and energy came from, as the preceding sentence on metabolism theorists makes clear, not whether selection had begun.
option_rationales.C: The weak claim concerns replicators assembling themselves, so the missing element is the supporting chemistry, not RNA itself.
option_rationales.D: This reads the phrase literally; paragraph 4 uses it for the replicator camp's weakest claim, that replicators formed without a supporting chemistry.

common_misconception: Taking the phrase literally, or confusing the missing chemistry with RNA.

correct_answer: (C) Accounts giving priority to replication or to self-sustaining chemistry are better read as describing successive stages than as rivals.
explanation: The passage sets out both camps, shows in paragraph 4 that each answers a different question, and concludes in paragraph 5 that the problem is 'one of sequence rather than of priority', with self-maintaining chemistry giving rise to inherited information.

option_rationales.A: This is the point of paragraph 4 only; the passage uses it as a step towards the claim in paragraph 5 that the two describe a sequence, so it is too narrow.
option_rationales.B: The author does not choose a side: paragraph 4 calls each answer 'hard to dispute' for its own stage, and paragraph 5 combines them.
option_rationales.D: The author does set aside 'which came first', but because it is the wrong framing, not because it is unanswerable; the lost rocks are mentioned only as limiting the details.

common_misconception: Choosing the paragraph 4 summary, which is accurate but only a step in the argument, or the 'unanswerable' option, which gives the right conclusion for the wrong reason.

correct_answer: (A) attacking claims that a staged account combining both views would not need to make.
explanation: The two weak claims are that replicators formed 'in a chemical vacuum' and that networks evolved 'indefinitely without anything like genes'. The sequence proposed in paragraph 5, chemistry first supplying the setting and replicators then taking over, asserts neither, so the points count only against the rival framing.

option_rationales.B: The unrecoverable details are mentioned in paragraph 5 as a limit on the author's own view; the easy points concern weak claims, not unanswerable questions.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says 'each side scores easy points' and names a weak claim on each side, so the points are not won by one camp alone.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 calls each camp's central answer 'hard to dispute' for its own stage; the points are scored against the 'weakest claim', not the central thesis.

common_misconception: Assuming the points refute a camp's main thesis, when the author says each thesis is hard to dispute.

correct_answer: (C) an end point reached by a route no one could repeat may still have been very likely to be reached.
explanation: The image follows the charge that contingency enthusiasts treat a particular history as 'proof that its outcome depended on that history, which does not follow'. A ball's unique path can still end in 'the only hollow', so a unique route is compatible with an all but inevitable result.

option_rationales.A: The image shows only that a unique history does not prove a contingent outcome; it does not claim that all outcomes are fixed in advance.
option_rationales.B: The point is that history alone does not prove dependence, not that history is useless; the author never dismisses lineage histories.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 accepts that a 'far larger number of forms' appeared once; the image targets a different inference made by the contingency school.

common_misconception: Overextending the image into a claim that outcomes are predetermined.

correct_answer: (B) even-handed, crediting each with a real insight while faulting how it treats evidence.
explanation: Paragraph 2 opens 'Each school has a strong case' and then criticises the convergence list as 'assembled after the fact' and the contingency inference as one that 'does not follow'. Paragraph 3 holds that both claims are compatible and 'probably true'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says 'each tends to treat the other's evidence as anecdote' as a fault of both, and paragraph 3 calls both views 'probably true'.
option_rationales.C: The author says only that 'much of the disagreement' dissolves, and treats the remaining question about intelligence as open and important.
option_rationales.D: The author criticises both schools' reasoning in paragraph 2 and offers a judgement of their own in paragraph 3, so the stance is not deferential.

common_misconception: Reading the reconciliation as refusal to judge, when it rests on criticism of both sides.

correct_answer: (D) Most supposed independent origins of eyes, wings and streamlined bodies turn out to descend from one shared ancestral form.
explanation: The functional-level half of the reconciliation, that a replay would 'very probably' produce seeing, swimming and flying organisms, rests on the recurrence of these designs as evidence that physical problems 'admit only a few good solutions'. If the recurrences were really inherited from a single origin, that evidence would vanish.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 states this as a limit on what the evidence shows; it bears on the separate question of intelligence, not on the two-level reconciliation.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 already grants this, and paragraph 3 assigns such unrepeated forms to the level of particular lineages, so it is consistent with the reconciliation.
option_rationales.C: This is what paragraph 3 itself predicts at 'the level of particular lineages', so it supports rather than weakens the reconciliation.

common_misconception: Choosing the unrepeated-forms option because it sounds like evidence for contingency against convergence.

correct_answer: (D) insufficient grounds for expecting a replay of evolution to produce a creature like us.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says the recurrence shows only that 'some problems have few solutions' and that on intelligence the evidence 'does not yet discriminate between the two views'. It is relevant to broad functions but not enough to predict a creature like us.

option_rationales.A: The author says 'a single case cannot reveal whether it was a likely destination or a fluke', so the author does not take the evidence to favour the fluke reading either.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the recurrence of eyes and wings 'does not tell us that every capacity we value is among those solutions', which denies this.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 uses that recurrence to predict that a replay would 'very probably' produce seeing and flying organisms, so it is relevant to some questions.

common_misconception: Choosing the 'fluke' option, which wrongly takes the author's scepticism about convergence as support for contingency.

correct_answer: (A) A town rebuilt after a flood would almost surely again have bakeries and schools, though chance would decide who ran them.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says broad functional roles recur because problems 'admit only a few good solutions', while 'which occupants of that space history happens to supply' is contingent. Bakeries and schools are the recurring roles; who runs them is the contingent occupancy.

option_rationales.B: Nothing in this case varies from year to year, so it shows only a fixed, recurring outcome; it lacks the second level at which chance decides the particular occupants of a recurring role.
option_rationales.C: This captures only contingency, with no level at which the replays reliably converge on the same broad outcome.
option_rationales.D: The similarity here comes from a shared source, which is not convergence on a solution arrived at independently.

common_misconception: Picking the river, which illustrates convergence alone, or the bridges, which mistake copying for convergence.

correct_answer: (B) argue that forest recovery should be judged by the lasting forest it produces rather than by the number of saplings that are planted.
explanation: Paragraph 1 states the thesis: counting saplings 'has quietly confused an input with an outcome'. Paragraphs 2 and 3 show the costs of that confusion and an alternative, and paragraph 4 concludes that success should be measured by land that 'becomes, and remains, a functioning forest'.

option_rationales.A: The minister with a spade in paragraph 1 illustrates why planting appeals to campaigns; the passage does not attack anyone's motives, and its target is the measure of success.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'None of this means that planting is always a mistake' and names cases where planting 'may be the only way to begin', so a blanket replacement contradicts the author.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 mentions why saplings die, but only as evidence that counting plantings hides losses; the passage offers no techniques for improving survival.

common_misconception: Overstating the argument into a rejection of all planting, which the last paragraph explicitly rules out.

correct_answer: (C) for several years after protection begins, the land looks like scrub and does not resemble visible progress.
explanation: Paragraph 3 ends: 'for some years the land looks like scrub, which is one reason it is undervalued: it does not look like progress.'

option_rationales.A: Grasslands appear in paragraph 2 as places where planting did harm; regeneration is said to need old roots, seed trees and living soil, not grassland.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says regeneration happens 'often more cheaply than planting', so the claim about higher cost reverses the passage.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the opposite: regenerating species are 'suited to the site because they arrived there by themselves'.

common_misconception: Reversing the cost comparison or the point about site suitability, both stated in the same paragraph.

correct_answer: (D) objects to the way the success of forest campaigns is measured, not to the act of planting trees itself.
explanation: The sentence follows the concession that planting is sometimes necessary. The 'spade' is planting itself, which the author accepts in some cases; the 'scoreboard' is the habit of measuring success by the number planted, which the next sentence replaces with the area of land that 'becomes, and remains, a functioning forest'.

option_rationales.A: The 'scoreboard' is the count of saplings used to report success; nothing in the passage describes campaigns competing with one another.
option_rationales.B: The spade stands for planting in general; the passage never compares volunteers with professionals.
option_rationales.C: Accepting the count is the opposite of the author's point; paragraph 4 replaces it with the area that remains forest after ten or twenty years.

common_misconception: Reading 'scoreboard' literally as competition rather than as the measure of success.

correct_answer: (C) One that fences off land near surviving seed trees, plants only on degraded plots with no seed source, and reports how much forest still stands after fifteen years.
explanation: The author wants campaigns judged by forest that 'becomes, and remains' after ten or twenty years, wants regeneration where seed trees and soil remain (paragraph 3), and accepts planting where no seed sources survive (paragraph 4). Only the correct answer combines all three.

option_rationales.A: Tending saplings addresses survival, but the programme still reports trees planted and plants everywhere, ignoring both the choice of site and the long-term measure the author proposes.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says that where soils are badly degraded or no seed sources survive, 'careful planting may be the only way to begin', so refusing to plant anywhere goes against the author.
option_rationales.D: Choosing a mix of species answers the problem of 'choice', but reporting saplings planted keeps the very scoreboard that paragraph 4 rejects, so losses would still go unrecorded.

common_misconception: Choosing the mixed-species option, which fixes one problem from paragraph 2 but keeps the count of saplings planted.

correct_answer: (A) the large area that such a predator needs, once protected, also shelters many other species living in it.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'A large predator needs a large area, and the forest or grassland that is protected for its sake also shelters thousands of less appealing species'.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says these species are ones 'no donor would have paid to save directly'; the benefit comes through shared habitat, not through donors changing their giving.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 mentions breeding programmes and collars as spending on the animal itself, precisely the case in which 'the advertising argument does not apply'.
option_rationales.D: The passage never describes the predator's effect on other animals; its point concerns the area protected 'for its sake'.

common_misconception: Supplying an ecological mechanism (predation) that the passage does not mention.

correct_answer: (B) give examples of habitats whose threatened species would gain nothing from the protection of a charismatic animal.
explanation: The list follows 'Some of the most threatened organisms live in habitats that no charismatic animal shares' and is followed by 'Protecting a tiger reserve will do nothing for them.' It marks the limit of the advertising defence.

option_rationales.A: Donors' refusals are not discussed in paragraph 3; the list describes where threatened organisms live, not where donors decline to give.
option_rationales.C: The author does not propose moving money from reserves; paragraph 4 keeps flagship species as 'a useful' tool and asks only that some effort follow need.
option_rationales.D: The passage compares no habitats for richness; the examples matter because no charismatic animal shares them, as the next sentence says.

common_misconception: Treating the examples as a recommendation to reallocate money, which the conclusion does not make.

correct_answer: (C) qualified approval: they are a useful means of raising attention and money but an incomplete guide to priorities.
explanation: Paragraph 2 defends flagship species, paragraph 3 limits the defence, and paragraph 4 concludes they are 'a tool ... and a useful one' while insisting 'Some part of the effort has to be directed by need rather than by appeal'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 draws an explicit conclusion of its own, 'The sensible conclusion is ...', so the author is not neutral.
option_rationales.B: The author accepts the advertising defence only 'up to a point' (paragraph 3) and lists species it leaves out, so the complaint is not answered.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the sensible course is 'neither to abandon flagship species' nor to rely on them alone, so the author does not want them dropped.

common_misconception: Choosing enthusiasm because of paragraph 2, without weighing the limits set out in paragraph 3.

correct_answer: (D) spent on protecting the habitat that the animal shares with many other species, rather than on the animal alone.
explanation: The defence in paragraph 2 works because the money 'is spent, at least in part, on soil, water and cover that serve everything living there'. Paragraph 3 says it fails when money is spent on the animal itself. So the donation does most for neglected species when it goes to the shared habitat.

option_rationales.A: The passage does not say drab species are generally more threatened, and the donor's awareness does not change what the money protects.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says that when money is spent 'on that animal directly, on breeding programmes', the advertising argument 'does not apply at all'.
option_rationales.C: Who appears in the pictures does not decide what is protected; the passage ties the benefit to how the money 'is spent'.

common_misconception: Picking the breeding option because it helps a threatened animal, missing that paragraph 3 excludes it from the defence.

correct_answer: (B) pay only for the market value of damaged crops and leave out losses such as sleep, schooling and constant fear.
explanation: Paragraph 3: schemes 'pay for the market value of a damaged crop while ignoring the sleepless nights, the children kept from school to guard fields and the fear that hangs over every harvest'.

option_rationales.A: The passage does not say who runs the schemes; their faults are delay, paperwork and narrow valuation.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says schemes pay 'a fraction of the loss', the reverse of overpayment, and never suggests they discourage guarding.
option_rationales.D: Nothing in paragraph 3 links payment to retaliation; the obstacles named are slowness and paperwork for poor households.

common_misconception: Inventing a reason (who runs the schemes) that sounds plausible but is not given.

correct_answer: (A) records that farmers have suffered a loss while leaving most of that loss with the farmers who suffered it.
explanation: The scheme pays 'a fraction of the loss, a year late'. The burden stays where it was (it is not shifted), and the payment serves only to acknowledge or record that the loss occurred.

option_rationales.B: The passage never mentions records of elephant movements; what is documented is the burden itself, the farmers' loss.
option_rationales.C: Paperwork is one fault mentioned earlier, but the passage does not compare its cost with the payment; 'documents' refers to recording the loss, not to forms costing money.
option_rationales.D: To 'not shift the burden' means the cost is not transferred; a scheme that paid in full, even late, would contradict the author's point about 'a fraction of the loss'.

common_misconception: Taking 'documents' literally as paperwork, a detail from the same paragraph.

correct_answer: (C) Farmers who had lost nothing to elephants were as likely to retaliate as those with heavy losses, and retaliation fell sharply after lessons on the animals' role.
explanation: The author argues that hostility reflects inability to bear costs, not lack of understanding (paragraph 2). If hostility were unrelated to losses and disappeared once farmers were taught about elephants, ignorance would be the better explanation, which weakens the claim.

option_rationales.A: This fits the author's distributive framing in paragraphs 3 and 4, since it ties hostility to how costs are borne rather than to ignorance.
option_rationales.B: This supports the author: a farmer may 'understand their ecological importance perfectly well' and still be hostile, so knowledge and hostility coexist.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 already concedes that tolerance 'is shaped by tradition as well as by loss', so this finding is consistent with the passage and does not show hostility is ignorance.

common_misconception: Choosing the tradition option, which sounds like a challenge but repeats the concession the author already makes.

correct_answer: (B) a remedy that lowers one village's losses may only pass them to neighbours, leaving the wider question of who pays unresolved.
explanation: Paragraph 4 grants that deterrents work locally but says they 'move the problem as often as they solve it'. The next sentence states that 'The underlying question remains political', so the remark shows that technical fixes redistribute costs among those already bearing them instead of transferring them to the wider society.

option_rationales.A: The author proposes no coordination; the conclusion turns instead to whether 'the wider society' will pay those who live beside elephants.
option_rationales.C: Moving damage from one village to the next does not make costs even, and paragraph 1 says they are 'concentrated on a few villages'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says that 'where these work they reduce losses at modest cost'; the remark is about losses moving, not about deterrents failing or elephants learning.

common_misconception: Reading the remark as saying deterrents do not work, when the passage says they do work locally.

correct_answer: (A) cleared away the material on the forest floor while leaving most of the older, thick-barked trees unharmed.
explanation: Paragraph 2: frequent low-intensity fires 'cleared the undergrowth, fallen branches and young trees that gather on the forest floor, while leaving the older, thick-barked trees largely unharmed'.

option_rationales.B: The low-intensity fires described in paragraph 2 came before suppression; deliberate burning appears only in paragraph 4 as a modern remedy.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the opposite: these fires cleared 'young trees' and undergrowth while 'leaving the older, thick-barked trees largely unharmed'.
option_rationales.D: Climbing into the crowns is what the later, large fires did after fuel accumulated; the earlier fires stayed small and on the forest floor.

common_misconception: Confusing the earlier small fires with the later crown fires described in the same paragraph.

correct_answer: (D) the planting of fast-growing, thin-barked trees in place of the older species of dry forests.
explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 name accumulated fuel, drought, heat and the spread of housing into wooded land. No change in tree species through planting is mentioned anywhere; the thick-barked trees are said to be killed by the large fires, not replaced by planting.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 lists 'the spread of housing into wooded land' among the causes of catastrophic fire besides suppression.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says 'drought, heat and the spread of housing into wooded land matter as well'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 describes exactly this accumulation of fuel, which allows a fire to 'climb into the crowns of the trees'.

common_misconception: Recognising 'thick-barked' from paragraph 2 and assuming the option restates it.

correct_answer: (D) a genuine danger to that forest, not a sign that fire is returning to its natural place there.
explanation: Paragraph 3: in 'some wet forests and many shrublands fire was historically rare, and a recent increase in burning there is a threat rather than a return to normal'. Whether a fire harms 'depends on the ecosystem in which it burns'.

option_rationales.A: Housing is named as one factor among several in paragraph 3; nothing allows the author to assign this single cause to an unspecified case.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the suppression lesson 'is sometimes drawn too broadly' and singles out wet forests as places where fire was rare, so the author would not extend it there.
option_rationales.C: The claim that fires do this in 'every forest' is the overbroad lesson the author rejects; paragraph 3 says the argument 'is not that fire is good'.

common_misconception: Applying the dry-forest lesson to every forest, the overgeneralisation that paragraph 3 warns against.

correct_answer: (B) a manager may keep suppressing fires even when aware that doing so raises the risk of catastrophic fire later.
explanation: The harm of acting (a planned burn) is 'visible and attributable', while the harm of not acting is 'deferred and diffuse', so 'the easiest course is to keep doing what made the problem worse'. This holds even for managers who recognise the problem, as the paragraph's first sentence implies.

option_rationales.A: The passage says the reverse: an escaped burn 'is blamed on the people who lit it' while a fuel-driven wildfire 'is blamed on nature'.
option_rationales.C: The passage says planned burns carry visible and attributable risks, not that their total harm exceeds that of large wildfires; the asymmetry concerns blame and timing.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph opens with 'Recognising this has not made the remedy easy', so the problem is incentives, not a lack of understanding.

common_misconception: Choosing the ignorance option, which overlooks 'Recognising this' at the start of the paragraph.

correct_answer: (A) Because exclusion carries certain costs and often only assumed benefits, removing residents from protected land should be justified in each case rather than treated as the default.
explanation: Paragraph 4 sums up: the critique establishes 'not a rule but a burden of proof'. Exclusion has 'certain and heavy costs' while its benefits 'are often assumed rather than shown', so it 'must be defended, case by case, rather than taken as the natural form of protection'.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 uses the romantic image only to qualify the critique; the passage keeps both protection and residents' share in management, rejecting neither.
option_rationales.C: The author concludes with 'not a rule but a burden of proof'; replacing parks with community management everywhere is itself a rule the passage does not propose.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 rejects the view that 'exclusion is never justified', and paragraph 4 allows exclusion where use is absent or demonstrably incompatible.

common_misconception: Picking the option that matches the critique in paragraph 2 and missing the qualification in paragraph 3.

correct_answer: (C) started an unplanned change in which some of the qualities that made the places worth protecting declined.
explanation: Paragraph 2: removal 'began a new and unplanned experiment, and in some cases the very qualities that had made the place worth protecting began to decline'.

option_rationales.A: Grasslands were kept open 'by grazing and deliberate burning' under the residents; the passage says nothing of grazing animals moving freely after removal.
option_rationales.B: The passage says these losses came 'often with little or no compensation', the reverse of fair compensation.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says removal 'did not return the land to an original state'; it began 'a new and unplanned experiment'.

common_misconception: Accepting the founding picture of the parks, which the paragraph says was 'historically false'.

correct_answer: (D) It guards the critique of fortress conservation against an opposite oversimplification before the author states a conclusion.
explanation: After paragraph 2 criticises the image of untouched wilderness, paragraph 3 warns that 'The romantic image of the timeless forest dweller can be as misleading', and concedes that some exclusion may be justified. This prepares the balanced 'burden of proof' conclusion in paragraph 4.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says a population 'may, under new pressures' overharvest; it is a possibility, not evidence about most communities.
option_rationales.B: The founders' picture is described in paragraph 1 and refuted in paragraph 2; paragraph 3 turns to a different error, the romantic image of the forest dweller.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says it would be 'too simple' to treat residents as always the best stewards; it does not make exclusion usually better, and paragraph 4 keeps the presumption in favour of residents with a compatible record.

common_misconception: Reading a concession as a reversal of the author's position.

correct_answer: (A) A cliff used by a seabird that deserts its nests at slight disturbance, where counts show breeding fails whenever people enter, and which no community has ever used.
explanation: Paragraph 4 allows exclusion 'Where that record is absent, or where a species' needs are demonstrably incompatible with human use'. The seabird case meets both conditions: no history of use, and evidence that any presence causes breeding to fail.

option_rationales.B: The fishing record is long and compatible with stable fish numbers; relying on a general belief is exactly the assumption paragraph 4 rejects as a basis for exclusion.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 suggests such grassland may depend on the herders' grazing and burning, and visitors' preferences are not a reason the passage accepts for exclusion.
option_rationales.D: The village has a long record of use and the harm is only 'probably' so, a benefit 'assumed rather than shown'; paragraph 4 puts the presumption with the residents here.

common_misconception: Choosing the forest case because it mentions rare birds, overlooking that the harm is only assumed and that use is long established.

correct_answer: (B) whether a species has outsized influence depends on the community and conditions in which it lives.
explanation: The sentence sums up paragraph 2: the same species 'may have a dominant influence in one place and a minor one in another, depending on what else lives there, on the climate and on the history of the site'.

option_rationales.A: This is the 'fixed attribute' view the sentence rejects; paragraph 2 says the same species may have 'a minor one in another' place.
option_rationales.C: 'Relationship' refers to a species' role within a given community, not to partnerships; the rocky-shore example concerns predators and prey in different places.
option_rationales.D: The rocky shore is one example of a setting; the passage does not limit keystones to any habitat type.

common_misconception: Taking 'relationship' in its everyday sense of a partnership.

correct_answer: (C) incomplete, since it leaves out the particular system in which the predator's influence was found.
explanation: Paragraph 4 warns against 'treating the label as a discovery about a species' nature rather than a finding about a particular system'. An unqualified statement does just that, so the author would see it as missing the setting.

option_rationales.A: Measuring it in one community is exactly what the author warns against generalising from, since the role may be 'minor' elsewhere.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'Some species really do have outsized and well-documented effects', so the author does not deny keystone effects.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says a keystone strategy 'may' neglect diffuse interactions; 'always' overstates it, and paragraph 4 values naming species.

common_misconception: Choosing 'false', which overstates the critique into a denial that keystones exist.

correct_answer: (B) In a meadow, removing any single species of grazing insect changed little, but removing several of them together altered the plant community sharply.
explanation: Paragraph 3 claims that in many communities 'influence is spread across several species, each of moderate importance, whose combined effects' keep the system stable. A case where no single removal matters but the joint removal does is direct evidence of such diffuse influence.

option_rationales.A: This supports paragraph 2's point that influence depends on the setting; it says nothing about influence being spread across several species, which is the claim of paragraph 3.
option_rationales.C: This is a classic keystone case of one species with outsized effect; it illustrates the concept the paragraph says is not the only pattern, so it does not strengthen that paragraph.
option_rationales.D: This illustrates the persuasive value of the label mentioned in paragraphs 1 and 4; it does not show that influence is diffuse or that diffuse interactions are neglected.

common_misconception: Choosing the two-coasts finding, which is true to the passage but supports paragraph 2 rather than paragraph 3.

correct_answer: (C) appreciative of its value as a memorable idea but wary of its being taken as a general model of communities.
explanation: The author credits the concept with being 'enormously useful' (paragraph 1) and refuses to discard it (paragraph 4) while warning against treating it as a fixed property or a general model.

option_rationales.A: The author cares a great deal about accuracy, devoting paragraphs 2 and 3 to its misleading assumptions.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 begins 'None of this means the concept should be discarded', so the author is not dismissive.
option_rationales.D: The final sentence says it should not be used 'as a model of how communities are generally built', the opposite of this view.

common_misconception: Treating the strong criticism in paragraphs 2 and 3 as a rejection.

correct_answer: (D) show that the label of invader turns on how a species travelled rather than on anything about the species or what it does.
explanation: Paragraph 1 argues that native status 'rests on a choice that is not itself ecological'. The two plants make the same crossing, and only the one carried by people is called an invader, so the label depends on the manner of arrival, not on the plant or its effects.

option_rationales.A: Speed and distance of spread are never compared; the example sets two plants making the same crossing side by side to show that only the means of travel differs.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 makes no recommendation about protection; the author's own position, given in paragraph 4, allows a presumption against newly arrived species.
option_rationales.C: The passage compares no harms in paragraph 1; the example concerns what the plant is called, and paragraph 3 later says even newcomers are not 'more likely to be harmful'.

common_misconception: Reading the example as a claim about harm or speed of spread, which the paragraph does not discuss.

correct_answer: (A) whether the effects of an introduced species can be known at the time when a decision about it has to be taken.
explanation: After two concessions, paragraph 3 states the objection: 'their alternative assumes that effects can be known at the moment a decision has to be made, and this is often false'. The rest of the passage builds on this point about timing and knowledge.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 opens 'The critics are right that origin is not itself a harm', so on this point the author agrees with them.
option_rationales.C: The author denies this in paragraph 3: the lack of shared history 'does not make the newcomer more likely to be harmful', so it is not what divides the author from the critics.
option_rationales.D: The author concedes this too, saying the critics are 'right that much eradication has been undertaken without asking whether the target was doing any damage'.

common_misconception: Choosing the option about newcomers being more harmful, which sounds like the traditional view the critics attack but which the author explicitly rejects.

correct_answer: (B) Introduced species that eventually caused serious harm could almost always still be removed cheaply once that harm became evident, even decades after they arrived.
explanation: The presumption is justified because 'the decision cannot wait for the evidence': paragraph 3 says that by the time harm is plain 'removal has usually become impossible'. If late removal were cheap and effective, decisions could wait for the evidence of effects, and the reason for acting on origin would fall away.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 already says long-established species should be judged by 'what it is shown to do'; the finding concerns that later stage and leaves the case for acting early untouched.
option_rationales.C: This adds to paragraph 1's point that the cut-off date 'is a convention', which the author accepts; the case for the presumption rests on uncertainty and the cost of delay, not on the date.
option_rationales.D: This supports paragraph 3, which says a newcomer's behaviour 'is harder to forecast than that of a species whose relationships have been worked out over a long time'.

common_misconception: Choosing the finding about long-established species being harmless, which bears on the critics' general view but not on the argument for acting early.

correct_answer: (D) weakens as the species' effects in its new home become observable, so that in time those effects should carry the decision.
explanation: Paragraph 4: origin's 'weight changes with time'. At arrival a presumption is reasonable; once a species is established and 'its effects can be observed', the case for removal 'should rest on what it is shown to do'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the newcomer's lack of shared history 'does not make the newcomer more likely to be harmful', so the case cannot rest on greater harm.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says of such a species that 'the presumption has done its work' and that 'the label alien then adds little', so its force does not stay equal.
option_rationales.C: The author places the presumption at arrival, before effects are known, because 'the decision cannot wait for the evidence'; waiting for rapid spread is what paragraph 3 warns against.

common_misconception: Choosing the option about rapid spread, which confuses the evidence the critics want with the moment the author thinks a decision must be made.

correct_answer: (C) taking away cover that native animals had come to rely on, as well as through chemicals and disturbed ground.
explanation: Paragraph 2: campaigns 'can do damage of their own, through herbicides, through disturbance of the ground, or by stripping out shelter on which native animals had come to depend'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 lists herbicides, ground disturbance and loss of shelter; the spreading of seeds during removal is never mentioned.
option_rationales.B: Pollinators appear in paragraph 2 as being fed by introduced species 'where native flowers have been lost', not as victims of removal campaigns.
option_rationales.D: Nothing in the passage refers to replacement species; the harms of campaigns named in paragraph 2 are money spent, herbicides, disturbance and lost shelter.

common_misconception: Picking the pollinator option because pollinators appear in the same paragraph.

correct_answer: (A) By declining to name an end state, rewilding does not remove human choice but moves it to the start of the process, which its advocates should admit.
explanation: Paragraph 5 states the conclusion: rewilding achieves 'not the withdrawal of human choice from the landscape but its relocation, from the end of the process to its beginning', and the method is 'more honest' when 'its advocates own those decisions'.

option_rationales.B: This is the objection of paragraph 3, which the author treats as partly answered; paragraph 5 says the argument 'is not an argument against rewilding' and calls it possibly 'the most sensible response'.
option_rationales.C: This is the advocates' case from paragraph 2; the author concludes that 'letting nature decide' conceals decisions people have already made, so outcomes are not left entirely to nature.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 calls this only 'a partial reply' and says it 'does not dissolve the difficulty', because choosing processes is itself a choice about outcomes.

common_misconception: Choosing the advocates' view or the critics' view, each of which the passage presents fairly before qualifying it.

correct_answer: (B) what a rewilding project will produce can often be foreseen from choices made at its start, even though no end state was named.
explanation: The example closes the argument that 'the choice of processes is itself a choice about outcomes' and that 'often these consequences can be foreseen': 'those who set the density know this'. So the outcome, though not named, is largely settled by the starting choices.

option_rationales.A: The passage makes no recommendation about density or about which landscape is preferable; the example shows only that different densities produce different landscapes.
option_rationales.C: The passage never ranks herbivore density against flooding; both are listed as processes whose choice shapes the outcome.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 calls process measures 'checkable commitments'; the example is used to show that processes shape outcomes, not that they cannot be measured.

common_misconception: Reading the example as advice on how to stock a site, when it is offered as evidence that outcomes are chosen in advance.

correct_answer: (A) One that promises to let a river overflow its banks in wet years and reports each year whether it did, without saying which habitats should result.
explanation: Paragraph 4 gives the model: 'one can ask whether the river is in fact allowed to flood ... These are checkable commitments'. The correct answer commits to a process and reports on it while leaving the resulting landscape open.

option_rationales.B: This measures success against a reference state, the traditional restoration approach of paragraph 1, which judges the outcome rather than the process.
option_rationales.C: This is the version paragraph 3 criticises as 'immune to criticism'; it offers no checkable commitment, so nothing can be held to account.
option_rationales.D: Visitors and donations are neither ecological processes nor outcomes; paragraph 4's examples concern flooding, herbivore numbers and dead wood.

common_misconception: Choosing the reference map option because it is measurable, without noticing that it measures an end state.

correct_answer: (D) a fixed target would make it harder to win support from funders and neighbours who prefer projects without set goals.
explanation: All the advocates' reasons appear in paragraph 2: the arbitrariness of a reference state, the effect of a changing climate, and the growing intervention an old picture would require. Funders and neighbours appear only in paragraph 3, as people the objection says are left without a way to hold the project to account; no one says they prefer projects without goals.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says doing so 'would require ever more intervention, mowing, planting, culling and weeding'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says choosing a reference state 'is to privilege one moment of its history over all the others'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says 'the conditions that sustained a historical community may no longer exist'.

common_misconception: Recognising 'those who fund it, live beside it' from paragraph 3 and assuming the option restates an advocate's reason.

correct_answer: (C) a project or claim deserves to be taken seriously only if some possible outcome would count against it.
explanation: The objection ends: 'a claim that nothing could count against is not much of a claim'. Its force rests on the principle that a project is open to judgement only if some outcome could tell against it.

option_rationales.A: The objection asks only for some standard against which a project could fail; paragraph 4 shows it can be partly met by process commitments, which use no earlier date.
option_rationales.B: Neighbours are named among those who cannot 'hold it to account'; the objection concerns accountability to a standard, not who should choose the outcome.
option_rationales.D: The meadow and the rare species are offered to make the objection 'sharper', not as evidence about how often projects fail; the objection is about whether failure can be recognised at all.

common_misconception: Choosing the reference-state option, which the objection might seem to favour but does not need.

correct_answer: (A) argue that seismology deserves credit for long-term probabilities that guide construction, rather than blame for failing to predict individual earthquakes.
explanation: Paragraph 1 states the common complaint, paragraph 2 separates prediction from forecasting, paragraph 3 shows that forecasts shape building codes, and paragraph 4 concludes that the discipline 'should not be judged by its failure' at prediction while 'its success at a quieter task goes unremarked'. The purpose is to shift how seismology is judged.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the opposite: 'Forecasts are what building codes are written from', and engineers already act on these probabilities.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 mentions these conditions only as a likely reason prediction is out of reach, and says seismologists 'suspect' it, not that measurement is impossible; the option is too narrow and too absolute.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says 'This does not mean that the search for warning signs should be abandoned', because a reliable sign 'would save lives that codes cannot', so the option reverses the author's position.

common_misconception: Taking the account of failed warning signs in paragraph 1 as the point of the passage, and missing the concession in paragraph 4.

correct_answer: (B) names a place, a magnitude and a short time window, while a forecast gives a probability over a longer period.
explanation: Paragraph 2: a prediction 'names a place, a magnitude and a narrow window of time', while a forecast 'states a probability over a longer period'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says engineers act on forecasts, not that they prepare them; the passage draws no distinction based on who issues each.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 defines the two by what they state, not by the data they use; historical records are never mentioned.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 gives a size for both: a forecast speaks of 'shaking above some level'; nothing restricts predictions to large events or extends forecasts to small ones.

common_misconception: Attaching a plausible but unstated difference (data source, audience) to the two terms.

correct_answer: (C) it arrives years before any earthquake and asks for spending rather than a decision to leave.
explanation: Paragraph 3 ends: nobody experiences it as a warning, 'since it arrives years before the event and asks for money rather than flight'. The correct answer paraphrases both halves of that reason.

option_rationales.A: The passage nowhere questions the accuracy of forecasts; it calls them 'far from useless' and the basis of building codes.
option_rationales.B: The passage never discusses how forecasts are worded; the reason it gives is that the warning 'arrives years before the event'.
option_rationales.D: Nothing in the passage says forecasts are hidden; paragraph 3 explains the lack of a felt warning by its timing and its demand for money.

common_misconception: Supplying an outside explanation (secrecy, jargon) instead of the reason the sentence itself gives.

correct_answer: (D) In most earthquake-prone regions, buildings are demolished or replaced within a few years of construction, long before a thirty-year hazard is likely to occur.
explanation: The reply in paragraph 4 rests on the claim that reinforcing a building is 'a decision about the lifetime of a building', over which a one-in-twenty chance in thirty years is large. If buildings last only a few years, that lifetime is short and the chance over it is small, so the reply loses its force.

option_rationales.A: This fits the author's claim in paragraph 3 that codes are written from forecasts; it supports rather than weakens the reply.
option_rationales.B: The author already says nobody should evacuate on a long-term probability; how residents respond to evacuation orders does not touch the argument about reinforcing buildings.
option_rationales.C: This concerns prediction, which the reply sets aside; a possible new warning sign leaves the case for acting on long-term probabilities untouched, and paragraph 1 shows such signs often fail later tests.

common_misconception: Choosing an option about evacuation or warning signs because those topics appear in paragraph 4, without locating the assumption the reply depends on.

correct_answer: (B) show how a single summary symbol throws away the information about uncertainty that running many forecasts provides.
explanation: Paragraph 3 opens by saying the gain 'is lost in the last step'. The icon is the illustration: it 'has quietly discarded the ensemble and kept only something like its average', so the spread, which paragraph 2 called 'the information', never reaches users.

option_rationales.A: The passage says the application 'kept only something like its average', meaning it simplifies the ensemble's output; it says nothing about the application running a different model.
option_rationales.C: The passage says a correct forecast of uncertainty is 'remembered as' wrong, which concerns how forecasts are judged, not how often they actually fail.
option_rationales.D: The passage offers no remedy of this kind; paragraph 3 describes a loss and calls the public's habit 'understandable' without recommending who should issue forecasts.

common_misconception: Reading the example as a claim about model quality or accuracy rather than about presentation.

correct_answer: (C) a poor test of a forecast that expressed uncertainty, since such a forecast allowed for more than one outcome.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says that under this habit 'a forecast that correctly said the outcome was uncertain is remembered as a forecast that was wrong'. The word 'correctly' shows the author thinks the one-day test misjudges such forecasts, because an uncertain forecast does not commit to a single outcome.

option_rationales.A: The passage never links the fairness of this test to the forecast's lead time; the two-week horizon in paragraph 1 concerns single calculated forecasts.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 presents the habit as one that 'trains the public to expect a kind of certainty the science has explicitly given up', which the author regrets rather than recommends.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says centres compare spread with 'the errors actually observed over many past forecasts', a record across many cases, not a verdict on one day's rain.

common_misconception: Confusing the public's one-day test with the forecasters' long-run comparison in paragraph 4, since both involve checking forecasts against the weather.

correct_answer: (D) appreciative but qualified: impressed that a limit became a method, yet alert to what the method cannot reveal.
explanation: Paragraph 2 praises the conversion of chaos into 'a way of measuring how much prediction a given situation permits', while paragraph 4 warns against treating the ensemble 'as a perfectly honest witness'. Both halves of the correct answer are needed.

option_rationales.A: Phrases such as 'What is striking' and 'It would be a mistake, however' express clear judgments, so the author is not neutral.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says an ensemble 'can therefore agree with itself and still be wrong', and paragraph 2 says the spread measures uncertainty rather than removing it.
option_rationales.C: The author calls the change 'striking' and says chaos 'became a way of measuring how much prediction a given situation permits', which is praise, not suspicion.

common_misconception: Seizing on either the praise of paragraph 2 or the warning of paragraph 4 alone.

correct_answer: (A) Every run of an ensemble forecasts a dry week for a valley because the shared model mishandles air rising over nearby hills, and heavy rain falls there.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says all runs share the same model, so 'errors built into the model are shared by all the members and do not show up as spread'; an ensemble 'can therefore agree with itself and still be wrong'. In the correct answer, the runs agree because of a shared mistake about hills, one of the features the paragraph names, and are wrong together.

option_rationales.B: This is the method working as paragraph 2 describes: the spread 'is the information'. No hidden error is involved.
option_rationales.C: This is the chaotic amplification of starting errors in paragraph 1, which ensembles are designed to handle; it is not an error shared by every member.
option_rationales.D: This is the presentation problem of paragraph 3, where the ensemble is reduced to 'something like its average', not a weakness of the ensemble itself.

common_misconception: Choosing the option that matches another paragraph's problem (chaos, presentation, wide spread), since each of those options is a faithful picture of something the passage discusses.

correct_answer: (C) the top layer of snow stays porous for a long time, letting surface air mix downward until the bubbles seal.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'the upper layer remains porous, and air from the surface continues to mix downward through it. By the time the bubbles finally close, the gas they hold is considerably younger than the ice'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says air mixes in before 'the bubbles finally close'; nothing says air is forced into ice that had already sealed.
option_rationales.B: The passage never mentions contamination during drilling; it explains the age difference by the porous upper layer that stays open, as paragraph 2 puts it, for 'decades, centuries or, at the driest sites, far longer'.
option_rationales.D: Melting is not mentioned anywhere; paragraph 2 attributes the difference to air mixing 'downward' through porous snow.

common_misconception: Supplying a plausible physical mechanism the passage does not give.

correct_answer: (D) the model used to date the air needs values of temperature and snowfall that the core itself is meant to supply.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says compaction 'depends on temperature and snowfall, the very quantities the core is being used to reconstruct'. The dating step therefore needs, as input, part of what the record is supposed to yield.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the gas is 'considerably younger than the ice that surrounds it', the opposite of the option.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says such traces 'can appear in cores drilled at opposite ends of the planet', which contradicts the option.
option_rationales.C: The passage says these proportions are used to infer temperature through a calibrated relationship; it never says they change after drilling.

common_misconception: Overlooking the phrase 'the very quantities' and choosing a detail-based option that misstates the passage.
