option_rationales.B: This assumes that each body has 'a single proper community to which it should be restored', the popular error paragraph 3 criticises.
option_rationales.D: The author credits the antibiotic programme with saving many lives and says the lesson is not a simple reversal; the campaign uses the ecological image to blur a question, not sharpen it.

common_misconception: Choosing the textbook revision because it moves away from war language, which the author also wants, without noticing that it adds no testable concept.

correct_answer: (C) present a case in which pain occurs although no tissue remains that could be damaged.
explanation: Paragraph 2 lists cases where 'the gauge picture fails', and says of amputated limbs that 'there is no tissue left to report anything'. The example shows pain without damaged tissue.

option_rationales.A: The passage does not discuss how common such pain is or blame surgery; it uses the case only to show pain where 'there is no tissue left to report anything'.
option_rationales.B: That point is made by the separate example of serious wounds felt little 'in moments of danger'; the amputation example concerns pain without tissue.
option_rationales.D: This reverses the role of the example, which is offered as a difficulty for the gauge picture, not as support for it.

common_misconception: Confusing the amputation example with the neighbouring example about moments of danger.

correct_answer: (D) a conclusion that the brain reaches by weighing several kinds of information together.
explanation: Paragraph 3 explains the term: tissue signals are 'one input among several', and the brain 'combines them with context, expectation and memory' and produces pain 'when it concludes' the body is under threat. A verdict is a conclusion drawn from evidence.

option_rationales.A: The passage treats the verdict as revisable: paragraph 4 suggests that treatment aimed at the protective system 'may help', so the verdict is not fixed.
option_rationales.B: This describes a 'reading', the gauge picture that the word 'verdict' is chosen to replace.
option_rationales.C: The legal sense of punishment is not intended; the passage describes the brain combining 'context, expectation and memory' to judge threat, not penalising injury.

common_misconception: Taking 'verdict' to mean something final and unchangeable, as in its courtroom sense.

correct_answer: (A) a scan that shows no damaged structure does not show that the pain is imaginary.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says a verdict produced by the nervous system 'is as real as any other bodily event' and that searching harder for a damaged structure may do little good. So the absence of a visible structure does not make the pain unreal.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says that 'operating on whatever turns up in a scan, may do little good' when the alarm itself is oversensitive.
option_rationales.C: This reasons from the gauge picture, which the passage rejects; on the verdict account, pain can outlast damage without the damage having been underestimated.
option_rationales.D: The author denies that the account means 'the pain is imaginary' and insists that the verdict 'hurts just as much'.

common_misconception: Choosing the persuasion option, which mirrors the misunderstanding the author explicitly rejects.

correct_answer: (B) Pain is better seen as the brain's judgement about threat than as a measure of injury, which bears on treating pain that outlasts healing.
explanation: Paragraph 1 sets out the gauge picture, paragraph 2 gives cases where it fails, paragraph 3 proposes the verdict account, and paragraph 4 defends it against the charge that it makes pain imaginary and draws a consequence for treatment. The correct answer covers both the thesis and its consequence.

option_rationales.A: This keeps the gauge picture; the author suggests the alarm itself 'has become oversensitive' and doubts that searching harder for damage will help.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says the gauge picture is 'roughly accurate' for 'a great many everyday injuries'; the passage says it fails in particular cases.
option_rationales.D: The author says the account is not 'a polite way of saying that the pain is imaginary' and that such pain 'hurts just as much'.

common_misconception: Choosing the option about imaginary pain because the passage discusses that interpretation at length.

correct_answer: (D) lengthens the survival recorded after her diagnosis without postponing her death.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'Nothing about her death has changed, but the survival figure has more than tripled, simply because the clock was started earlier.' Her survival after diagnosis rises from two years to seven while she still dies at seventy.

option_rationales.A: The case stipulates that the tumour 'will kill a woman at seventy whatever is done', so no years are added to her life; only the measured survival grows.
option_rationales.B: The passage says nothing about the timing being too late; the point of the case is that the timing makes no difference to when she dies.
option_rationales.C: Slow tumours are the 'second distortion', introduced after the example; the woman's case illustrates the earlier starting of the clock, not tumour speed.

common_misconception: Reading the seven years of survival as five extra years of life.

correct_answer: (B) the way it is made favours screening whether or not screening saves lives, though nobody intends this.
explanation: The author immediately qualifies 'rigged' with 'by the arithmetic of detection rather than by anyone's intent', and then shows how lead time and tumour speed improve the figures regardless of benefit.

option_rationales.A: The passage criticises survival after diagnosis as a measure of screening; it makes no claim about every other use of survival comparisons.
option_rationales.C: The author says the comparison is rigged 'by the arithmetic of detection rather than by anyone's intent', which rules out deliberate manipulation.
option_rationales.D: The passage attributes the better survival to when the clock starts and to what is found, 'rather than what was done', not to differences in treatment.

common_misconception: Taking 'rigged' in its usual sense of deliberate fraud, ignoring the qualification that follows it.

correct_answer: (A) explaining why the harm of overdiagnosis tends to build support for screening rather than doubts about it.
explanation: The sentence leads straight into 'Screening thus produces its own most sincere advocates, and the more it overdiagnoses, the more grateful survivors it creates.' Its role is to show that overdiagnosis, a harm, is experienced as a benefit and so generates support.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the cells 'are what the pathologist says they are'; the patients' error, if any, concerns whether they were in danger, not whether they had the abnormality.
option_rationales.C: The same sentence says 'no individual can know' that his or her tumour was harmless, so the passage cannot be recommending that patients be told.
option_rationales.D: The passage calls these advocates 'sincere' and describes an unintended effect; it attributes no strategy or motive to the programmes.

common_misconception: Choosing the option about patients being wrong to believe they had cancer, which confuses being 'never in danger' with never having had the abnormality.

correct_answer: (C) When comparable populations were assigned at random to be screened or not, fewer people in the screened population died of the disease.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says the right question is 'whether fewer people in the population it serves die of the disease', and cites 'carefully conducted trials comparing large screened and unscreened populations' as the evidence that justifies some programmes. A randomised comparison of mortality between populations is that kind of evidence.

option_rationales.A: This is the survival comparison that paragraph 4 says 'cannot answer that question', because lead time, slow tumours and overdiagnosis inflate it even when no death is prevented.
option_rationales.B: The author asks whether fewer people 'in the population it serves' die, a question answered only by 'comparisons between whole populations'; attenders and non-attenders are self-selected parts of one population, so the gap may reflect who chooses to attend rather than what screening does.
option_rationales.D: More and earlier diagnoses are exactly what overdiagnosis and the bias towards slow tumours would produce, so this finding cannot distinguish benefit from distortion.

common_misconception: Choosing the attenders comparison because it measures deaths, without noticing that it compares self-selected groups rather than whole populations.

correct_answer: (D) It occurs when a pathologist mistakes harmless cells for cancerous ones under the microscope.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says overdiagnosis 'is not an error in the usual sense, since the cells are what the pathologist says they are', and that 'The error lies in the prediction that they would have mattered'. A misreading by the pathologist is therefore exactly what overdiagnosis is not.

option_rationales.A: Consistent: paragraph 3 says such people 'are treated, sometimes with surgery or radiation', though 'they were never in danger'.
option_rationales.B: Consistent: overdiagnosed patients 'appear in the statistics as survivors', and paragraph 4 lists overdiagnosis among the influences that improve survival 'even when not a single death has been prevented'.
option_rationales.C: Consistent: paragraph 3 says 'no individual can know that his or her own tumour was of this harmless kind'.

common_misconception: Assuming that overdiagnosis must be a laboratory mistake, since the word suggests a wrong diagnosis.

correct_answer: (B) rests on few patients, has no comparison group and is shaped by memorable cases.
explanation: Paragraph 3 calls a doctor's experience a trial 'without randomisation, with a small sample, no comparison group and a memory that favours vivid cases'.

option_rationales.A: Whether experience can be recorded or shared is never discussed; the weaknesses listed concern sample size, comparison and memory.
option_rationales.C: The passage says memory 'favours vivid cases', which may be successes or failures; it does not say the bias runs towards harms.
option_rationales.D: The passage says the sample is small, not that it is too small to yield any impression; doctors do form impressions, which the passage calls a 'poor instrument'.

common_misconception: Turning 'vivid cases' into a specific bias towards harms.

correct_answer: (C) showing how evidence from trials about groups should, and should not, guide decisions about individual patients.
explanation: Paragraph 1 sets up the gap between the group question and the individual question; paragraphs 2 to 4 reject two errors and a tempting remedy; paragraph 5 states the author's position on how averages should be used. The correct answer covers that whole structure.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says subgroup analysis is not 'as reliable as it appears' and produces 'mirages' by chance.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 presents reliance on clinical judgement as 'The second error' and calls the clinician's impression 'a poor instrument'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 5 says such designs suit only 'some chronic conditions' and 'are not always practical'; they illustrate what individual evidence requires.

common_misconception: Picking the option about clinical judgement because the passage criticises over-literal use of averages in paragraph 2.

correct_answer: (A) the trial result fits patterns of benefit under which that patient's own risk would not fall by three points.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says the same average 'would result if a small minority benefited a great deal and everyone else not at all, or if many benefited modestly while a few were harmed'. Under these patterns a given patient might gain far more, nothing, or be harmed, so promising three points claims 'knowledge the trial does not contain'.

option_rationales.B: The passage says the average may conceal a minority who 'benefited a great deal', so individual risks can change; what the trial cannot reveal is whose risk changes and by how much.
option_rationales.C: The passage says only that the same average could arise 'if many benefited modestly while a few were harmed'; it never says harms outnumber benefits.
option_rationales.D: The passage does not question the trial's estimate of the average; its objection is to applying a correct average to each patient.

common_misconception: Choosing the option that no individual's risk can be changed, which mistakes uncertainty about whose risk changes for a claim that no individual's risk changes.

correct_answer: (B) One who departs from the trial-based default for a patient whose genetic variant is known to block the drug's mechanism, an effect confirmed in a later trial.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says departures from the average need 'a plausible mechanism together with a difference that recurs in a fresh trial', and paragraph 5 says departures should be justified by reasons. A known mechanism plus a confirming later trial meets both conditions.

option_rationales.A: This relies on a small, unrandomised sample and on 'a memory that favours vivid cases', which paragraph 3 calls a poor instrument.
option_rationales.C: A single striking subgroup among many divisions is the kind of finding paragraph 4 says may be a chance 'mirage' and has 'often failed to reappear when tested again'.
option_rationales.D: This is 'The first error' of paragraph 2: applying the average 'as though it were a fact about each patient'.

common_misconception: Choosing the subgroup option because it appears to use trial evidence rather than intuition.

correct_answer: (C) indicate what a genuinely individual conclusion would demand, by contrast with a mere claim that a patient is different.
explanation: The paragraph says such designs 'show what an answer to the individual question would actually require, and how little the bare assertion of individuality provides'. The reference sets a standard against which the second error of paragraph 3 falls short.

option_rationales.A: The design is described for conditions whose symptoms 'come and go quickly', not stable ones, and is said to be 'not always practical'; no replacement is proposed.
option_rationales.B: The author calls the average 'the best default available when nothing more is known'; the single-patient design adds information rather than showing the average worthless.
option_rationales.D: A single-patient trial uses alternating treatment and placebo and compares results, which is the opposite of relying on intuition.

common_misconception: Reading the example as a recommendation of a new standard method rather than as an illustration of what individual evidence requires.

correct_answer: (D) argue that electronic computers took over a way of organising calculation that human computing offices had already developed.
explanation: Paragraph 1 says the electronic computer 'inherited an idea that human computing offices had already worked out in detail'; paragraphs 2 and 3 describe that idea (division of labour, rules, checking by redundancy) and show it anticipated programming; paragraph 4 qualifies but keeps the continuity. The purpose is to argue this continuity.

option_rationales.A: The change in the word's meaning is only the opening observation of paragraph 1; the passage does not trace the history of the word but uses it to introduce a claim about how calculation was organised.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 denies that 'the machines merely did faster what people had done slowly' and says their speed 'changed which problems were worth posing at all'.
option_rationales.C: The passage never compares the reliability of offices and machines; paragraph 3 says only that designers borrowed the offices' 'conception of what it meant to make a calculation reliable'.

common_misconception: Mistaking the opening remark about the word for the purpose, or reading the passage as belittling the machines.

correct_answer: (A) The same column was worked out by two people separately, and any mismatch sent it back to be redone.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'two people would compute the same column independently, and any disagreement sent the column back.' The correct answer restates this.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 mentions such tables as the products of the offices' work, not as a means of checking it; the checking method in paragraph 2 is duplicate computation.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says errors were caught 'not by insight but by procedure'; a planner reviewing sheets through understanding is the opposite of what is described.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the workers 'did not have to understand why a step was there' and that the scheme was designed so that they would not need to.

common_misconception: Assuming that checking must involve someone who understands the problem.

correct_answer: (C) head off an overstatement that the passage's stress on continuity might otherwise invite.
explanation: Having argued for continuity between offices and machines, the author forestalls the inference that machines were nothing more than faster offices, and then explains that speed changed which problems were posed, before reaffirming that 'the continuity matters'. The sentence is a qualification.

option_rationales.A: The borrowing is described in paragraph 3; this sentence does not summarise it but guards against reading the continuity as mere sameness.
option_rationales.B: The passage says nothing about what is usually assumed about the offices' speed or accuracy; the sentence qualifies the author's own argument.
option_rationales.D: The same paragraph goes on to say 'But the continuity matters', so the earlier claim is kept, not replaced.

common_misconception: Reading a qualifying sentence as a change of thesis.

correct_answer: (A) an intended feature of the method, since the procedure was meant to yield correct results without that understanding.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says the scheme was 'designed so that they would not need to' understand, and that the result was 'a method in which correctness no longer depended on anyone grasping the whole'. Non-understanding was therefore built in, not a flaw.

option_rationales.B: Nothing in the passage suggests the arrangement was abandoned; it is presented as the defining feature of the offices, later carried over into programming.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the scheme 'was in fact designed so that they would not need to' understand; nothing is said about a shortage of trained workers or about planners merely tolerating the arrangement.
option_rationales.D: The passage never links errors to the workers' lack of understanding; duplicate computation catches disagreements whatever their cause, and the passage treats non-understanding as part of the design.

common_misconception: Assuming that lack of understanding must be a defect, which makes the error-source option tempting.

correct_answer: (D) show how an accidental early advantage can grow into a large gap when ranking rewards prior engagement.
explanation: The example follows directly on the description of the feedback loop and shows 'the small, accidental difference' hardening 'into an enormous gap'. It illustrates the mechanism of concentration.

option_rationales.A: Fragmentation is the familiar view of paragraph 1 that the author revises; the example shows concentration on one song, the opposite tendency.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the second song may disappear 'not because anyone judged it worse but because no one was shown it'.
option_rationales.C: The example is hypothetical and concerns exposure, not listeners' powers of discrimination; the passage proves nothing about what listeners can tell apart.

common_misconception: Confusing the example with the fragmentation view it is meant to correct.

correct_answer: (B) making a vast catalogue available does little for obscure work if ranking keeps people from encountering it.
explanation: Paragraph 3: the hope 'depended on people actually encountering that work', and ranking that rewards popularity 'makes such encounters rarer than the size of the catalogue suggests'. Availability without exposure does not help obscure work.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 speaks of 'the vast catalogue that digital distribution made available'; the problem is that it 'sits largely unvisited', not that it is small.
option_rationales.C: This is the fragmentation picture of paragraph 1; the author says the characteristic risk is 'less fragmentation than concentration'.
option_rationales.D: The author locates the cause in a ranking system 'that rewards prior popularity', not in users' preferences; the two-songs example stresses that neglect need not reflect anyone's judgement.

common_misconception: Blaming users' tastes, or reverting to the fragmentation account the author has set aside.

correct_answer: (B) When the same new songs were ranked separately for several groups of listeners, different songs became hits in each group, depending on early chance.
explanation: If identical songs become hits or flops depending on early chance, popularity is in part produced by the loop rather than reflecting fixed appeal. That is exactly what 'partly manufacturing it' claims.

option_rationales.A: This supports the concession in paragraph 4 that concentration is not new, but it says nothing about whether automated rankings shape demand.
option_rationales.C: Narrowing of individual taste bears on the fragmentation view of paragraph 1 and does not show that rankings produce the popularity they appear to report.
option_rationales.D: Greater enjoyment of suggestions is consistent with the ranking merely reporting real preferences; it does not show that exposure created the demand.

common_misconception: Choosing an option that is on topic (recommendation, concentration) but does not separate created demand from reported demand.

correct_answer: (D) It would ask whether apparent popularity shows real preference or just the prominence an item had earlier.
explanation: The final sentence locates any remedy in 'asking how much of what looks like popular demand is an echo of earlier exposure', that is, whether popularity reflects preference or prior prominence. The correct answer says this in other words; it neither promises success nor prescribes a mechanism.

option_rationales.A: The author says the remedy lies 'less in protecting users from their own tastes'; limiting matches to past taste is the response to fragmentation that the author downgrades.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'It would be wrong to present this as something algorithms invented'; the author also proposes no removal of popularity signals.
option_rationales.C: The author hedges ('if there is one') and identifies invisibility as well as speed as what is new; nothing suggests that slowing the loop would be enough.

common_misconception: Taking one of the two new features (speed) as the whole problem, or reading the remedy as protection from one's own tastes.

correct_answer: (C) may disclose facts about relatives, some of whom may not even know that the test was taken.
explanation: Paragraph 2: such a person 'reveals facts about parents, siblings and cousins, some of whom may not know the test was taken.'

option_rationales.A: Legal ownership of samples is never discussed; 'ownership' in paragraph 1 is an image of privacy, not a legal claim about samples.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the person 'reveals facts about parents, siblings and cousins', whatever notice they have read.
option_rationales.D: No such option is described; the passage's point is that the disclosure about relatives happens through the test itself.

common_misconception: Bringing in outside ideas about legal ownership or research consent.

correct_answer: (A) consent has been relied on to provide more protection than individual choices are able to supply.
explanation: The 'load' is the 'whole burden of protection' that paragraph 3 says the framework places on individual decisions. Because data is collective, individual consent cannot bear that burden alone, though it still matters.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 opens 'This does not make individual consent worthless' and says 'Being asked still matters'; rules are to be added, 'not merely' substituted.
option_rationales.C: The length or complexity of forms is never mentioned; the problem described is structural, that others' choices reveal what a refuser withholds.
option_rationales.D: Fatigue with consent requests is an outside idea; the passage's argument holds even for people who decide carefully.

common_misconception: Reading the sentence as a rejection of consent, against the opening of paragraph 4.

correct_answer: (D) A household that stops burning wood in its stove still breathes smoky air, because most of the town keeps burning wood.
explanation: Paragraph 4 describes privacy as 'a condition that each person's conduct affects for others, and that no one can secure for themselves by private choice alone'. The household's private choice cannot secure clean air while others keep burning wood, mirroring a refuser whose traits are inferred from others' data.

option_rationales.A: This concerns the cost of refusing, not the futility of refusing; the tenant's refusal does secure what it aims at, freedom from the lease.
option_rationales.B: This is deception, which paragraph 4 treats as a separate wrong that 'the collective character of data does not erase'; it is not a case of others' conduct defeating a private choice.
option_rationales.C: Here the private choice succeeds in protecting its maker, the reverse of a condition that 'no one can secure for themselves by private choice alone'.

common_misconception: Choosing the deception case because it is about consent, though the analogy concerns collective conditions.

correct_answer: (B) Traits inferred about non-sharers from others' data prove so unreliable that they seldom reveal what a refuser meant to hide.
explanation: Paragraph 3 concludes that a refusal 'has secured very little' on the condition 'If it can be known anyway, through the choices of others'. If inferences about non-sharers are unreliable, the fact cannot in practice be known anyway, and the refusal does protect it.

option_rationales.A: This is the author's own concession in paragraph 4 and does not bear on whether refusals protect anything.
option_rationales.C: This illustrates the relational character of data described in paragraph 2 and leaves untouched the claim that a refusal secures little.
option_rationales.D: Growing accuracy makes it more likely that a refused fact 'can be known anyway', which strengthens rather than weakens the argument.

common_misconception: Picking the true-sounding concession about deception, which is consistent with the argument.

correct_answer: (A) argue that failures blamed on operators often stem from how automation shapes their role, and to suggest design responses.
explanation: Paragraphs 1 to 3 explain how automation leaves operators the hardest situations while eroding their skill and attention, so that 'human error' misplaces the fault; paragraph 4 proposes designing systems 'around the people who must step in'.

option_rationales.B: The passage shifts blame from the individual to 'the design of the whole arrangement'; it does not call operators careless.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'None of this is a case against automation', which has removed 'many kinds of mistake'.
option_rationales.D: The passage notes that reports end with 'human error' but says nothing about any requirement to name a single cause.

common_misconception: Reading criticism of the 'human error' label as criticism of automation itself.

correct_answer: (C) Attention drifts when nothing happens for long stretches, and a reliable machine makes such stretches longer.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'Attention drifts when nothing happens for hours, and the more reliable the machine, the longer the stretches in which nothing happens.'

option_rationales.A: The passage describes drifting attention, not a deliberate decision to stop watching; trust is never mentioned.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says skill decays through lack of exercise, not that training was reduced; and that point concerns control, not monitoring.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 suggests better displays as a remedy, but paragraph 2 does not give complex displays as the reason monitoring is poor.

common_misconception: Importing the familiar idea of over-trust in machines, which the passage does not use.

correct_answer: (C) leave its overseers worse equipped for unusual crises, so that their lapses come as more of a shock.
explanation: Paragraph 3: 'The better the automation works in ordinary conditions, the less prepared its human supervisors may be for the extraordinary ones, and the more surprising their failure will look when it comes.'

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the reverse: a more reliable machine lengthens the stretches in which 'nothing happens', during which attention drifts.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says what remains for humans are the situations 'in which the machine gives up'; nothing suggests better ordinary performance removes these.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the rare moments 'are the ones in which the most is at stake', so rarity does not make skill unimportant.

common_misconception: Assuming that better automation must make the whole system safer in every respect.

correct_answer: (D) sceptical of it as an explanation of failure, while granting that it is accurate in a narrow sense.
explanation: Paragraph 1 calls the phrase 'accurate in a narrow sense' but says it 'hides the way the situation was produced'; paragraph 3 says it 'locates the fault in the individual' when the design deserves scrutiny. This is qualified scepticism.

option_rationales.A: The author says the label 'hides the way the situation was produced' and that 'the design of the whole arrangement deserves scrutiny'.
option_rationales.B: The author holds that the label misdirects scrutiny 'at the very moment' it is needed, which is not indifference.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 grants that 'a person did do the wrong thing'; the author does not deny the operator's part, only that it is the whole story.

common_misconception: Overstating the author's criticism into a denial of any operator responsibility.

correct_answer: (A) satellites that relay stored data between continents when undersea links fail.
explanation: Paragraph 2 lists buildings of servers, cooling water, cables across sea floors and along railway lines, and sites chosen for power, taxes or ground. Satellites are never mentioned.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says servers 'must be kept cool, often with water drawn from local supplies'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 mentions 'particular sites chosen for cheap power, favourable taxes or stable ground'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 mentions 'cables laid across sea floors and along railway lines'.

common_misconception: Accepting a plausible piece of real-world infrastructure that the passage does not name.

correct_answer: (B) It answers a defence of the metaphor by separating what users need from what those who govern the infrastructure need.
explanation: Paragraph 4 opens with what 'Defenders of the metaphor might point out', accepts it for users, and replies that abstraction 'becomes a liability' for 'citizens, regulators and planners'. It is an objection and a reply by distinction.

option_rationales.A: No new evidence about costs appears in paragraph 4; it addresses an objection about the value of abstraction.
option_rationales.C: The author grants the point ('That is true') but adds 'it confuses two audiences', so the criticism is kept and narrowed, not withdrawn.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says 'Nobody wants to think about the location of a server before sending a message' and calls abstraction 'a gift to the user'.

common_misconception: Taking the concession ('That is true') for a retreat from the thesis.

correct_answer: (C) the image invites a belief that services are widely spread, when they may hinge on a few points of failure.
explanation: Paragraph 3 contrasts the suggestion of resilience with the fact that 'a large share of the services people rely on may depend on a small number of companies and sites, so that a single failure can ripple outward'. The image of diffusion hides concentration.

option_rationales.A: That users need not know where files go is the part of the metaphor the author accepts in paragraph 1; it does not bear on resilience.
option_rationales.B: Energy cost is a separate effect of the metaphor ('A cloud uses nothing'); it is not what makes the impression of resilience misleading.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says sites are chosen partly for 'stable ground'; the resilience point concerns concentration in few companies and sites.

common_misconception: Mixing up the three separate ways the metaphor misleads in paragraph 3.

correct_answer: (D) Using a tap without a thought for reservoirs is a convenience, but a water board that planned as if water came from taps would plan badly.
explanation: The reply in paragraph 4 is that abstraction is 'a gift to the user at the moment of use' but 'a liability' for those who must decide about the infrastructure. The tap is convenient for the user and misleading only if carried into planning, matching that two-audience structure.

option_rationales.A: The author says the cloud image 'is not simply wrong' and serves users well; an abstraction that misleads every audience is the opposite of the reply.
option_rationales.B: The author accepts that users need not know what lies behind the abstraction; the reply concerns a different audience, not users' competence.
option_rationales.C: This concerns the cost of hiding infrastructure physically; it lacks the distinction between an abstraction that helps one audience and harms another.

common_misconception: Choosing the buried power lines because it is about hidden infrastructure, though it lacks the two-audience distinction.

correct_answer: (A) show that both sides in the debate wrongly treat understanding as all-or-nothing, and to propose mapping separate abilities instead.
explanation: Paragraph 2 identifies the 'shared assumption' that understanding is 'a single property'; paragraph 3 concludes that 'The useful work lies in mapping which abilities are present'. The correct answer captures both moves.

option_rationales.B: This is the second reported answer; the author says its verdict 'merely manipulates symbols' flattens the profile 'in the opposite direction'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says the question of experience 'should not be allowed to stand in for' the tractable question of what a system can do.
option_rationales.D: This is the first of the 'Two answers' in paragraph 1, which the author reports; paragraph 3 says the verdict 'really understands' tells us little.

common_misconception: Taking one of the reported views for the author's own.

correct_answer: (B) reduces an uneven pattern of strengths and weaknesses across abilities to a single yes or no judgement.
explanation: The 'profile' is the description just given: some abilities 'to a high degree and others hardly at all'. A verdict of 'really understands', like its opposite, collapses this into one answer that 'tells us little'.

option_rationales.A: The author says the opposite verdict 'does the same in the opposite direction', so the fault is not exaggeration in one direction but collapsing the profile either way.
option_rationales.C: Nothing in paragraph 3 concerns emotion; the contrast is between a detailed map of abilities and a single verdict.
option_rationales.D: The 'profile' is the system's pattern of abilities, not a body of vocabulary; the passage does not discuss popularisation.

common_misconception: Reading 'flattens' as 'flatters', that is, as exaggeration, which the parallel with the opposite verdict rules out.

correct_answer: (A) The abilities by which we judge understanding always come together, each present to exactly the degree the others are.
explanation: The argument rests on the premise that the abilities 'can come apart' (paragraph 2), which is why a single verdict is 'badly posed' (paragraph 3). If they always occurred together in matching degrees, understanding would behave like a single property and a single verdict would lose little.

option_rationales.B: This is exactly the uneven profile paragraph 3 describes, so it supports rather than weakens the argument.
option_rationales.C: This repeats the mechanic example of paragraph 2 and confirms that the abilities 'can come apart'.
option_rationales.D: This concerns the objection of paragraph 4, which the author sets aside as a separate question; it leaves paragraphs 2 and 3 untouched.

common_misconception: Picking the option about inner experience because it sounds like a challenge to the author.

correct_answer: (B) perhaps a real question, but not one peculiar to machines or one on which most practical decisions turn.
explanation: 'Perhaps it does' concedes the question may be untouched by mapping abilities; 'arises equally for any being' shows it is not specific to machines; and the final sentence says practical decisions depend on the other question. The correct answer combines these.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says the question 'should not be allowed to stand in for' the tractable one on which 'most practical decisions' depend.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says it 'arises equally for any being whose inner life we cannot inspect', so it is not peculiar to machines.
option_rationales.D: The author answers the objection with 'Perhaps it does', allowing that the question may be real and 'whatever its answer' may matter.

common_misconception: Reading the author's setting aside of the question as a dismissal of it.

correct_answer: (C) the groups differ in how often their members actually default and the predictions are less than perfect.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'When the groups' underlying default rates differ and the prediction is less than perfect', the criteria conflict; it 'follows from the arithmetic of prediction under unequal base rates'.

option_rationales.A: The number of measures a lender uses is never mentioned; the condition given concerns base rates and imperfect prediction.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 raises earlier unfairness as a consideration in choosing which criterion gives way, not as the condition under which the conflict arises.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the conflict 'is not a defect of any particular system that better engineering might remove'.

common_misconception: Confusing the condition for the conflict with a consideration relevant to resolving it.

correct_answer: (D) support the claim that a conflict between two demands does not show that either demand is empty.
explanation: The sentence reads: 'Discovering that two values can conflict is not the same as discovering that one of them is empty, any more than the occasional conflict between honesty and kindness shows that one of these is an illusion.' The analogy rebuts the conclusion that fairness is incoherent.

option_rationales.A: The comparison concerns whether conflicting values are real, not which should prevail; the author says which criterion yields depends on harm to those affected.
option_rationales.B: The author holds that fairness 'bundles together several demands' that are each meaningful; the comparison defends, rather than dismisses, everyday notions.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 rejects leaving the choice to builders as a technical matter; it says nothing about their personal virtues.

common_misconception: Reading the analogy as ranking the values instead of defending their reality.

correct_answer: (B) would rest partly on how heavily each kind of mistaken decision falls on those who must bear it.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says the choice 'depends on what the decision does to the people it touches: who bears the cost of being wrongly refused, how severe that cost is', and calls these 'questions about harm and responsibility, not about arithmetic'. The correct answer captures this concern with how the burden of errors falls on applicants.

option_rationales.A: This is close to the 'incoherent' conclusion the author rejects; paragraph 3 names the principles, harm and responsibility, on which the choice should rest.
option_rationales.C: The author ties the choice to 'who bears the cost' and 'how severe that cost is'; a total count of errors ignores how costs are distributed and is the kind of technical rule the author resists.
option_rationales.D: This is the second of the 'two conclusions' that paragraph 3 rejects: 'Nor does the need to choose make the choice technical'.

common_misconception: Choosing the total-error rule, which sounds neutral but replaces questions about who bears harm with a single technical figure.

correct_answer: (A) appreciative of its having exposed a hidden trade-off, but wary that the clarity it brings may be wasted.
explanation: Paragraph 4: 'the formal analysis has done something valuable' by making the conflict explicit, but 'The danger is that the explicitness is squandered'. The attitude is appreciation with a caution.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the loan officer 'does not have to declare which criterion is being sacrificed, and may not know', so the dilemma had not been openly acknowledged.
option_rationales.C: The analysis shows the opposite: it 'removed the comfortable belief that a sufficiently careful decision maker could satisfy every reasonable demand at once'.
option_rationales.D: The author fears the choice may be 'buried again' under technical vocabulary, a danger to be avoided, not a purpose the analysis was designed to serve.

common_misconception: Turning the author's warning about a future danger into an accusation about the analysis itself.

correct_answer: (C) sacrifices at least one of the criteria just as a scoring system must, though possibly without knowing which one.
explanation: Paragraph 4: the officer 'faces exactly the same trade-off' but 'does not have to declare which criterion is being sacrificed, and may not know'. The correct answer combines both parts.

option_rationales.A: The passage makes no comparison of fairness between officers and algorithms; its point is that both face the same dilemma.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the officer 'faces exactly the same trade-off'; not declaring the criterion does not remove the conflict.
option_rationales.D: The author says the analysis 'removed the comfortable belief that a sufficiently careful decision maker could satisfy every reasonable demand at once'.

common_misconception: Assuming that a choice not made explicitly is not made at all.

correct_answer: (D) can be read later only if the disk, a machine able to read it and software able to interpret the file all survive.
explanation: Paragraph 2: a file 'depends on the disk surviving, on a machine that can still read the disk, and on software that can still interpret the file'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the opposite: 'A single digital copy is, if anything, more perishable than a sheet of paper. Paper survives neglect'.
option_rationales.B: This is what paragraph 2 says of 'a letter left in a drawer', not of a file on a disk.
option_rationales.C: The passage gives no time limit and says the dependencies decay 'on its own schedule'; it does not say care is useless.

common_misconception: Transferring the description of the paper letter to the digital file.

correct_answer: (B) Whether digital material lasts turns on reasons to copy it, which explains both complaints and makes preservation an institutional task.
explanation: Paragraph 2 locates persistence in 'whether enough people, or enough systems, have reasons to keep making copies'; paragraph 3 shows this explains both complaints; paragraph 4 concludes that preservation is 'less a technical problem than an institutional one'.

option_rationales.A: The author accepts that embarrassing material does persist; the argument reconciles the two complaints rather than denying one.
option_rationales.C: The passage contrasts single copies with paper but never recommends printing; it locates persistence in copying and institutions, not in a change of medium.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says archives 'must choose' because of 'the sheer volume of material'; copying everything is presented as impossible.

common_misconception: Choosing an option that takes one half of the opening puzzle for the conclusion.

correct_answer: (A) material may matter a great deal for later understanding and still be among the first things to be lost.
explanation: Paragraph 3 follows the phrase with 'the material most likely to vanish is often the unglamorous record that matters most to a historian a generation later'. Value and persistence can come apart.

option_rationales.B: This reverses the claim: if copying tracks attention 'rather than value', the number of copies is not a reliable measure of value.
option_rationales.C: The passage says persistence follows attention 'rather than value', not that attention and value are inversely related.
option_rationales.D: 'Always' overstates the passage, which says such material is 'often' most likely to vanish, and paragraph 4 describes institutions that can preserve it.

common_misconception: Turning 'rather than' into an inverse relation, or reading 'often' as 'always'.

correct_answer: (C) It sets out two complaints that seem to contradict each other, a tension that the following paragraphs then resolve.
explanation: Paragraph 1 presents the two complaints and ends 'it is puzzling to hear the same medium accused of both'; paragraph 2 begins 'The puzzle dissolves'.

option_rationales.A: The author goes on to say that 'the two complaints describe the same mechanism working on different material', so both are kept, not rejected.
option_rationales.B: The author says in paragraph 2 that a single digital copy is 'more perishable than a sheet of paper'; paragraph 1 states no thesis of its own.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 opens 'The puzzle dissolves', so the author does resolve it.

common_misconception: Assuming that an author who presents two views must reject at least one of them.

correct_answer: (D) print archives never had to choose what to keep, since the volume of print was small enough to preserve in full.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says archives face 'a difficulty that print archives faced less acutely', which implies print archives faced it to some degree; 'never had to choose' is not supported.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says preservation needs an organisation that 'will go on paying for that duty when the material has ceased to be interesting'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'every choice about what to copy is also, in effect, a choice about what to let disappear'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the photograph 'is duplicated faster than any single copy can be deleted', which depends on the capacity to copy described in paragraph 2.

common_misconception: Reading 'less acutely' as 'not at all'.

correct_answer: (B) anonymous review becomes hard to defend chiefly when secret reports also decide whether a paper is published at all.
explanation: Paragraph 3 states the thesis: anonymity is not itself the problem; 'What makes it dangerous is its combination with gatekeeping power.' Paragraph 4 restates it: if review only improves papers 'a mask does little harm', but if it decides 'which papers exist' it deserves suspicion.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 notes that such arrangements 'are not free of costs' and uses them only to reveal an assumption; the author never ranks them above every alternative.
option_rationales.C: This is the 'usual defence' reported in paragraph 1, which the author grants force but then qualifies; it is one step in the argument, not its central claim.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says 'Most referees, of course, do nothing of the kind', and paragraph 3 says it would be 'wrong to infer' that 'anonymity is, in itself, the problem', so both the call for abolition and the claim of routine abuse misstate the author.

common_misconception: Choosing the option that sounds most critical of anonymous review and missing the qualification in paragraph 3.

correct_answer: (C) lets less powerful researchers criticise the work of influential authors without having to fear for their own careers.
explanation: Paragraph 1 says a young researcher 'may hesitate to point out its flaws if her name is attached', since the powerful author 'may one day sit on the committee that decides her promotion'. Anonymity 'allows candour to flow upward'.

option_rationales.A: The passage concerns hiding the referee's name, not the author's; nothing in paragraph 1 says anonymity shields authors' reputations from view.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 mentions that a referee need not 'explain himself in public', but as a danger of anonymity, not as the defence offered for it.
option_rationales.D: The passage never discusses how editors choose referees or personal ties; paragraph 1 grounds the defence in the junior referee's fear for her promotion.

common_misconception: Picking the option taken from paragraph 2, which describes a cost of anonymity, not its defence.

correct_answer: (A) honest criticism travelling from junior researchers toward the people who hold power over them.
explanation: The phrase sums up the example just given: a young researcher can criticise 'the most powerful figure in her field' only if her name is hidden. Candour flows 'upward' from the less powerful to the more powerful.

option_rationales.B: Promotion is mentioned only as something the powerful figure could later affect; paragraph 1 does not say that refereeing speeds anyone's promotion.
option_rationales.C: This reads 'upward' as improvement in quality; the sentence is about who may safely criticise whom, as the preceding example of the young researcher shows.
option_rationales.D: The editor is not the subject of the defence; paragraph 1 concerns a young researcher assessing 'the most powerful figure in her field', and editors are not described as speaking upward.

common_misconception: Taking 'upward' literally as improvement or advancement instead of as direction in a hierarchy.

correct_answer: (D) every paper is published, with the unsigned referee reports printed beside it and the authors free to reply.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says that when a report 'merely advises', being 'published alongside the paper as one reader's criticism that the authors can answer', the critic's identity 'matters far less'. Reports printed beside papers that are published regardless, with a right of reply, fit that description even though the reports are unsigned.

option_rationales.A: This is exactly the arrangement paragraph 3 condemns: a report that 'decides, in secret, whether anyone will read the paper', where 'the absence of a name becomes the absence of accountability'.
option_rationales.B: Choosing junior referees might answer the remark in paragraph 2 that 'the established' usually referee, but the reports would still decide in secret, which paragraph 3 identifies as the real danger.
option_rationales.C: Greater secrecy does nothing to remove the gatekeeping power that, according to paragraph 3, makes anonymity dangerous; if anything it reduces accountability further.

common_misconception: Choosing the junior-referee option because it seems to fix the problem of the established refereeing, while missing that the author locates the danger in secret gatekeeping.

correct_answer: (B) overestimate both how frequently the effect being studied occurs and how strong it tends to be when it does.
explanation: Paragraph 1 says the reader 'will then overestimate how often, and how strongly, the effect in question occurs, since the failures that would have tempered the estimate never reached print.'

option_rationales.A: Sample size appears only in paragraphs 3 and 4 as a matter of study design; nothing in paragraph 1 links the missing failures to beliefs about sample size.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says the reader 'will then overestimate' the effect, which is the opposite of doubting the positive findings.
option_rationales.D: The passage attributes no such assumption to readers; the preference of editors is part of 'the complaint' about journals, not a belief readers form.

common_misconception: Choosing the option about readers' suspicion, which reverses the effect described.

correct_answer: (C) she herself often cannot tell what the absence of the expected effect actually means.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says a null result 'is mute about its own meaning': it may reflect no effect, a small sample, contamination or a misread protocol, and the researcher 'is often the person least able to tell which'. An uninterpretable finding is not worth the weeks of writing.

option_rationales.A: Fear of contradicting colleagues is never mentioned; paragraph 3 explains abandonment by the ambiguity of the result and the poor return on writing it up.
option_rationales.B: This is the conventional account that paragraph 2 says 'places the drawer in the wrong office'; the study is abandoned 'before any journal had a chance to reject it'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 begins 'The reason is not laziness' and locates the reason in the result being 'mute about its own meaning'; being busy is not the explanation offered.

common_misconception: Picking the journal-rejection option because it is the familiar explanation, though the passage argues against it.

correct_answer: (A) In fields where sample sizes and procedures must be declared before data are collected, researchers submit a far larger share of their null results.
explanation: Paragraph 4 claims that the drawer 'will empty only when null results become informative', which depends on decisions 'made before any data are collected', such as adequate samples and procedures 'specified in advance'. A finding that such pre-declared design is followed by many more null results being submitted directly supports this causal claim.

option_rationales.B: This suggests that journal rejection persists even for informative null results, which supports the conventional account and so tends to weaken the author's claim that design is what empties the drawer.
option_rationales.C: This points to career incentives, not interpretability, as the obstacle; it offers a rival explanation to the one in paragraphs 3 and 4 rather than support for it.
option_rationales.D: Citation after publication does not bear on the claim that null results are published once they become informative; it concerns how such results are received.

common_misconception: Choosing an option that is on topic but supports a different explanation (journal bias or career incentives) from the one the author defends.

correct_answer: (D) a hypothesis framed too loosely for any experiment to count against it.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says a null result 'may show that the effect does not exist, or that the sample was too small to detect it, or that a reagent was contaminated, or that a student misread the protocol'. A loosely framed hypothesis is not among these possibilities.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 lists 'that the sample was too small to detect it', so this is mentioned.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 lists 'that a student misread the protocol', which this paraphrases, so this is mentioned.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 lists 'that a reagent was contaminated' among the possibilities, so this is mentioned.

common_misconception: Overlooking a paraphrase of one listed item and choosing it as the exception.

correct_answer: (A) illustrate the kind of error that critics expected untrained volunteers to make when recording what they saw.
explanation: Paragraph 1 reports 'the objection most often raised' that amateurs would err; the warbler example shows the kind of misidentification feared: the expert distinguishes two species that the walker 'may not know' exist.

option_rationales.B: The passage makes no comparison between song and appearance; the fragment of song only shows what the trained expert can do.
option_rationales.C: Photography is mentioned in paragraph 2 as a later response to hard identification; the warbler example belongs to the critics' objection in paragraph 1.
option_rationales.D: Accuracy is never compared across groups of organisms, and the claim of proof is far stronger than anything in paragraph 1.

common_misconception: Linking the example to the photographing practice of paragraph 2 rather than to the objection it sits in.

correct_answer: (B) may appear common there partly because the suburbs are where many observers happen to be.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says a map of sightings is 'partly a map of the observers', and the bird 'may simply be living where the watchers live'. Its apparent abundance may reflect where people look.

option_rationales.A: This is misidentification, which paragraph 3 explicitly sets aside: the stubborn problem 'lies not in what volunteers see but in where and when they look'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says that 'no amount of skill in identification' will correct this distortion, and it compares the places observers visit, not their skill.
option_rationales.D: The passage mentions farmland and industrial estates only as places volunteers visit less; it makes no claim about birds moving between habitats.

common_misconception: Reverting to misidentification, the problem the paragraph has just moved past.

correct_answer: (C) sympathetic to why it was raised, while holding that another weakness of volunteer data matters more.
explanation: Paragraph 2 grants that 'The worry was reasonable' but says it was 'aimed at the lesser target'; paragraphs 3 and 4 identify sampling as the 'more stubborn' problem. The attitude is respectful but corrective.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 calls the sampling problem 'more stubborn' and paragraph 4 says it is 'harder to correct than misidentification', so the author does not rank misidentification first.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says 'Errors do not vanish' and calls the worry 'reasonable'; the author never claims volunteers are as accurate individually as specialists.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 opens 'The worry was reasonable', which shows the author understands the doubt perfectly well.

common_misconception: Taking the author's answer to the objection in paragraph 2 as outright dismissal, or as full agreement.

correct_answer: (D) A frog survey in which each volunteer visits an allocated pond on set evenings, wherever that pond happens to lie.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says projects that take the sampling bias seriously 'ask some volunteers to survey assigned locations at fixed times', giving 'a sample whose shape is known'. Allocated ponds on set evenings do exactly this.

option_rationales.A: Checking improbable records is the paragraph 2 remedy for misidentification; it does not change where and when observations are made.
option_rationales.B: Open recording from chosen places reproduces the bias of paragraph 3, since people walk 'along popular footpaths' and near their homes.
option_rationales.C: Training improves identification, but paragraph 3 says 'no amount of skill in identification' separates the map of species from the map of observers.

common_misconception: Choosing an option that improves accuracy of identification, which answers the earlier concern, not the one in paragraphs 3 and 4.

correct_answer: (D) regarded ordinary people as defined only by an absence of knowledge that experts were expected to fill.
explanation: Paragraph 1 says the model assumed resistance came from not understanding, to be fixed by 'supplying the missing facts', and it 'treated the public as a vessel with a hole in it, defined entirely by what it lacked'. The image means the public was seen only as a lack to be filled.

option_rationales.A: The image describes how the model saw the public, not a failing of scientists; that criticism comes later and is the author's, not the model's.
option_rationales.B: This reads the hole as a leak; the same sentence glosses the image as being 'defined entirely by what it lacked', which is about emptiness, not about failing to retain.
option_rationales.C: The press is never mentioned; the image concerns the supposed emptiness of the public mind.

common_misconception: Taking 'hole' to mean a leak and so choosing the option about retaining facts.

correct_answer: (C) Public resistance to expert conclusions often reflects judgements about trust and risk, so supplying facts is at best a partial remedy.
explanation: Paragraph 2 shows that knowledge does not guarantee acceptance, paragraph 3 that scepticism may be 'a judgement about whom to trust and who pays', and paragraph 4 concedes that explanation is sometimes what is needed but rejects making it 'the whole story'.

option_rationales.A: The dam example in paragraph 3 illustrates why scepticism may be rational; the passage proposes no legal remedy, so this adds an outside prescription.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says only that it is 'easy to find' well-read people who reject the consensus; it makes no claim that the well informed are generally more likely to do so.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says some people need 'a good explanation' and that good communication 'will sometimes end in explanation', so giving up explaining contradicts the author.

common_misconception: Overstating the author's critique into a rejection of explanation altogether.

correct_answer: (B) show that scepticism can rest on considerations of trust and fairness that a technical briefing leaves out.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says the villagers understand the hydrology but also know that past assurances failed, that benefits go elsewhere and that they would bear the loss. Their scepticism is 'a judgement about whom to trust and who pays', which the engineers' presentation 'omits'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 introduces 'The deeper failure', a different point from paragraph 2; the villagers' doubts rest on past assurances and the distribution of benefits and losses, not on extra reading.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says only that the villagers 'may follow the hydrology perfectly well'; it does not rank their understanding above the engineers'.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says the scepticism 'may be quite rational even when the hydrology is sound', so the example does not depend on the dam being unsafe.

common_misconception: Assuming the example must show the dam to be dangerous, and missing 'even when the hydrology is sound'.

correct_answer: (A) a briefing under the deficit model can be accurate and still address a question other than the one troubling its audience.
explanation: In paragraph 3 the engineers explain hydrology, which the villagers already follow, while omitting the matters of trust and loss that drive their doubt. To 'at least explain the right thing' implies that the alternative can explain something true but beside the point, as in the dam example.

option_rationales.B: The author says communication should begin by 'asking what an audience already knows, fears and has experienced'; restricting explanation to direct questions is an extreme rule the passage does not state.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says such communication 'will sometimes end in explanation', not that acceptance will follow; the option promises an outcome the author does not.
option_rationales.D: Nothing in the passage says deficit-model explanations were inaccurate; in paragraph 3 the hydrology may be 'sound'. The phrase 'the right thing' concerns relevance, not accuracy.

common_misconception: Reading 'right' as 'factually correct' rather than 'relevant to the audience's actual concern'.

correct_answer: (C) her account of past events hangs together and explains the scattered evidence she has found.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says the geologist assembles 'a history from traces' and that 'her standard of success is the coherence of a narrative that accounts for scattered evidence'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the geologist 'is not testing a hypothesis by experiment' at all, so this cannot be her standard.
option_rationales.B: This is the ingenuity paragraph 2 attributes to the astronomer, who 'cannot intervene' and must find suitable natural cases.
option_rationales.D: Making instruments work is what paragraph 2 says occupies the chemist; it is not given as the geologist's standard.

common_misconception: Confusing the three scientists of paragraph 2 with one another.

correct_answer: (D) a description broad enough to fit every science would be too vague to tell any researcher what to do next.
explanation: Paragraph 1 offers a dilemma: a single recipe 'either excludes much of their work or becomes so general that it no longer guides anyone'. The second horn means that a recipe stretched to cover astronomy, geology and chemistry alike would say too little to direct anyone's work.

option_rationales.A: The passage calls the sequence 'tidy' and 'easy to examine', the opposite of too complicated; the remark describes a hypothetical broader recipe.
option_rationales.B: The author does not recommend separate recipes; paragraph 4 says what the sciences share are norms that 'cannot be captured in a flowchart'.
option_rationales.C: The passage never says scientists rely on intuition or luck; the remark concerns the usefulness of a description, not how researchers actually proceed.

common_misconception: Choosing the option about separate recipes, which turns a criticism into a prescription the author does not make.

correct_answer: (A) gives too much weight to criticism by colleagues as a way of testing scientific claims.
explanation: The textbook sequence makes no mention of criticism by colleagues; in paragraph 4 the author names exposure 'to colleagues who are expected to attack' claims as one of the norms the sciences genuinely share. The author therefore could not object that the sequence overstates it.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the chemist spends much time on something 'the textbook sequence ignores entirely: making instruments and procedures work at all', so this is an objection.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the sequence 'leaves the public poorly prepared' for research in which 'experts disagree for long periods', so this is an objection the author makes.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the sequence 'encourages the view that sciences which cannot experiment are somehow lesser', so this is one of the author's objections.

common_misconception: Missing that the correct answer reverses the author's own positive account in paragraph 4.

correct_answer: (B) In one long-established and productive science, central claims are customarily shielded from colleagues' attacks and are not expected to be revised in the light of evidence.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says what 'unites' the sciences is a set of communal norms: claims are exposed to attack, stated so that evidence could tell against them, and given up when it does. A productive science in which the community itself does not hold these expectations would show that the norms are not common to the sciences.

option_rationales.A: The author claims such students would 'understand science better', not that they would perform procedures better; tests of procedure do not touch the claim about shared norms.
option_rationales.C: This agrees with paragraph 2, which describes the geologist as assembling 'a history from traces'; it confirms the variety of methods rather than weakening the claim about shared norms.
option_rationales.D: The norms are things scientists are 'expected' to do; individual lapses are compatible with the norm, and paragraph 3 already allows that experts may 'disagree for long periods'.

common_misconception: Choosing the option about stubborn individuals, which concerns lapses from a norm rather than the absence of the norm.

correct_answer: (A) responding sensibly to the impossibility of reading everything that is published in their field.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says the literature is 'far larger than anyone could read', that a familiar name is 'a cheap signal' of worth, and that readers who rely on it 'are not being foolish'.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says the unknown co-author 'did much of the work' in one illustrative case; readers' awareness is never discussed, and 'usually' generalises the example.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says forbidding readers to notice names 'would be both futile and costly', so the author would not recommend training them to ignore names.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 rejects 'Condemning it as mere snobbery' and explains the habit as 'a reasonable strategy for coping with abundance', which is a practical consideration.

common_misconception: Assuming the author condemns the readers because the effect is unfair to unknown researchers.

correct_answer: (C) accepting it as accurate as far as it goes, while holding that it misses the more serious harm.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says the fairness description 'is correct within its limits, but it understates what is at stake'. Paragraphs 3 and 4 then identify the larger cost: a field's resources are committed for 'reasons that are partly accidental'.

option_rationales.A: Nothing in the passage scorns the fairness view or its holders; the author calls it accurate and builds on it.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 calls the description 'correct within its limits', and paragraph 3 shows careers diverging for reasons 'partly accidental', so the author does not think credit tracks merit.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the effect is 'less an injustice done to individuals than a distortion in how a field allocates its bets', so the author does not regard it chiefly as an injustice.

common_misconception: Choosing the 'endorsing it fully' option because the author agrees that the effect is unfair.

correct_answer: (D) A funding agency that assesses a share of the applications it receives with the applicants' names and records removed.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says the remedy is 'to loosen the link between attention and money', for example 'to judge some grant proposals without knowing who wrote them'. Blind assessment of some applications does this.

option_rationales.A: This addresses credit owed to individuals, which paragraph 4 calls the lesser issue; it does nothing to loosen the link between attention and money.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the remedy 'is not to forbid readers from noticing names, which would be both futile and costly'; hiding authors from readers is exactly that.
option_rationales.C: A citation ranking advertises the attention already received and would strengthen, not loosen, the conversion of attention into resources.

common_misconception: Choosing the anonymous journal because it also hides names, without noticing that the author rejects hiding names from readers.

correct_answer: (B) a field may commit its resources to some ideas and neglect others for reasons that have little to do with their merit.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says compounding advantage means a field 'has placed a heavy bet on one line of work for reasons that are partly accidental', while ideas from less visible researchers go untested. Paragraph 4 states that the effect is 'less an injustice done to individuals than a distortion in how a field allocates its bets'.

option_rationales.A: Departure from science is not mentioned; the passage describes ideas waiting 'years for a hearing', not people leaving the profession.
option_rationales.C: The passage never discusses what eminent researchers believe about themselves; the harm it describes lies in how resources are allocated.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 warns against treating a name as 'a reason to believe', but paragraph 2 calls attention to names reasonable, and the passage says the effect is above all 'a distortion in how a field allocates its bets'.

common_misconception: Choosing the option about readers' credulity, which draws on the last sentence but is not what the author ranks as the main harm.

correct_answer: (A) separating proposals that are scientifically sound from those that are not, at the threshold of quality.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says judgement 'is exercised in full at the threshold, where panels are reasonably good at separating the sound from the unsound'.

option_rationales.B: Paragraphs 1 and 2 say the opposite: near the top, the line 'often separates projects that no one present could distinguish with any confidence'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the biases at the margin need not be 'deliberate', which suggests panels may not notice them, not that they recognise them.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 describes panels as wary of 'projects whose payoff is uncertain'; nothing says they predict payoffs well.

common_misconception: Assuming that panels which judge soundness well must also rank well, which paragraphs 1 and 2 deny.

correct_answer: (C) grant it but set it aside as a weak justification before presenting what the author considers the stronger one.
explanation: Paragraph 2 reports the efficiency defence, grants it ('This is true'), calls it 'the weakest part of the case', and then says 'The stronger argument is about honesty'. Its role is to be set aside in favour of the honesty argument.

option_rationales.A: The author does not argue that savings outweigh anything; the efficiency case is called 'the weakest part of the case', and paragraph 4 denies that judgement is lost.
option_rationales.B: The passage never says why agencies adopted lotteries; paragraph 1 links the experiments to the 'predicament' of indistinguishable proposals, not to workload.
option_rationales.D: The author accepts this view ('This is true'), so the purpose is not to refute it.

common_misconception: Choosing the 'concede' option, which captures the grant but invents a weighing the author never performs.

correct_answer: (D) when merit cannot settle a decision, the outcome is shaped by systematic leanings rather than by pure luck.
explanation: Paragraph 3 explains the sentence: when merit cannot separate proposals, 'other preferences fill the gap', which together 'tilt the funding line toward the safe and the recognisable'. The 'chance' in ranking is therefore not random but leans in a consistent direction.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the biases are mild and that 'none need be deliberate', so deliberate favouritism misstates it.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says a lottery 'removes this tilt at the margin'; the threshold is described in paragraph 4 as the place where panels judge well, not as a source of bias.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says ranking 'already contains a large element of chance'; the sentence adds that this chance is tilted, not that it is small.

common_misconception: Reading 'not neutral' as deliberate unfairness, or as a criticism of lotteries.

correct_answer: (B) Projects ranked just above the funding line have consistently gone on to outperform those ranked just below it.
explanation: The reply in paragraph 4 rests on the premise that the belief that reward follows merit 'is, at the margin, already false'. If projects just above the line reliably outperform those just below, the ranking near the line does track merit, and a lottery would then replace a meaningful judgement; the premise, and with it the reply, collapses.

option_rationales.A: This supports the reply, which holds that the loser of a draw 'has at least been told the truth'; a preference for that outcome strengthens rather than weakens it.
option_rationales.C: This concerns the efficiency argument of paragraph 2, which the author calls the weakest part of the case; it does not touch the reply about motivation.
option_rationales.D: This bears on the claim that panels judge well at the threshold, which answers a different objection in paragraph 4; occasional disagreement is also compatible with being 'reasonably good'.

common_misconception: Choosing the option about disagreement at the threshold because it is about panels' judgement, without noticing that it addresses a different objection.

correct_answer: (B) Where panels cannot reliably separate good proposals, drawing lots is preferable to a ranking that disguises chance as judgement.
explanation: Paragraphs 2 to 4 argue that near the funding line ranking 'already contains a large element of chance' that is hidden and tilted, so an open lottery above a threshold is more honest; paragraph 5 limits this to cases 'where judgement has reached its limit'. The correct answer keeps both the claim and its scope.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 offers publication as something agencies 'that decline to draw lots might still learn'; the author does not recommend it in place of lotteries, which the passage defends where 'judgement has reached its limit'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 calls efficiency 'the weakest part of the case'; the author's central argument is about honesty.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says panels judge well 'at the threshold', and paragraph 5 says lotteries are not recommended 'everywhere', so both the call for wholesale replacement and the claim of bias at every stage overstate the case.

common_misconception: Choosing the option drawn from paragraph 5 because it echoes 'the pretence of precision', without seeing that it reverses the author's support for lotteries.

correct_answer: (A) a competent reader who follows a paper's written methods will be able to obtain the findings it reports.
explanation: Paragraph 1 says 'the implicit promise is that anyone competent who follows them will see what the authors saw', and paragraph 2 says this promise 'is only partly kept' because tacit skills cannot be written down.

option_rationales.B: Sharing materials is never mentioned; the promise in paragraph 1 is that anyone 'who follows' the listed methods 'will see what the authors saw'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 describes knowledge as 'independent of the particular people who first produced it', which concerns independence from persons, not the correction of their errors.
option_rationales.D: This is the 'natural suspicion' that paragraph 1 says follows from the promise; it is a consequence of believing the promise, not the promise itself.

common_misconception: Choosing the 'natural suspicion', which is closely tied to the promise but is what follows from it.

correct_answer: (C) may have acquired the decisive skill without identifying which part of the procedure it concerned.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says the successful groups often could not 'say afterwards what the crucial difference was', because even the original authors 'did not know which of the many things they did without thinking were the things that mattered'. The skill was transferred without being identified.
