option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says such knowledge 'is not secret', and paragraph 3 says the authors themselves 'did not know' which of their actions mattered, so nothing was deliberately withheld.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says 'the written instructions were not wrong', only incomplete, so there were no errors to discover.
option_rationales.D: The passage attributes success to contact with the original laboratory, not to greater care; paragraph 2 says the missing knowledge is 'acquired by doing and by watching others do'.

common_misconception: Assuming that success after a visit must mean that information was hidden or that the published account was mistaken.

correct_answer: (D) Cooks using a baker's detailed recipe keep failing to match her bread until one spends a week in her kitchen, after which he succeeds without knowing what he changed.
explanation: Paragraph 3 describes groups that fail from written descriptions alone and succeed after time in the original laboratory, 'often without being able to say afterwards what the crucial difference was', while the instructions themselves 'were not wrong'. Only the baker's kitchen case has all three features: accurate but insufficient instructions, success through presence, and an unidentified difference.

option_rationales.A: This depends on deliberate secrecy, whereas paragraph 2 says the knowledge 'is not secret' and paragraph 3 says even the authors did not know what mattered.
option_rationales.B: In paragraph 3 the readers of the instructions fail; here they succeed, so the situation reverses the pattern the passage describes.
option_rationales.C: Here the instructions are wrong and a written correction fixes them; paragraph 3 says 'the written instructions were not wrong', and the missing element could not be written down.

common_misconception: Choosing the secret-ingredient case because a visit or an insider also brings success there, overlooking that the passage rules out secrecy.

correct_answer: (C) A field could report its techniques far more fully than it now does and still find that some of its results are hard to reproduce elsewhere.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says longer methods sections 'will capture the explicit portion of a technique more fully while leaving the tacit portion exactly where it was'. Fuller reporting is worthwhile, but tacit skill would still be missing, so some results could remain hard to reproduce.

option_rationales.A: The author explains why replication can fail even for sound claims but never says failures should as a rule be blamed on replicators; the option turns a possibility into a general verdict.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 5 says this 'is not a reason to distrust that knowledge, since skills can be tested by their results as surely as statements can'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says 'A great deal that is now left out of papers could be written down' and that omitting it 'deserves the criticism it receives', so reporting reform is not wasted.

common_misconception: Choosing the option that dismisses reporting reform, which ignores the concession at the start of paragraph 4.

correct_answer: (D) lengthening methods sections until each of them captures the whole of the technique it describes.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says that 'Demanding ever longer methods sections will capture the explicit portion of a technique more fully while leaving the tacit portion exactly where it was'. A methods section that captures the whole of a technique, tacit portion included, is what the author argues is impossible, so this is not endorsed.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 proposes 'funding researchers to visit one another's laboratories', so this is endorsed.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 proposes 'treating the training of a replicator as part of the cost of a replication', so this is endorsed.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says much that is left out 'could be written down' and that omitting it 'whether to save space or to protect an advantage, deserves the criticism it receives', so the author endorses including it.

common_misconception: Treating the endorsement of fuller reporting as an endorsement of complete reporting, and so picking the option about omitted details as the exception.

correct_answer: (A) argue that an unreliable narrator's deepest effect is to make readers question the trust they give to all narration.
explanation: Paragraph 1 states the usual view (a puzzle), paragraph 2 calls it 'thin', and paragraph 3 gives the author's position: the best uses of the device bring 'a change in how the reader regards narration as such'. Paragraph 4 is a concession that supports the same point.

option_rationales.B: This is the 'game of detection' of paragraph 1, which paragraph 2 calls 'thin'; the passage moves beyond it rather than setting out to explain it.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says such books 'can be thrilling once', so they do give pleasure; the paragraph is a concession, not the purpose of the passage.
option_rationales.D: The passage never ranks the two kinds of novel; paragraph 3 mentions the calm third-person narrator only as a voice we trust too readily, not as a superior model.

common_misconception: Taking the detection view the author reports, or the concession in paragraph 4, for the passage's purpose.

correct_answer: (B) the one question they raised has been answered, leaving the reader nothing to wonder about.
explanation: Paragraph 4: 'On a second reading, however, they tend to go flat, because the only question they posed has been answered.' The correct answer restates this reason.

option_rationales.A: The passage says nothing about clues becoming obvious; it explains the flatness by the answered question alone.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 contrasts lying with selecting only when discussing ordinary narrators; that contrast is not the reason given for these novels going flat.
option_rationales.D: Resentment is never mentioned; paragraph 4 gives a different reason, that 'the only question they posed has been answered'.

common_misconception: Supplying a plausible reason from general reading experience instead of the one the passage states.

correct_answer: (D) the reader's version of what really happened rests on testimony that the reader has already decided to doubt.
explanation: Paragraph 2 goes on to say that the true story we assemble is 'built from the materials of the account we have decided to distrust'. The correct answer states this consequence.

option_rationales.A: The narrator's intentions are never discussed; the point concerns where the reader's evidence comes from, not what the narrator means to reveal.
option_rationales.B: The passage makes no recommendation to novelists; it describes the reader's position without proposing a remedy.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the opposite: 'we have no other witness'.

common_misconception: Reading the remark as a claim about the narrator's intentions rather than about the reader's evidence.

correct_answer: (C) A juror who catches one witness contradicting himself starts to ask what the apparently consistent witnesses may also have left out.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says that having learned to read one voice against itself, 'we begin to notice how much we ordinarily grant to voices that give no sign of strain'. The juror who turns his scrutiny to the consistent witnesses mirrors this extension of attention from one untrustworthy voice to all voices.

option_rationales.A: This matches the view in paragraph 1, where the reader who spots the discrepancy 'has finished the work'; the author rejects that as the device's best effect.
option_rationales.B: This replaces a bad witness with trusted ones, which is the 'thin' detection picture; the author's point is that distrust should extend to voices 'that give no sign of strain'.
option_rationales.D: The effect the author describes is awareness that every narrator will 'select, arrange and omit' (paragraph 3), a sharper attention to all voices, not a wholesale rejection of one genre.

common_misconception: Choosing the detective or the first juror, who stop at catching one liar, which is the view the author calls thin.

correct_answer: (C) illustrate how a story makes an unstated history felt through what it chooses to show and leave out.
explanation: The example comes straight after the claim that 'selection pressed hard enough becomes a kind of meaning in itself', and the passage says the eleven years 'are present precisely because they are withheld'. It illustrates meaning made by omission.

option_rationales.A: One example cannot establish what stories most often concern, and the passage makes no claim about the usual subjects of stories.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 argues the reverse: giving the woman 'a history' makes the photograph 'one detail among many'.
option_rationales.D: The photograph matters because of what it implies, not because objects of that kind are better than others; the passage ranks no types of detail.

common_misconception: Reading the example literally, as a point about subject matter or objects, rather than about method.

correct_answer: (B) the length of time over which the reader lives alongside its characters and watches them change.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'A novel accumulates; it earns its effects through duration, letting the reader live alongside its people for enough days that change in them can be felt as change.'

option_rationales.A: Information is discussed only in paragraph 3, as what weakens an expanded story; it is never named as the novel's source of effect.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 assigns selection to the short story: 'What it has instead is selection'. The novel is contrasted with it.
option_rationales.D: Subplots and minor characters are not mentioned; the passage names duration, not variety, as the novel's resource.

common_misconception: Confusing the novel's method with the story's, since the two are described in adjacent sentences.

correct_answer: (D) a compliment that measures the story by a standard that belongs to a different form.
explanation: Paragraph 1 cites the phrase as an example of the habit of treating the story as a smaller novel, and paragraph 4 concludes that 'judging it by the novel's standards will reliably mistake its strengths for omissions'. The praise is such a judgement.

option_rationales.A: The passage criticises the standard such critics apply, not their attentiveness, and a claim about most critics goes beyond anything stated.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says the praise treats 'richness of that kind' as the measure of success 'as though' it were, signalling disagreement; the story's force lies elsewhere.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says publishers regard collections as 'harder to sell' and that the habit is 'reinforced' by them, so the praise belongs to the same habit, not to a change in it.

common_misconception: Taking the praise at face value because it sounds generous to the story.

correct_answer: (A) Readers comparing admired stories with later full-length versions by the same writers mostly found the longer versions stronger, because of the added history.
explanation: Paragraph 3 claims that 'expanding a fine story so rarely improves it' because filling the gaps with information weakens implication. Evidence that expanded versions are generally found more powerful, precisely because of the added history, strikes at both the claim and its reason.

option_rationales.B: Sales concern the trade's habit in paragraph 1, not whether expansion improves a story; the fact is irrelevant to the claim.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 already concedes that 'more than one long novel began as a few pages', so this is consistent with the argument and does not show that expansion improves fine stories.
option_rationales.D: This supports, if anything, the value of the story's method and says nothing about whether expanded stories are better or worse.

common_misconception: Choosing the novels that grew from short pieces, which the author has already conceded.

correct_answer: (B) show that an unhappy ending forced on a story from outside is as arbitrary as a contrived happy one.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says the fault of contrived happy endings is that 'nothing in the preceding chapters made them necessary', and then offers the carriage death as 'A catastrophe imposed in the same way', 'no less arbitrary'. The example extends the fault to unhappy endings.

option_rationales.A: The author says such a catastrophe is 'no more truthful', not less, and paragraph 4 allows that some tragic endings are honest; the option overstates and ranks.
option_rationales.C: The period setting is incidental; the point is that the death is imposed 'because the author wanted the book to feel weighty', not that accidents are unbelievable.
option_rationales.D: This is the view of paragraph 1 that the example is meant to unsettle; the carriage death is called 'arbitrary', not courageous.

common_misconception: Taking the example as a general verdict on tragic endings rather than as a parallel case.

correct_answer: (D) leaves the reader reassured about the world that the novel has depicted.
explanation: Paragraph 3 defines the term: 'Some endings also console; they leave the reader reassured about the world the book has shown.' The correct answer paraphrases this definition.

option_rationales.A: This is an everyday sense of consoling, but the passage defines the word differently, as leaving the reader 'reassured about the world the book has shown'.
option_rationales.B: Rewards and punishments are not mentioned; the passage defines consolation by its effect on the reader's view of the world.
option_rationales.C: This is what the passage calls closing: 'it marks the point after which the story will not be told'. The author separates it from consoling.

common_misconception: Choosing the definition of closure, which sits in the preceding sentence, or the everyday sense of the word.

correct_answer: (A) readers ought to prefer novels that end in marriage or reconciliation to novels that end in failure.
explanation: The author's test in paragraph 4 is indifferent to tone: an ending is honest 'whether that place is a marriage or a grave'. Nowhere does the author rank happy endings above unhappy ones; the passage defends happy endings only against blanket suspicion.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says readers 'are right to feel cheated' by endings that 'arrive from outside the story', so the author does make this claim.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 calls closure 'a formal necessity, since a story must stop somewhere', so the author makes this claim.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the unhappy note 'can be just as comfortably familiar to readers who have learned to expect gloom', so the author makes this claim.

common_misconception: Mistaking the defence of happy endings against prejudice for a preference for them.

correct_answer: (C) Such a reader treats a dislike of reassurance as if it were an objection to bringing a story to a definite end.
explanation: Paragraph 3: the suspicious reader 'objects to the consolation, and then mistakes the objection for an argument against closure itself'. The correct answer restates this confusion of the two functions the author has just distinguished.

option_rationales.A: The author never endorses the objection to consolation, calling consolation merely 'a choice'; the option assigns the author a verdict the passage does not give.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says unhappy endings are 'credited with courage', but a requirement on every serious novel is far stronger than anything attributed to the reader.
option_rationales.D: The phrase 'as though the honest book would be the one that refused to finish' is the author's account of where the reader's confusion leads, not a preference the reader holds; paragraph 1 shows this reader admiring tragic endings.

common_misconception: Reading the author's 'as though' clause as a description of the reader's actual taste.

correct_answer: (A) the reader already knows the point in the poem at which a turn is expected.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'a turn in the ninth line registers as a turn only because the reader knows where turns are expected'. The correct answer restates this.

option_rationales.B: The passage does not describe what a turn contains or how readers are taught; it says only that they know 'where turns are expected'.
option_rationales.C: Line length is never mentioned; the passage says only that the length of the whole poem is fixed.
option_rationales.D: The passage says nothing about abandoning the rhyme scheme; it attributes the effect to the reader's expectation.

common_misconception: Supplying outside knowledge about sonnets instead of the reason the passage gives.

correct_answer: (B) show that literary fiction also depends on inherited conventions that can be followed mechanically.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says the hardening of conventions into formula is 'the same' in literary fiction, 'which has its own conventions', and gives these devices as examples, adding that some writers 'complete them dutifully'. They support the conclusion that no books lack conventions.

option_rationales.A: This is the view of paragraph 1 that the author rejects; the devices are offered as conventions, and the author adds that some writers 'complete them dutifully', so they are not inventions.
option_rationales.C: The author says 'the same is true' of literary fiction, an equivalence, not a claim that it is more formulaic than every genre.
option_rationales.D: Borrowing between the two is never discussed; the devices are presented as literary fiction's own conventions.

common_misconception: Reading the examples as an attack that ranks literary fiction below genre fiction.

correct_answer: (C) depending on close knowledge of the conventions against which a particular book can be measured.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says devoted readers, having read 'a hundred novels built on the same frame', notice the smallest variation, and that their pleasure is 'the active one of comparison'. Comparison requires knowledge of the frame against which each book is measured.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 describes alertness to 'the smallest variation', not to compliance; checking rules is closer to the formula writer's 'checklist' in paragraph 4.
option_rationales.B: The passage never compares these pleasures; it says only that the unconventional novel cannot make departures felt so precisely.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the pleasure is 'not the passive pleasure of repetition', which this option describes.

common_misconception: Equating familiarity with repetition, which the passage explicitly rules out.

correct_answer: (D) How sharply a departure is felt depends on how firmly the reader expected the thing departed from.
explanation: The author's reason is that 'the unconventional novel has no settled expectation to depart from'. For that to explain the difference in precision, the strength of a felt departure must depend on the strength of the prior expectation, which is what the correct answer states.

option_rationales.A: The author explains the difference by the absence of 'settled expectation', not by inattention; the argument would stand even if both readers were equally attentive.
option_rationales.B: The claim concerns how precisely a departure is felt, not how much the book is valued; the argument needs no ranking of books.
option_rationales.C: Breadth of reading is not needed; even a reader of a few detective stories knows that 'the culprit must be among the people introduced'.

common_misconception: Picking an option about readers' qualities instead of the link between expectation and effect that the reason requires.

correct_answer: (C) refusing to leave at all, until the next line narrows her refusal to the weather.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'For the length of the pause the woman refuses to leave at all; the next line shrinks the refusal to a matter of weather.'

option_rationales.A: Nothing in the example suggests anyone else forbids her; the refusal is her own ('she said').
option_rationales.B: This is the reading the whole sentence finally gives; paragraph 2 says that during the pause 'the woman refuses to leave at all'.
option_rationales.D: Sincerity is never raised; the example concerns how the line break changes the scope of the refusal.

common_misconception: Choosing the meaning of the completed sentence instead of the meaning the single line has during the pause.

correct_answer: (B) give a text the look of verse while adding nothing to its meaning or its pace.
explanation: The sentence defines the term by its condition: 'If nothing is lost, if no meaning that the breaks created has vanished and no pace has been flattened, then the breaks were decoration.' Decorative breaks are those that contribute neither meaning nor pace.

option_rationales.A: Rhyme and metre are what free verse has given up (paragraph 1); decorative breaks are defined by doing no work, not by reintroducing them.
option_rationales.C: The author uses 'decoration' as a verdict of failure ('then the breaks were decoration') and nowhere calls appearance a legitimate aim.
option_rationales.D: The word refers to the breaks, not to the poem's vocabulary; ornamental diction is never discussed.

common_misconception: Reading 'decoration' in its neutral everyday sense rather than as the failure the test detects.

correct_answer: (A) When the poem is printed as a continuous paragraph, a second sense that one of its lines had carried disappears.
explanation: Paragraph 4's test is to 'set the poem out as prose, read it again, and ask what has gone'; the breaks were doing work if some 'meaning that the breaks created has vanished'. A lost second sense, of the kind shown in paragraph 2, is exactly such a meaning.

option_rationales.B: If the prose version is just as effective, nothing has been lost, which by the author's test would show the breaks were 'decoration'.
option_rationales.C: The test in paragraph 4 is applied to the text by a reader, not to the poet's account of intentions; care in choosing does not show the breaks work.
option_rationales.D: Unequal lines show only that breaks exist; the author's test asks whether anything is lost when they are removed, which this does not establish.

common_misconception: Taking visible features of the lines, or the poet's testimony, as evidence instead of applying the author's own test.

correct_answer: (D) qualified acceptance: it is fair against many poems but cannot become a verdict on the form itself.
explanation: The author answers the objection with the principle of the line as 'a unit of attention' (paragraph 2), yet concedes in paragraph 4 that for much published free verse 'the objection is simply correct'. The test, however, 'cannot do' the work of condemning 'the form as such'. The attitude is acceptance limited to particular poems.

option_rationales.A: The final sentence says the test 'cannot do' this: it cannot 'condemn the form as such'. The option makes the objection a general verdict with exceptions, which reverses the author's position.
option_rationales.B: The author grants that poets give a weak answer ('deserves a better answer than poets usually give it') but then supplies one in paragraphs 2 and 3.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'A good deal of what is published as free verse' fails the test and that there 'the objection is simply correct'.

common_misconception: Choosing the partial agreement option, which sounds balanced but makes the objection right about the form in general.

correct_answer: (B) Flat characters do work of their own in fiction, so treating roundness as the only mark of achievement misreads many novels.
explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 give flat characters functions (registering a society, comedy, fidelity to how others appear), and paragraph 4 concludes that flat and round 'are not grades of achievement but different tools' and that a criticism rewarding only one 'will misread every novel in which both are at work'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says that one particular effect depends on first taking a figure as simple; it does not say round characters in general succeed only this way.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 offers this only as 'a case that' flatness is closer to experience, and paragraph 4 says 'This is not to invert the hierarchy'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the inner-life tradition is 'one powerful tradition' among others; the author does not rank the two kinds of novel.

common_misconception: Choosing the option that inverts the hierarchy, which the author explicitly declines to do.

correct_answer: (C) show how a character's comic effect can depend on his being unable to act in any other way.
explanation: The example follows the claim that fiction's comedy 'depends on repetition', and the passage says the man is funny 'precisely because he could not have done otherwise'. It illustrates comedy arising from fixity.

option_rationales.A: No historical claim about satire is made; the almanac simply gives the man a fixed habit to repeat.
option_rationales.B: The passage makes no claim about the casts of comic novels; it shows how one flat figure produces comedy.
option_rationales.D: The passage says such deepening 'may be a gain, but it is a different book'; it does not claim the novel always gains.

common_misconception: Treating the follow-up remark about deepening him as the purpose of the example.

correct_answer: (A) embodying an unyielding social world against which the changing characters can be measured.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says their fixity 'is how the novel registers the pressure of a world that does not bend, against which its few changing figures can be measured'. The correct answer restates this role.

option_rationales.B: Delivering a message is the use the dismissive view in paragraph 1 allows flat characters; paragraph 2 gives them a different role.
option_rationales.C: Nothing in paragraph 2 links these figures to the reader's position; they represent the society, not the outsider.
option_rationales.D: That effect belongs to the figure 'we had thought simple' in paragraph 4; the aunt and the official are valued for their 'fixity'.

common_misconception: Assigning to these figures a function the passage reserves for other characters or for the view it rejects.

correct_answer: (D) Readers of novels about whole societies report learning the society's pressures almost entirely through the changing main characters, and barely recall the fixed minor ones.
explanation: Paragraph 2 claims that 'a society is felt in fiction partly through the people who never change'. If readers in fact grasp the society through the changing characters and scarcely notice the fixed ones, the proposed function of flat characters is undercut.

option_rationales.A: How often a kind of novel is studied is irrelevant to whether fixed characters convey a society's pressure.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 is about how such novels work, not about which books critics like; a critic's taste does not bear on how a society is felt in fiction.
option_rationales.C: This is consistent with paragraph 3, which links flatness to comedy, and does not challenge the claim that such figures register a society.

common_misconception: Choosing an option about critics' preferences, which touches the passage's subject but not the mechanism paragraph 2 asserts.

correct_answer: (C) opens with a thesis and restates it at the close, after setting out evidence and dealing with objections.
explanation: Paragraph 2: it 'opens with a thesis, marshals evidence in its favour, dispatches objections and restates the thesis at the close'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the reverse: writers learn to treat 'any movement of thought' as a defect 'to be removed in revision'.
option_rationales.B: The passage calls it 'a miniature treatise', not a replacement for one, and says nothing about its origin.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says its virtues 'are real virtues, and there are good reasons to teach them'.

common_misconception: Overlooking the author's concession that the school essay has real virtues.

correct_answer: (D) a voice that presents its claims as if they did not depend on anyone's particular position or experience.
explanation: The phrase is set against the essayist's 'I', which 'marks the scope of a claim: this is how the matter looks from here'. The treatise's impersonal voice instead claims no particular location, which is why its claims are 'harder to locate'.

option_rationales.A: The phrase concerns where the claims are made from, not what they are about; the treatise is credited with 'clarity of claim' in paragraph 2.
option_rationales.B: This reads the phrase literally; the contrast is with the essayist's 'I', a matter of voice, not of authorship.
option_rationales.C: That describes the 'meandering essay' of paragraph 5, not the impersonal treatise, which states its conclusion plainly.

common_misconception: Confusing the impersonal treatise with the evasive essay of paragraph 5.

correct_answer: (A) Its manner of presentation can make a conclusion seem more inevitable than the evidence by itself warrants.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'The treatise presents its conclusion as if it were the only place the evidence could lead', and paragraph 4 adds that its objectivity is 'always also a manner' that can be adopted by writers 'whose claims have not earned it'. Together these imply that the form can lend a conclusion more inevitability than it has.

option_rationales.B: Self-display is said of the essay's 'I'; paragraph 4 allows that the treatise's objectivity 'is sometimes real', so calling it a disguise in every case contradicts the passage.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 grants that its virtues are real and that 'there are good reasons to teach them'; the author regrets what was lost, not that the treatise is taught.
option_rationales.D: The author contrasts how visible the route to a conclusion is, not how reliable conclusions are; nothing is said about which form reaches truer conclusions.

common_misconception: Turning the author's comparison of forms into a verdict on their reliability or their place in teaching.

correct_answer: (B) Readers shown an argument that included an alternative the writer had rejected could state reasoned objections to its conclusion more readily than readers shown the conclusion alone.
explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that by 'showing the alternatives it passed through' the essay equips the reader to contest its conclusion. A finding that readers who see a rejected alternative can object more readily is direct evidence for that mechanism.

option_rationales.A: Greater acceptance does not show readers were better able to disagree; if anything it points the other way.
option_rationales.C: Enjoyment is not the claim; the question is whether seeing the route to a conclusion equips readers to contest it.
option_rationales.D: This bears on the virtues of the school essay granted in paragraph 2, not on the reader's capacity to disagree with a provisional essay.

common_misconception: Choosing the finding about abandoned paths and agreement, which shares the correct answer's setup but measures the wrong outcome.

correct_answer: (B) guard the argument against being taken as a defence of writing that never commits itself to a claim.
explanation: Paragraph 5 opens 'None of this licenses formlessness' and distinguishes genuine provisionality from 'the meandering essay that circles its subject without ever risking a claim'. Its role is to block a misreading of the argument as a defence of non-commitment.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 says the meandering essay is 'less useful' than the rigid one; it does not say the thesis-first essay is more useful than the provisional essay at its best.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 5 does not return to schooling or to history; it sets a limit on the author's own thesis.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph answers the objection itself: a thought must be 'stated with enough definiteness to fail', and the best essay is 'argument conducted in the open'.

common_misconception: Reading the comparison with the 'rigid' essay as a reversal of the author's preference.

correct_answer: (A) making it easier to find their place in the story after a month away from it.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'recurring figures with distinctive habits of speech helped her find her place', the reader in question being one 'returning after a month's absence'.

option_rationales.B: The passage says nothing about foreshadowing; the figures help a returning reader 'find her place'.
option_rationales.C: Padding is discussed in paragraph 4 as a cost of fixed lengths, but the passage never links it to recurring characters.
option_rationales.D: Resemblance to readers is never mentioned; the habits of speech help readers recognise characters, not identify with them.

common_misconception: Linking the recurring figures to padding because both concern serial length.

correct_answer: (C) the serial novel that readers actually have falls short of a better book its author would otherwise have written.
explanation: Paragraph 1: 'The implication is that the real novel, the one the author would have written in better conditions, lies somewhere beneath the one we have'. The correct answer restates this hidden assumption.

option_rationales.A: The view blames deadlines and payment, external pressures, not indifference; it excuses authors rather than accusing them.
option_rationales.B: The view objects to 'a contrived moment of suspense', and paragraph 4 objects only to cliffhangers 'the story did not need'; the claim that such endings are always a fault in any kind of novel goes far beyond either.
option_rationales.D: The first readers' care is never compared with critics'; paragraph 1 concerns how critics explain the novels' faults.

common_misconception: Reading the excuse as an accusation against the authors.

correct_answer: (D) even-handed, since the author grants it as one possible reading while offering an alternative that is equally reasonable.
explanation: Paragraph 3: 'A purist may regard this as a surrender of artistic control. It can as easily be seen as a kind of conversation'. The phrase 'as easily' grants the purist's reading while presenting an equally available alternative.

option_rationales.A: The author engages the question directly and reframes it; nowhere is it called irrelevant.
option_rationales.B: The author writes 'A purist may regard this as a surrender of artistic control', which allows the reading; there is no contempt and no claim about what critics still hold.
option_rationales.C: The author immediately offers the alternative of 'a kind of conversation', which does not endorse the purist's verdict.

common_misconception: Mistaking the author's reframing for outright rejection.

correct_answer: (B) the ideal of the unified novel arose because serial publication had made novels too long to plan in advance.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says only that the ideal 'has a history of its own' and 'gained much of its authority later, among writers and critics who worked for a different market and under different conditions'. The passage gives no cause for its rise, and certainly not the length of serial novels.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says some cliffhangers 'read awkwardly once the parts were bound together', which supports this.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says authors 'sometimes did' adjust their plans 'in light of how readers responded', which supports this.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says such material could, 'at the pace of first reading, serve as the texture of a world one returned to', which supports this.

common_misconception: Supplying a causal story for the unified-design ideal because the passage places it after the serial era.

correct_answer: (D) point out that qualities once excused in the instalment novel are now admired when they appear in a similar form.
explanation: Paragraph 5 calls it 'an irony in the critical embarrassment': television dramas are praised 'for the very qualities' that 'the instalment novel was once thought to need excusing for'. The comparison reinforces the claim of paragraph 4 that the unified-design standard converts differences into faults.

option_rationales.A: The passage makes no claim about which medium dominates; the comparison concerns how critics judge the same qualities.
option_rationales.B: The author's point is that the old standard was misapplied, not that today's critics have lowered theirs; the irony targets the earlier embarrassment.
option_rationales.C: Discussion between episodes is mentioned as a shared feature, not as a necessary condition; 'only' is unsupported.

common_misconception: Reading the irony as a complaint about falling standards rather than as support for the author's critique of the old standard.

correct_answer: (A) explain each supposedly untranslatable word clearly in the very language said to have no equivalent for it.
explanation: Paragraph 2 notes that each entry pairs the foreign word with an English explanation that readers grasp at once: 'The list, in other words, translates every word it calls untranslatable.' The lists thus refute the claim they are meant to illustrate.

option_rationales.B: The passage never complains about missing usage examples; its point in paragraph 2 is that the lists succeed in explaining the words.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says 'most of the words in them are real', so the author does not fault the lists for inventing words.
option_rationales.D: The author claims neither that all experiences are identical nor that the words are unnecessary; paragraph 3 even treats a word's existence as cultural information.

common_misconception: Choosing a criticism that sounds reasonable in general but is not the one the passage makes.

correct_answer: (C) the way one language bundles into a single word a meaning that another language spreads across several words.
explanation: The sentence says 'one language packages in a single word what another expresses in a phrase', and the next calls this 'a fact about how vocabularies happen to be divided up'. The word therefore means bundling a meaning into one word.

option_rationales.A: That idea belongs to paragraph 3; in paragraph 2 the word contrasts a single word with a phrase expressing the same meaning.
option_rationales.B: Footnotes appear only in paragraph 3, and there they fail to restore losses; 'packages' describes how vocabularies are divided, not a translator's technique.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 does call the lists charming, but in paragraph 2 the subject of 'packages' is a language, not an article.

common_misconception: Carrying over associations of the word (marketing, wrapping) instead of reading the sentence it sits in.

correct_answer: (D) It concedes that something is lost in translation, while locating that loss in qualities other than a word's basic sense.
explanation: Paragraph 3 begins 'This is not to say that nothing is lost' and lists ease of use, register, sound and associations as what a paraphrase cannot reproduce. The meaning itself was shown in paragraph 2 to cross, so the concession relocates the loss rather than reversing the thesis.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the opposite: 'no amount of explanation in a footnote restores them'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 opens 'But the losses are of degree, not of kind', so the concession limits the argument rather than abandoning it, and paragraph 3 never says experiences cannot be grasped.
option_rationales.C: No particular poem is discussed; the paragraph speaks generally of 'a translator working on a poem'.

common_misconception: Reading a concession as a reversal of the author's position.

correct_answer: (A) A translation may render a word's sense accurately and yet fail to carry over much of what that word does in the original.
explanation: Paragraph 2 holds that meaning crosses between languages, and paragraph 3 that a word's register, sound, ease and associations are lost even so. Together these support the correct answer; paragraph 4 sums it up as 'always possible and never complete'.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the losses 'are not peculiar to exotic words' and occur whenever any word is rendered by another.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the way vocabularies are divided 'tells us very little about what their speakers are able to think or feel', which contradicts this.
option_rationales.D: This is too absolute: paragraph 3 says a word's existence is 'a small piece of cultural information', and paragraph 2 says vocabulary tells us 'very little', not nothing.

common_misconception: Picking the absolute version of the author's claim over the hedged one.

correct_answer: (C) arguing that adaptations should be judged by whether they achieve what their source achieved, not by how little they change.
explanation: Paragraph 1 rejects the checklist standard, paragraphs 2 and 3 argue that a film must find 'its own means of doing what the book did', and paragraph 4 restates fidelity as 'a matter of purpose rather than of inventory'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says the complaint against such films 'is fair', so the author does not defend them.
option_rationales.B: The unreliable narrator is an illustration, and paragraph 3 describes how a director could adapt such a novel well.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says a film 'must find something for the camera to look at', and paragraph 3 shows it can succeed; the author never ranks the media.

common_misconception: Taking the central example or the concession for the purpose of the whole passage.

correct_answer: (B) A novel can linger over or summarise events as it likes, whereas a film moves at a pace the viewer cannot slow.
explanation: Paragraph 2 states: 'A novel handles time loosely, lingering or summarising as it likes, while a film runs at a pace the viewer cannot slow.'

option_rationales.A: The 'ready-made audience' in paragraph 4 is what a famous title brings to some films; it is not offered as a general difference between the media.
option_rationales.C: The passage never says novels must preserve incidents; dropped subplots are mentioned only as items on the critics' checklist.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 describes a director framing scenes so the viewer doubts them, so the passage denies that film can show events only from the outside.

common_misconception: Choosing an option that reuses passage phrases in a claim the passage does not make.

correct_answer: (D) A play based on a novel told in letters, which cuts several letters but has each actor speak straight to the audience, so each character's partial view is felt.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says the right question is 'whether the film has found its own means of doing what the book did'. The play drops material but invents a stage device that reproduces the novel's effect of partial, first-person views, so it is the faithful adaptation in the author's sense.

option_rationales.A: This keeps the inventory and loses what the book does, which is exactly the failure paragraph 2 describes.
option_rationales.B: This matches paragraph 4's case of 'keeping the label and throwing away the substance', which the author calls a fair target of complaint.
option_rationales.C: The book's effect lies in the child's confusion; explaining every quarrel from outside discards it, much as the plain staging in paragraph 2 loses the unreliable narrator.

common_misconception: Equating faithfulness with keeping scenes, which the author rejects as a checklist.

correct_answer: (C) justified, though for a reason that a checklist of departures from the book does not capture.
explanation: Paragraph 4: the complaint 'is fair', 'But it is fair for a different reason than the checklist suggests': these films changed 'the wrong things', keeping the label and discarding the substance.

option_rationales.A: The passage never discusses films sending viewers to books, and it calls the complaint fair, not unfair.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'the complaint against them is fair', and the opening sentence 'None of this means that every liberty is defensible' rules this out.
option_rationales.D: Counting departures is the checklist reasoning the author rejects; paragraph 4 says such films fail 'not because they changed things'.

common_misconception: Accepting the right verdict with the wrong reason, the very move the author warns against.

correct_answer: (B) the space available for criticism is scarce and should go to books that deserve attention.
explanation: Paragraph 1: so many books appear that 'the space a journal devotes to criticism is therefore precious', and spending it on a bad book 'is to deny it to a book that deserves attention'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 mentions only 'the pleasure that some critics take in wounding', not personal scores, and this is not the core of the argument.
option_rationales.C: The devaluation of praise is the author's own point against silence in paragraph 3, not part of the argument for it.
option_rationales.D: Sales and publishers' risks are never mentioned in the argument for silence in paragraph 1.

common_misconception: Attributing the author's counter-argument to the side the author is answering.

correct_answer: (A) a reasoned negative argument can be of use even to a reader whom it fails to persuade.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says a careful negative account makes standards public for readers to 'test, dispute and apply'. The reader who 'may end unconvinced' still gains those standards, so the argument is useful even where it does not persuade.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 rejects the view that guiding choice is the only job of criticism; the alertness meant is a way of reading, not a way of choosing.
option_rationales.C: The passage does not advise distrust of one's own admiration; it says the reader gains standards to test and dispute.
option_rationales.D: The sentence allows that the reader 'may end unconvinced'; nothing says he will later be converted.

common_misconception: Reading 'next novel' as a buying decision and so choosing the guide-to-choice view the author rejects.

correct_answer: (A) Criticism exists solely to help readers decide which books are worth their time.
explanation: Paragraph 2 opens: 'it quietly assumes that the only job of criticism is to guide readers in choosing what to read.' The correct answer restates that assumption.

option_rationales.B: The argument appeals to the number of books and the scarcity of space, not to the proportion that are bad; the author never says it assumes most books are poor.
option_rationales.C: The passage never discusses sales; the argument says a neglected book 'simply sinks' but does not compare it with an attacked one.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 mentions that 'some critics' enjoy wounding as the only thing lost by silence; it is not something the argument depends on.

common_misconception: Choosing a premise that sounds congenial to the argument but that the author does not identify.

correct_answer: (C) criticism that never says no can inform readers just as well as criticism that sometimes dissents, provided its praise is carefully argued.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'A notice that can only ever say yes tells the reader very little, because its enthusiasm is not the outcome of a judgement that could have gone the other way.' Careful argument does not remedy this, since the problem is that the verdict could never have been negative. The author would reject this statement; the other three restate paragraphs 2 and 4.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 calls contesting a reputation that shapes public taste 'among the most useful things criticism can do'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 grants that restraint 'does have force' for a modest first novel 'which few people will encounter anyway'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says such an account 'is also an account of what success would have looked like', so the author agrees.

common_misconception: Taking careful argument as enough to rescue praise, and missing that paragraph 3 locates the problem in the impossibility of dispraise.

correct_answer: (D) matters because so many later works respond to it, not because it has been judged to excel.
explanation: The surrounding sentences say a work becomes canonical 'because later writers cannot leave it alone' and is 'the one you must have read in order to understand a great many others'. A medal is a verdict of excellence; a position in a network is defined by the replies the work receives.

option_rationales.A: This takes 'medal' literally; the passage never mentions prizes or attacks by readers.
option_rationales.B: The replies are by 'later writers' who rewrite and parody the work, not by critics, and no rise and fall is described.
option_rationales.C: This reverses the direction: paragraph 2 describes later writers replying to the canonical work, not the work replying to its predecessors.

common_misconception: Missing the direction of the replies, which run from later works to the canonical one.

correct_answer: (B) On the conversational account it would probably not be canonical, however excellent it is judged to be.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says canons 'exclude works of great finish that simply provoked no answer', since status comes from being answered, not from being judged excellent.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says a committee 'cannot make a book canonical by placing it on a reading list'.
option_rationales.C: The author does not dispute judgements of quality; the claim is only that quality does not explain canonical status.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says such works 'simply provoked no answer'; paragraph 4 describes exclusion in general, and 'must' asserts a cause the passage does not.

common_misconception: Choosing a causal story from paragraph 4 and treating it as necessary.

correct_answer: (C) qualify the conversational account by showing that it inherits, in a new location, the exclusions that critics of the canon object to.
explanation: Paragraph 4 opens with 'Yet the conversational canon is not thereby cleared' and argues that access to education, publishing and preservation shaped who joined the conversation, so the conversational canon still reflects exclusion, now located in the conditions of writing.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the account 'relocates' the complaint; it does not abandon the account or return to the list model.
option_rationales.B: No programme is proposed; the paragraph says only where 'the remedy, if there is one, must be sought'.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph moves the complaint away 'from the judgements of tastemakers' to the conditions under which people could write.

common_misconception: Taking a qualification for a rejection, or the hedge 'if there is one' for a proposal.

correct_answer: (B) Many works that all parties agree are canonical turn out to have been almost never quoted, imitated, parodied or answered by later writers.
explanation: The account claims a work is canonical because later writers 'answer it, parody it, borrow its situations'. If many undisputed canonical works received no such replies, canonical status would not track replies, which strikes at the account's central claim.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says committees cannot confer canonical status, so changing lists are compatible with the account and do not bear on it.
option_rationales.C: Popularity with readers is not canonical status on either model discussed; the account only predicts such works are not canonical, which this does not deny.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 cites exactly this as something the conversational account explains and the list model cannot, so it supports the account.

common_misconception: Choosing the option about polished but unanswered works because it sounds like a counter-example, without noticing that it concerns popularity rather than canonical status.

correct_answer: (D) a translation uses the idiom of its own time, which changes, while the original is read with allowance for its age.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'The usual answer is linguistic: a translation is written in the language of its own moment', whose idioms change, whereas the original is read 'as a historical text' whose strangeness is forgiven.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says 'retranslation is not a sign that earlier translators failed', and the usual answer in paragraph 2 concerns language, not skill.
option_rationales.B: This is close to the author's own 'deeper reason' in paragraph 3, which is offered precisely because the usual answer 'cannot be the whole story'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says readers return to originals 'century after century'; nothing restricts them to scholars.

common_misconception: Confusing the usual answer with the author's deeper explanation.

correct_answer: (A) Translations date because each must settle what its original leaves open, and so preserves one period's reading of it.
explanation: Paragraph 3 gives the 'deeper reason': translation 'forces choices', each choice 'settles a question the original left unsettled', and the result 'records one generation's reading'. Paragraph 4 draws the consequence for retranslation.

option_rationales.B: This is the 'usual answer', which paragraph 2 says 'cannot be the whole story'.
option_rationales.C: Too narrow, and the author does not rank translations; this reversal is called 'occasional' in paragraph 4.
option_rationales.D: Too absolute: the author treats each translation as a valuable reading and retranslation as a way 'a classic stays alive'.

common_misconception: Choosing the explanation the author qualifies, or overstating the author's claim into impossibility.

correct_answer: (C) the decisions it made about undecided passages reflect concerns its present readers no longer share.
explanation: Paragraph 2 offers the observation as evidence against the purely linguistic answer, and paragraph 3 supplies the explanation: a translation's choices are 'shaped by what the translator's own age finds plausible or important', and 'When the concerns of that generation fade' it looks like an interpretation.

option_rationales.A: The state of the original text is never discussed; this is outside the passage.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the translator's choices 'are not arbitrary'; mistranslation is never suggested.
option_rationales.D: This restates the linguistic explanation, which the author introduces this very observation to show is incomplete.

common_misconception: Falling back on the linguistic answer for a fact the author cites against it.

correct_answer: (D) Actors staging an old play must decide how each ambiguous line is spoken, so every production shows its own era's reading while the script stays open.
explanation: Paragraph 3: the original 'can leave such places open', but writing in another medium 'forces choices at every point', shaped by the interpreter's age. A performance must likewise fix tone where the script does not, and the script remains open for the next production, as the original remains for the next translator.

option_rationales.A: This tracks change in the language itself, which corresponds to the 'usual answer' of paragraph 2, not the deeper reason of paragraph 3.
option_rationales.B: Here the phrase had a settled meaning that she corrects; paragraph 3 concerns places 'where its sense is undecided', which a translator must settle without being wrong.
option_rationales.C: This is physical decay with a recoverable original state; the passage concerns choices forced on an interpreter where the original has no single settled sense.

common_misconception: Choosing the historian, who is also reading across time, without noticing that she recovers a fixed meaning rather than settling an open one.

correct_answer: (B) partial acceptance of each, joined to the claim that both rest on the same mistaken picture of intention.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'each is right about what it denies', and paragraph 3 says 'The mistake common to both is to picture intention as a private event lying behind the text'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 rejects a premise the anti-intentionalist shares, and paragraph 4 keeps a role for the author, so the author does not side with either camp.
option_rationales.C: The author answers the question in paragraphs 3 and 4 by redefining intention; nothing says it is unanswerable.
option_rationales.D: The passage is not neutral: paragraph 3 names 'The mistake common to both' and offers the author's own account.

common_misconception: Taking the even-handed paragraph 2 as the author's final stance.

correct_answer: (A) evidence worth weighing, which counts only insofar as it helps to reveal patterns that are present in the work.
explanation: Paragraph 2 denies such statements 'special authority over the book', yet paragraph 4 says notebooks may help 'as the testimony of a witness may help a court, but the evidence is then the pattern, not the testimony'. A public statement is thus admissible but subordinate to what the work shows.

option_rationales.B: This is the private-event picture paragraph 3 rejects, and paragraph 2 says authors 'misremember' and 'misjudge what they have made', so sincerity does not settle meaning.
option_rationales.C: This is the anti-intentionalist view; paragraph 4 says the view 'does not make the author irrelevant' and that notebooks 'may help us see a pattern'.
option_rationales.D: This reverses the author's view that intentions 'are public because the work is' and that the work's design can be taken 'more seriously' than the author's account.

common_misconception: Collapsing the author's middle position into one of the two positions the passage reports.

correct_answer: (D) show that a work can mean more than its author meant without that reading being a defiance of the work's design.
explanation: The example follows the claim that 'a work may carry implications its author never foresaw', and the paragraph concludes that pointing these out 'is not to defy the author's intention but to take the work's design more seriously than its author's later account of it'.

option_rationales.A: The example concerns one hypothetical novel and what it can reveal; it makes no general claim about novelists' awareness.
option_rationales.B: The notebooks appear in the previous sentence as an aid to seeing patterns in the work; the novel example involves no notebooks at all.
option_rationales.C: The author says the reading takes 'the work's design more seriously', so purpose embodied in the work still matters; this is not the anti-intentionalist claim.

common_misconception: Reading an example of meaning beyond the author's foresight as support for the anti-intentionalist view.

correct_answer: (C) the intentions that matter to criticism lie hidden behind a text, which can at best report them faithfully.
explanation: Paragraph 3 identifies 'The mistake common to both' as picturing intention 'as a private event lying behind the text, which the text either reports faithfully or conceals'. The correct answer states exactly that picture, so it is inconsistent with the author's account.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says a work may carry implications 'its author never foresaw and would perhaps have disowned'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says noticing 'that a repetition is deliberate' is 'already to treat the text as the product of choices'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 grants that 'A writer's notebooks may help us see a pattern we had missed', and a diary serves the same role.

common_misconception: Choosing the diary option because paragraph 2 denies such entries 'special authority', missing that paragraph 4 still allows them an evidential role.

correct_answer: (A) forming judgements of characters that the book later shows to be mistaken.
explanation: Paragraph 2: on a first reading we 'form judgements of characters that the book later overturns'.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 presents this as a discovery made on rereading, not during a first reading.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says that on a first reading 'We skim descriptions to reach events'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 lists returning images among what we can attend to 'Only when we know the ending'.

common_misconception: Picking a rereading experience because it appears in the same list.

correct_answer: (B) such details gain significance once a reader can see what they were preparing for.
explanation: The 'details' meant are the preparing scene, the returning image and the idle remark that 'turns out to state the novel's theme'. Their importance 'has not yet been revealed' on a first reading; knowing the ending reveals it, so the details are filled with meaning.

option_rationales.A: Nothing in the passage concerns readers inventing material; the details meant are those already in the text.
option_rationales.C: This is close to the opposite: the sentence denies that knowledge of the outcome empties the details.
option_rationales.D: The rereader does know the events, but the sentence is about what that knowledge does to 'these details', namely make them meaningful.

common_misconception: Choosing an option that is true of rereading in general but is not what the sentence says about the details.

correct_answer: (A) a reader's growing experience can reveal qualities in a book that were present but unseen before.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says the reader 'has acquired experiences that let different passages speak', and the marriage story becomes 'almost unbearably exact'. The exactness was there; the young reader lacked the experience to see it.

option_rationales.B: The older reader finds the story 'almost unbearably exact', so the passage implies the young reader missed something.
option_rationales.C: The example contrasts a younger and an older reader, not married and unmarried ones; this generalises beyond the passage.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the book 'has not altered a word' and locates the change in 'the person reading it', not in the culture.

common_misconception: Attributing the change to the book or the culture rather than to the reader.

correct_answer: (B) critical, though willing to grant that a first reading has a real value of its own.
explanation: Paragraph 2 argues against the nostalgia view, and paragraph 4 concedes that the first reading has 'an innocence about what is coming that the writer counted on'.

option_rationales.A: The author argues for 'the opposite view' in paragraph 2 and does not share the lament.
option_rationales.C: The author argues that 'in an important sense only rereading is reading' and ends by urging distrust of first-reading verdicts.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the first reading 'has a quality nothing later can supply', so the author is not dismissive of it.

common_misconception: Missing the concession and choosing an extreme, or mistaking the concession for neutrality.

correct_answer: (C) Readers who already know how it ends report finding more in it on a third reading than on a second.
explanation: Paragraph 4 makes the test whether a book 'offers nothing on a second reading' or 'gives more each time'. Only the correct answer reports what readers find after the ending is known, and it shows the book giving more each time.

option_rationales.A: Compulsive reading is what suspense produces; it is a first-reading effect and is what a mere mechanism would also achieve.
option_rationales.B: These are verdicts reached 'from inside a first reading', which the author says we should distrust.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says such a twist 'can surprise only once'; it is an effect designed for the first reading and says nothing about later ones.

common_misconception: Choosing the twist because recasting earlier chapters sounds like what rereading does, though it happens on the first reading.

correct_answer: (D) A frequency count cannot register the irony or dramatic context on which a word's meaning depends.
explanation: Paragraph 2: 'The meaning of a word depends on its context, on irony, on the dramatic situation in which it is spoken, none of which a frequency table records.'

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 complains of 'a modest result dressed in charts', a point about the modesty of results, not the difficulty of charts.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 presents processing a century's output as what the method makes possible; no one in the passage objects that it cannot be done.
option_rationales.C: The passage never says this; paragraph 4 credits the method with reaching 'the much larger body of books that the canon left out'.

common_misconception: Choosing an option that echoes the word 'charts' or 'century' from the passage.

correct_answer: (B) point readers towards particular books that then repay being read closely.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says the anomalies matter because they send someone 'back' to read, and 'it is that return which produces understanding'. 'The count poses a question; it does not answer one.'

option_rationales.A: The anomalies are said to mean 'little until someone goes back and reads the books'; they prove nothing by themselves.
option_rationales.C: This contradicts paragraph 3: 'Such a finding means little until someone goes back and reads the books in question'.
option_rationales.D: The features are ones 'nobody had thought to examine', not ones humans cannot perceive; the claim is too strong.

common_misconception: Overstating what the anomalies show, or confusing features nobody examined with features nobody could perceive.

correct_answer: (D) Computational reading cannot interpret texts by itself, but it can pose questions for close reading and test claims drawn from a biased sample.
explanation: Paragraph 3 gives the method the role of posing questions that close reading answers, and paragraph 4 its 'independent contribution' of testing generalisations against the books 'the canon left out'.

option_rationales.A: The author grants that some objections 'are serious' but calls the debate 'a false picture of the choice' and credits the method with real contributions.
option_rationales.B: The passage diagnoses the sampling problem but never recommends abandoning study of the canon; this adds a prescription.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says distant reading 'does not replace close reading', so this contradicts the author.

common_misconception: Choosing the strong prescription built on paragraph 1, or the objections the author reports and answers.

correct_answer: (C) The novels available in digital form for analysis are mostly the same books that later readers chose to keep in print.
explanation: Paragraph 4 says the method can test canonical generalisations against 'the much larger body of books that the canon left out'. If the machine-readable corpus is largely the kept-in-print canon, the machine would be testing claims against the same selection, and the independent contribution would vanish.

option_rationales.A: This is the kind of anomaly paragraph 3 describes, and it presupposes access to obscure novels, so it is consistent with the claim.
option_rationales.B: This fits the author's view that the two kinds of reading work together and has no bearing on the sampling claim.
option_rationales.D: This is the objection of paragraph 2 about trivial results; it does not touch the claim about testing generalisations against a wider sample.

common_misconception: Choosing the objection from paragraph 2 because it is critical of distant reading, without checking whether it bears on the specific claim.

correct_answer: (A) while offered as a history of a form, in fact describes the preferences that decided which books were kept.
explanation: Paragraph 4 completes the sentence: the claim was 'about the tastes of the readers who did the selecting'. A generalisation from a selected sample describes the selection and hence the selectors' preferences, not the whole form.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says no scholar can do this, and the author proposes testing by machine instead, so this is not implied.
option_rationales.C: The passage says such a claim may 'describe' the surviving books accurately; it does not say they differ in every respect.
option_rationales.D: The author questions generalisations about the form, not the existence of the form; this over-reads the sentence.

common_misconception: Reading 'never a claim about the novel' as 'false', when the point concerns what the claim is about.

correct_answer: (B) propose that a label should be judged by whether it sends the visitor back to the work, not by its length.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says both camps wrongly treat quantity as the label's 'only variable'; paragraph 3 replaces that with the question of 'what the label asks the visitor to do'; paragraph 4 concludes that information belongs on the wall 'when it changes what the visitor notices'. The purpose is to reframe how labels should be judged.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 describes the habit of reading first and glancing after, but the passage never compares the understanding of two groups of visitors; the claim invents a finding.
option_rationales.C: Audio guides and screens appear in paragraph 1 only as part of the expansionist camp's proposal, which the author goes on to criticise in paragraph 2; the author recommends nothing of the kind.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 rejects the purist assumption, saying an unexplained altarpiece makes a visitor feel 'excluded', and paragraph 4 keeps a place for historical information on the wall.

common_misconception: Taking one camp described in paragraph 1 as the author's own position.

correct_answer: (C) leave many visitors feeling shut out, so that they pass the work more quickly instead of studying it.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says that a visitor faced with an unexplained altarpiece 'feels excluded and walks faster'. Removing labels would produce exactly this case.

option_rationales.A: This is the purist's assumption, which paragraph 2 contradicts: an unexplained work does not make a visitor 'look harder'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 sends only facts that do not change what one notices to the catalogue, and the passage never predicts that visitors would turn to catalogues.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says the opposite: labels are read often while the paintings are 'looked at as little', with only a glance to confirm what the label said.

common_misconception: Accepting the purist premise that less text automatically means more looking.

correct_answer: (A) contrast a statement that can be taken in without looking with one that sends the reader to the canvas.
explanation: The paragraph introduces the contrast between labels that 'close' and labels that 'open' a picture, and the closing sentence makes the point of the example: 'The first sentence can be absorbed without raising one's eyes; the second cannot be finished without looking.'

option_rationales.B: The author objects to facts that merely 'sit beside the object', not to biography as such, and paragraph 4 explicitly defends information that changes what is noticed.
option_rationales.C: The passage does not rank the marriage against the ledger and glove; the example concerns what each sentence makes the reader do, not which fact matters more.
option_rationales.D: The second sentence asks the reader to decide which hand is lit more brightly; it makes no general claim about painters, and the portrait is only 'imagined'.

common_misconception: Reading the example for its content (the merchant, his marriage) rather than for its role in the argument.

correct_answer: (D) Figures by the window are in quick, broken strokes, those in shadow smooth; which group does your eye reach first?
explanation: Paragraph 3 praises a label that directs 'attention to something that can be checked against the canvas itself' and that 'cannot be finished without looking'. The correct label points to a visible contrast in brushwork and asks the viewer to test it.

option_rationales.A: A verdict borrowed from critics directs the eye to nothing checkable on the canvas, so it fails the test in paragraph 3 that a label should 'open' the picture.
option_rationales.B: This label would 'close' the picture by telling the viewer what it means; it can be absorbed without looking, which paragraph 3 counts against it.
option_rationales.C: A chain of owners is the kind of fact paragraph 2 says gives 'a great deal to know and very little to see'; by paragraph 4 it belongs in the catalogue.

common_misconception: Choosing the label that sounds most informative or most authoritative.

correct_answer: (A) the statues offer no built-in occasion for reconsideration, so disagreement is held back until it bursts out all at once.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says a permanent work 'asks only to be accepted' with 'no procedure built into it for being reconsidered', and so 'When disagreement finally arrives, it therefore arrives as a crisis'.

option_rationales.B: Cost is never raised; the passage treats durable materials as a statement of respect and of permanence, not as an expense to be protected.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says many such figures become unrecognised, but paragraph 2 locates the cause of the crisis in the absence of any 'procedure' for reconsideration, not in ignorance.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 opens by denying exactly this: 'The problem is not that later generations are fickle.'

common_misconception: Picking the explanation the author explicitly rules out (fickleness), or taking a detail from paragraph 1 as the cause.

correct_answer: (D) A memorial to the dead of a disaster, since its purpose is to resist forgetting.
explanation: Paragraph 4: 'a memorial to the dead of a war or a disaster is meant to resist the passing of time, because forgetting is precisely the danger it guards against.'

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 describes murals 'painted on the understanding that it will be painted over'; fondness is part of the conversation, not a reason to fix the work.
option_rationales.B: The passage nowhere exempts secure reputations; paragraph 1 warns that any monument may outlast the judgement it records.
option_rationales.C: Attracting visitors is mentioned in paragraph 4 only as a danger of temporary art sliding into spectacle, not as a reason for permanence.

common_misconception: Assuming the author would protect works that are popular or long-respected.

correct_answer: (B) is an event that invites the public to respond and argue, not a settled judgement handed down to be accepted.
explanation: The next sentence explains the phrase: people 'argue about the new piece, grow fond of it or feel relieved to see it go', practising the 'collective judgement' that a permanent statue, which 'asks only to be accepted', forecloses.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 stresses the 'collective judgement' of the public while the work is up; experts and post-removal judgement are not mentioned.
option_rationales.C: The passage does not say temporary art is neutral; its value is that people 'argue about the new piece', which implies it can provoke disagreement.
option_rationales.D: The phrase is not about festivals; paragraph 3 explains it as people arguing about, liking or being relieved to lose a work.

common_misconception: Reading 'occasion' as a special celebration instead of as an event that prompts response.

correct_answer: (C) A city with a rotating plinth for decades still endured years of bitter petitions over removing a nearby statue.
explanation: Paragraph 2 claims that a city used to change 'would already possess a habit of revisiting' and so would avoid crisis. A city with exactly that habit that still suffered a prolonged crisis is a direct counterexample.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 welcomes argument about the new piece; lively debate over a temporary work is the habit the author wants, not the crisis he warns against.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 already grants that memorials to the dead aim at permanence for good reason, so this agrees with the author rather than weakening him.
option_rationales.D: Forgetting a temporary work after it leaves is compatible with the author's view that such works matter as the 'conversation' they start, so it does not touch the claim.

common_misconception: Treating any public argument as the 'crisis' the author predicts, when he welcomes argument about temporary works.

correct_answer: (A) Varnish yellows with age, so preferring the darkened colours can mean preferring an accident to the painter's choice.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'Natural resin varnishes do yellow and darken with age' and adds that 'to prefer the olive because one is used to it is to prefer an accident over a decision.'

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 denies this directly: cleaning 'does not take it back to the day it left the studio' because pigments have also changed.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 reports the mourners' suspicion that cleaners have removed final glazes, and the author never dismisses it, so the passage gives no such guarantee.
option_rationales.D: The author reports the 'truth and sentiment' framing as 'tempting' and grants only part of it; he never says the mourners have no reason, and paragraph 1 records their worry about lost glazes.

common_misconception: Stretching the author's partial concession into full agreement with the cleaners.

correct_answer: (D) may present colour relationships the painter never saw, because faded and unfaded parts now appear together.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says cleaning 'produces a new object, one in which unchanged passages and altered ones sit side by side in proportions the painter never saw'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says cleaning reveals 'colours far brighter', and the passage makes no claim that cleaned pictures are less harmonious overall.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the bright painting 'may therefore be no closer to the original', and the author never claims which state is usually closer.
option_rationales.C: The author recommends reversibility, documentation and honest language in paragraph 4, not a return to the old appearance.

common_misconception: Assuming the author favours either the cleaned state or the darkened state, when he denies that either is the original.

correct_answer: (C) qualified support: he accepts their practice and results but rejects the strength of their central claim.
explanation: Paragraph 2 grants that cleaning has shown painters to be 'bold colourists'; paragraph 3 says the claim to restore the 'original state' is 'harder to sustain than it sounds'; paragraph 4 says cleaning should continue but be 'described honestly'.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 asks restorers to 'abandon the language of revelation' and calls 'this is what the painter meant' a claim beyond the evidence.
option_rationales.B: The charge of 'zeal' belongs to the mourning party in paragraph 1; the author himself says the lesson is 'not that cleaning should stop' and credits it with real discoveries.
option_rationales.D: The author takes clear positions: he endorses the point about varnish in paragraph 2 and rejects the claim of original state in paragraph 3.
